Do not let the worthy remain hidden,
then numbness will not occur.
Do not let the common people sing and criticize,
then unrest will not arise.
For the important ministers and the multitude of subordinates,
are the heart, abdomen, limbs, and body of the ruler.
If the heart, abdomen, limbs, and body are free from illness,
then the ruler is free from illness.
Thus, without a worthy physician,
none can cure it.
Everyone has these twelve ailments,
and if a worthy physician is not employed,
then the state will cease to be a state.
The Book of Songs says:
"If it grows fierce and fierce,
it cannot be cured by medicine."
It will inevitably end in destruction.
Therefore, if a worthy physician is employed,
the masses will be free from illness,
how much more so the ruler?
3.10 The Tradition says:
In times of peace,
there are no mute, deaf,
lame, blind,
hunchbacked, crippled,
dwarfs,
or those with broken limbs,
fathers do not weep for sons,
elder brothers do not weep for younger brothers,
and on the roads, there are no abandoned infants carried on the back.
Yet each ends their life in their proper order,
due to the employment of worthy physicians.
Thus, to achieve stability and uprightness,
there is no other way to eliminate ailments
than to employ the worthy.
The Book of Songs says:
"There are blind musicians, there are blind musicians,
in the court of Zhōu."
They are the remnant people of Zhòu.
3.11 The Tradition says:
If the rites of mourning and sacrifice are abandoned,
then the kindness between ministers and sons is weakened.
If the kindness between ministers and sons is weakened,
then those who betray and flee from death are many.
The Minor Odes says:
"From son to grandson,
do not discontinue but prolong it."
3.12 When human affairs are ordered, they accord with the spirits and gods,
accord with the spirits and gods,
then blessings are bestowed abundantly.
The Book of Songs says:
"To offer and to sacrifice,
to seek great blessings."
3.13 King Wǔ waged war against Zhòu,
arriving at Xíngqiū,
where shields broke into three pieces,
and rain fell for three days without ceasing.
King Wǔ felt fearful in heart,
summoned Tàigōng and asked,
saying:
"Does it mean that Zhòu should not be attacked?"
Tàigōng replied:
"Not so.
The shields breaking into three pieces
mean the army should be divided into three.
The rain falling for three days without ceasing
is to wash our weapons."
King Wǔ said:
"Then what should be done?"
Tàigōng said:
"Love the person,
and extend it to the crows on their roof;
hate the person,
and despise even their retainers.
Utterly destroy the enemy,
leaving none remaining."
King Wǔ said:
"Alas!
The world is not yet settled."
The Duke of Zhōu hurried forward and said:
"Not so.
Let each measure their dwellings,
and till their fields,
without distinguishing old or new.
If the common people have faults,
they lie with me alone."
King Wǔ said:
"Alas!
The world is already settled."
Then he cultivated martial arts and drilled troops at Nìng,
renamed Xíngqiū as Huáiníng,
and called it Xīuwǔ,
marching to defeat Zhòu in the wilderness of Mù.
The Book of Songs says:
"Vast is the wilderness of Mù,
splendid the sandalwood chariots,
mighty the team of chestnuts.
The Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ,
was like an eagle soaring,
assisting that King Wǔ,
to smite great Shāng,
and at dawn all was clear."
After returning from Shāng,
upon descending from the chariot,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì at Kuǎi,
enfeoffed the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Zhù,
enfeoffed the descendants of Shùn at Chén.
Descending from the chariot,
he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xiàhòu clan at Qǐ,
enfeoffed the descendants of Yīn at Sòng,
built a tomb for Bǐgān,
released the imprisonment of Jīzǐ,
and honored the lane of Shāngróng.
Crossing the river and heading west,
he released the horses on the sunny side of Huàshān,
to show they would not be ridden again.
He released the oxen in the wilderness of Táolín,
to show they would not be used for labor again.
Chariots and armor were smeared with blood
and stored in the treasuries,
to show they would not be used again.
Thereupon, he disbanded the army and practiced suburban archery,
shooting to the left to the tune of "Lí Shǒu,"
shooting to the right to the tune of "Zōu Yú,"
after which the world knew King Wǔ would not use arms again.
Sacrificing in the Míngtáng, the people learned filial piety;
holding court audiences, the feudal lords learned respect.
Seating the three elders in the Great Academy,
the Son of Heaven held
the sauce and served them,
held the cup and offered them drink,
thereby teaching the feudal lords brotherly respect.
These four things
are the great teachings of the world.
Is it not fitting that the martial achievements lasted long?
The Book of Songs says:
"He overcame Yīn and stopped the slaughter,
firmly establishing your merit."
It speaks of attacking Zhòu and the demise of Yīn's martial power.
3.14 Mèngcháng Jūn requested to learn from Mǐnzǐ,
sending a carriage to welcome Mǐnzǐ.
Mǐnzǐ said:
"In rites, there is coming to learn, not going to teach.
Sending a teacher to learn means one cannot learn;
going to teach means one cannot transform the ruler.
You are what is called unable to learn,
I am what is called unable to transform."
Thereupon, Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"I respectfully heed your command."
The next day, he adjusted his attire and requested to receive instruction.
The Book of Songs says:
"Daily progress, monthly advance."
3.15 A sword, though sharp,
will not cut without whetting.
Talent, though fine,
will not rise high without learning.
Though there be fine wine and delicacies,
one cannot know their flavor without tasting.
Though there be good ways,
one cannot achieve their merit without learning.
Thus, one learns and then knows insufficiency;
one teaches and then knows incompleteness.
Insufficiency,
so one feels ashamed and strives.
Incompleteness,
so one fully follows the teacher and becomes proficient.
From this perspective,
teaching and learning promote each other.
Zǐxià asked about the Book of Songs,
learning one to understand two.
Confucius said:
"He who enlightens me
is Shāng.
Now I can begin to discuss the Book of Songs with him!"
Confucius was virtuous among heroes and complete in sagehood,
his disciples bathed in his light and their virtue shone.
The Book of Songs says:
"Daily progress, monthly advance."
3.16 In all ways of learning,
honoring the teacher is difficult.
When the teacher is honored,
then the Way is revered.
When the Way is revered,
then the people know to respect learning.
Thus, in the rites of the Great Academy,
even when receiving instruction from the Son of Heaven,
the teacher does not face north,
to honor the teacher and esteem the Way.
Thus, without speaking, there is trust;
without anger, there is authority—
this is what is meant by a teacher.
The Book of Songs says:
"Daily progress, monthly advance,
through learning, accumulate brightness to achieve illumination."
3.17 The Commentary says:
When Sòng suffered a great flood,
the people of Lǔ came to offer condolences, saying:
"Heaven has sent excessive rain,
damaging the grain offerings,
which has extended to your land,
causing concern for those in governance,
so I have been sent to respectfully offer condolences."
The people of Sòng responded:
"Our ruler lacks benevolence,
fails to maintain proper purification rituals,
and employs the people at inappropriate times.
Heaven has thus sent this disaster,
and has further caused you concern.
We humbly accept your condescending message."
Confucius heard of this
and said:
"The state of Sòng is nearly there!"
His disciples asked:
"What do you mean?"
Confucius said:
"In the past, Jié and Zhòu did not acknowledge their faults,
and their downfall was swift.
Chéng Tāng and King Wén knew to acknowledge their faults,
and their rise was vigorous.
To recognize errors and correct them
is to be without error."
When the people of Sòng heard this,
they rose early and retired late,
mourning the dead and inquiring after the sick,
exerting themselves for the realm.
After three years,
the harvests were abundant and governance stable.
Had the people of Sòng not heard Confucius's words,
the grain would not have been plentiful,
and the state would not have been tranquil.
The Book of Songs says:
"Support me with your shoulders,
and show me bright virtue."
3.18 Duke Huán of Qí set up courtyard torches
to facilitate those wishing to seek audience.
A year passed, yet no scholars came.
Then, a man from the eastern wilds sought an audience with his knowledge of the multiplication table.
The Duke teased him,
saying:
"Is the multiplication table sufficient for an audience?"
The rustic replied:
"I heard that you set up courtyard torches to await scholars,
yet after a year, none have come.
The reason scholars have not come
is that you,
as a worthy ruler of the realm,
are considered by scholars everywhere to be beyond their reach,
hence they do not come.
The multiplication table
is but a minor skill,
yet you still treat me with courtesy;
how much more would you treat those more worthy than the multiplication table?
Mount Tài does not reject pebbles,
rivers and seas do not refuse small streams—
this is how they achieve their greatness.
The Book of Songs says:
'The ancients had a saying:
Consult the grass and firewood gatherers,'
meaning to seek broad counsel."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
He then firmly treated him with courtesy.
Within a month,
scholars from all directions came guiding one another.
The Book of Songs says:
"From the hall to the foundation,
from the sheep to the oxen."
This illustrates achieving greatness through small means.
3.19 In times of great peace,
the people on corvée labor do not exceed their time,
men and women do not miss their time to marry,
filial sons do not miss their time to provide for parents.
Outside, there are no unmarried men;
inside, there no pining women.
Above, there are no unloving fathers;
below, there are no unfilial sons.
Fathers and sons support each other,
husbands and wives protect each other.
The world is harmonious,
the state is tranquil.
With human affairs well-ordered below,
heavenly principles respond above.
Thus, heaven does not alter its course,
earth does not change its form,
the sun and moon shine brightly,
the constellations remain constant.
Heaven bestows, earth transforms,
yin and yang harmonize,
movement comes with thunder and lightning,
moisture comes with wind and rain,
regulated by mountains and rivers,
balancing cold and heat.
The myriad people are nurtured,
each finding their place,
and state resources are managed.
Thus, the state finds stability,
the land finds its masters.
The sages hollowed wood to make boats,
sharpened wood to make oars,
to connect the goods of all regions,
ensuring marsh-dwellers had enough water,
mountain-dwellers enough fish,
and surplus wealth could circulate.
Thus, fertile lands do not enjoy pleasure alone,
nor barren lands suffer hardship alone.
Even in years of famine,
or floods and droughts like under Yǔ or Tāng,
the people show no signs of cold or hunger.
Thus, in life they lack no necessities,
in death their bodies are not abandoned.
This is what is called happiness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Oh, brilliant royal forces,
nurturing in times of darkness."
3.20 One who can govern the world
must be able to nurture the people.
To nurture the people
is to nurture oneself.
Food and drink should suit the organs,
flavors should suit the qi,
labor and rest should suit the sinews and bones,
cold and warmth should suit the skin and flesh.
Then the qi and organs will be balanced,
the mind will be orderly,
thoughts will be appropriate,
joy and anger will be timely,
daily life will be leisurely and joyful,
affairs will be timely and resources sufficient.
This is what is called being able to nurture oneself.
Thus, when sages avoid excess and extravagance,
it is not because they despise pleasures or treasure wealth.
Nurturance has its proper measure;
exceeding it brings no joy,
so they do not do it.
Therefore, they do not bathe frequently in summer,
not because they begrudge water.
They do not warm themselves often in winter,
not because they begrudge fire.
They do not build high towers and pavilions,
not for lack of timber and earth.
They do not cast large bells and tripods,
not for lack of metal and tin.
They do not indulge in wine,
nor covet sensual pleasures,
not to avoid ugliness.
They simply follow what suits their nature,
and their standards can serve as models for the world.
Thus, their expenditures do not waste wealth,
sufficient to sustain their lives,
and the world praises their benevolence.
Their nurturance does not harm their nature,
sufficient to complete their teaching,
and the world praises their righteousness.
Satisfied with their emotions and avoiding excess,
not seeking what is not theirs,
the world praises their integrity.
Their conduct, once formed, cannot be concealed;
their punishments, when ceased, cannot be violated.
Holding to one Way and lightly regarding all things,
the world praises their courage.
With these four virtues residing in the people,
they are gentle and pleasant in peace,
and victorious over enemies in anger.
Thus, examining the means of nurturance completes the tools of governance.
With the tools of governance complete, near and far are gathered.
The Book of Songs says:
"Oh, brilliant royal forces,
nurturing in times of darkness."
This speaks of mutual nurturance reaching even to darkness.
3.21 Gōngyí Xiū served as prime minister of Lǔ and loved fish.
Someone from the state offered him fish, but he refused it.
His younger brother admonished him:
"You love fish yet refuse it—
why?"
He replied:
"Precisely because I love fish,
I refuse it.
If I accept the fish and lose my position,
I could no longer provide myself with fish.
If I do not accept it and keep my position,
I can always provide myself with fish."
This shows his understanding of fish as a matter of self-interest.
Thus, the Lǎozǐ says:
"He puts himself last, yet comes first;
he disregards himself, yet is preserved.
Is it not because he is selfless
that he can achieve his private ends?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Thoughts without depravity."
This expresses the same idea.
3.22 The Commentary says:
In Lǔ, there was a father and son engaged in a lawsuit.
Kāngzǐ wished to execute them.
Confucius said:
"They cannot be executed.
For the people, when fathers and sons sue each other, this has long been an act of unrighteousness;
this shows that those above have lost the proper way.
If those above possessed the Way,
such people would not exist."
When the litigants heard this,
they requested to drop the lawsuit.
Kāngzǐ said:
"To govern the people, one uses filial piety.
To kill one unrighteous person in order to punish the unfilial—
is that not acceptable?"
Confucius said:
"No.
To judge their case without having taught them
is to kill the innocent.
When the three armies suffer a great defeat,
one cannot punish them all.
When legal cases are not properly managed,
one cannot apply punishments.
If those above display the teachings and first practice them themselves,
then the common people will follow like the wind.
If personal conduct does not lead to compliance,
only then await it with punishments,
and the people will know their offenses.
Consider a wall one ren high:
the people cannot climb over it,
but a hundred-ren high mountain
even a child can climb and play upon—
this is because of its gradual slope.
Now, the decline of benevolence and righteousness has been long;
can one say that the people do not transgress?
The Book of Songs says:
'So that the people are not迷迷迷.'
The noblemen of old
guided their people and did not let them be迷迷迷,
thus authority was stern but not tested,
punishments were set aside and not used.
Therefore, they manifested their benevolence and righteousness,
carefully attended to their teachings and the Way,
made the people see it clearly with their eyes,
made the people hear it clearly with their ears,
made the people understand it clearly in their hearts,
then the Way was not迷迷迷, and the people's will was not confused.
The Book of Songs says:
'Show me bright virtuous conduct.'
Thus, if the Way and righteousness are not easy,
the people will not follow them.
If rites and music are not clear,
the people will not see them.
The Book of Songs says:
'The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow,'
speaking of its ease.
'What the nobleman treads,
the commoner looks upon,'
speaking of its clarity.
'Turning back to look upon it,
tears flow down,'
lamenting that they did not hear the rites and teachings but faced punishments and execution.
To neglect the fundamental teachings and rely on penal laws
is like breaking open the pen and shooting with poisoned arrows—
is it not pitiable!
Therefore, I said they cannot be executed.
In the past, the former kings led the people with rites,
comparing it to driving a carriage.
Punishments
are the whip.
Now, it is like driving without bit and reins, using only the whip.
To want the horse to advance,
you whip it from behind;
to want it to retreat,
you whip it in front;
the driver toils and the horse is also much injured.
Now, it is just like this.
Those above worry and toil, and the people mostly suffer punishments.
The Book of Songs says:
'If a man has no courtesy,
why does he not quickly die?'
If those above have no courtesy,
they cannot avoid calamity.
If those below have no courtesy,
they cannot avoid punishment.
If both above and below have no courtesy,
why should they not quickly die?"
Kāngzǐ left his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"Although I am not clever,
I ask to receive these words."
Confucius withdrew from court,
and his disciple Zǐlù questioned him:
"For a father and son to sue each other—
is that the Way?"
Confucius said:
"No."
Zǐlù said:
"Then why did you, Master, as a nobleman, spare them?"
Confucius said:
"To demand achievement without warning
is harmful.
To issue orders negligently and insist on deadlines
is tyrannical.
To execute without teaching
is brutal.
A nobleman in governance
avoids these three.
Moreover, the Book of Songs says:
'With a cheerful countenance and a smile,
not angry but teaching.'"
3.23 During Shùn's time,
the Yǒumiáo did not submit.
The reason for their not submitting
was that Héng Shān was to the south,
Qí Shān to the north,
the waves of Dòngtíng to the left,
the waters of Péngzé to the right—
they relied on these barriers.
Because they did not submit,
Yǔ requested to attack them,
but Shùn did not permit it,
saying:
"My instructive teachings have not yet been exhausted."
After prolonged instructive teaching,
the Yǒumiáo people requested to submit.
When the world heard of it,
all belittled Yǔ's righteousness
and praised Shùn's virtue.
The Book of Songs says:
"With a cheerful countenance and a smile,
not angry but teaching."
This refers to Shùn.
Someone asked:
"Then was Yǔ's virtue inferior to Shùn's?"
The answer was:
"Not so.
The reason Yǔ requested to attack
was to make Shùn's virtue evident.
Thus, goodness is attributed to the ruler,
faults to oneself—
this is the duty of a minister.
If Yǔ were the ruler
and Shùn the minister,
it would also be like this.
Yǔ can be said to have understood the great principle of being a minister."
3.24 When Jìsūnzǐ governed Lǔ,
he executed many people, always matching their crimes,
and punished many, always fitting their offenses.
Zǐgòng said:
"How violent is this governance!" Jìsūn heard this,
and said:
"I execute people only when it matches their crimes,
punish people only when it fits their offenses—
why do you, Sir, consider it violent?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Why not be like Zǐchǎn's governance of Zhèng?
In one year, the faults requiring punishment decreased;
in two years, crimes deserving execution vanished;
in three years, the prisons held no detained people.
Thus, the people turned to him like water flowing downward,
loving him as filial sons respect parents.
When Zǐchǎn was ill and near death,
all the people sighed and said:
'Who can die in place of Zǐchǎn?'
When he inevitably died,
officials wept for him at court,
merchants wept in the market,
farmers wept in the fields.
Those mourning Zǐchǎn
all acted as if bereaved of parents.
Now, I have privately heard that when you, Master, fall ill,
the people are pleased;
if you recover, the people are all alarmed.
To congratulate on death,
to fear survival—
if not violent, what is it?
I, Cì, have heard:
to rely on laws for governance is called violence;
to set deadlines without warning is called cruelty;
to execute without teaching is called brutality;
to overcome others with one's person is called oppression.
The oppressive lose their persons,
the brutal lose their ministers,
the cruel lose their governance,
the violent lose their people.
Moreover, I have heard that no one in high position practicing these four has avoided ruin."
Thereupon, Jìsūn bowed his head to the ground and apologized:
"I reverently heed your instruction."
The Book of Songs says:
"With a cheerful countenance and a smile,
not angry but teaching."
3.25 The questioner asked:
"Why do the wise take delight in water?"
The reply was:
"Water follows principle in its flow,
leaving no small crevice unfilled,
resembling the wise.
Moving downward,
it resembles the courteous.
Treading depths without hesitation,
it resembles the courageous.
Cleared by barriers,
it resembles those who understand destiny.
Traversing dangers to reach afar,
ultimately achieving without destruction,
it resembles the virtuous.
Through it heaven and earth are formed,
all things come to life,
the state is pacified, all affairs are balanced,
and all creatures are rectified.
This is why the wise take delight in water."
The Book of Songs says:
"How we delight in the Pàn water,
where we gather the mallow.
The Marquis of Lǔ has arrived,
drinking at the Pàn."
This refers to delighting in water.
3.26 The questioner asked:
"Why do the benevolent take delight in mountains?"
The reply was:
"Mountains are what the myriad people look up to.
Grasses and trees grow there,
all things are planted there,
flying birds gather there,
running beasts rest there,
and all directions benefit from taking and giving there.
They emit clouds and guide winds, towering between heaven and earth.
Through them heaven and earth are formed,
the state is pacified,
this is why the benevolent take delight in mountains."
The Book of Songs says:
"The Tài mountain is lofty and rugged,
gazed upon by the state of Lǔ."
This refers to delighting in mountains.
3.27 The Tradition says:
Duke Wén of Jìn once went into exile and, upon returning to his state,
distributed rewards three times without reaching Táo Shūhú.
Táo Shūhú said to Jiù Fàn:
"I followed him into exile for eleven years,
my complexion darkened,
my hands and feet calloused.
Now that the lord has returned and distributed rewards three times without including me,
has he forgotten me?
Or have I committed some great fault?
Please try to speak on my behalf."
Jiù Fàn spoke to Duke Wén,
who said:
"Alas!
How could I forget this man?
Those of supreme brilliance and worthiness,
with fully accomplished will and conduct,
who immerse me in the Way,
persuade me with benevolence,
transform my actions,
enlighten me,
making me a complete person—
these I consider the highest reward.
Those who respect me with ritual,
guard me with righteousness,
support and aid me,
preventing me from wrongdoing—
these I consider the next.
The fiercely brave and strong in warfare,
with an imposing presence that controls itself,
who take the front when danger is ahead,
the rear when it is behind,
saving me from perilous situations—
these I consider the next.
Then come those who toil and labor."
The Book of Songs says:
"Following the path without overstepping,
thus observing and fully expressing."
Now, if one does not inwardly admit faults,
nor please the common people,
what reward should be given?
3.28 Those who deceive say,
"Ancient and modern circumstances differ,
and the ways to order and chaos vary."
They think all people are foolish and ignorant,
crude and without measure,
easily deceived in what they see,
let alone after a thousand years!
Those deceivers
even practice deceit in their own courtyards,
how much more so with events a thousand years ago?
Then how is it that sages cannot be deceived?
The answer is:
Sages measure others by themselves.
They measure heart by heart,
emotion by emotion,
kind by kind—
ancient and modern are one.
If the kind does not contradict,
even after long, the principle remains the same.
Thus, nature follows principle without confusion.
Before the Five Emperors, no individuals are transmitted.
Not that there were no worthy men,
but due to the long time.
From the Five Emperors' era, no governance is transmitted,
not that there was no good governance,
but due to the long time.
The Yú and Xià have transmitted governance,
but not as detailed as the Yīn and Zhōu.
Not that there was no good governance,
but due to the long time.
Transmission becomes sketchier with time,
more detailed with proximity.
Sketchy accounts highlight the major,
detailed ones the minor.
Thus, the foolish hear the major without knowing the minor,
hear the minor without knowing the major.
Hence, over time, discrepancies arise.
The Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
represent the pinnacle of governance.
The Book of Songs says:
"The divine command was not disobeyed,
reaching to Tāng in unity."
This means ancient and modern are one.
3.29 Shùn was born in Zhūféng,
moved to Fùxià,
and died in Míngtiáo—
a man of the Eastern Yi.
King Wén was born in Qízhōu,
died in Bìyǐng—
a man of the Western Yi.
The distance between their lands
was over a thousand lǐ,
the time between their eras, over a thousand years,
yet their realized ambitions in the Central States
matched like tally and token.
Confucius said:
"Earlier sages and later sages,
their measure is one."
The Book of Songs says:
"The divine command was not disobeyed,
reaching to Tāng in unity."
3.30 Confucius observed in the Zhōu temple
a tilting vessel.
He asked the temple keeper:
"What vessel is this called?"
The reply was:
"This is probably the 'seat of caution' vessel."
Confucius said:
"I've heard of the seat of caution vessel:
full, it overturns;
empty, it tilts;
half-full, it stands upright.
Is this true?"
The reply:
"Yes."
Confucius had Zǐlù fetch water to test it:
full, it overturned;
half-full, it stood upright;
empty, it tilted.
Confucius sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
How can anything full not overturn?"
Zǐlù asked:
"May I ask if there is a way to maintain fullness?"
Confucius said:
"The way to maintain fullness
is to suppress and reduce it."
Zǐlù asked:
"Is there a way to reduce it?"
Confucius said:
"Those with abundant virtue and conduct
maintain it with reverence.
Those with vast land
maintain it with frugality.
Those with high rank and great eminence
maintain it with humility.
Those with numerous people and strong soldiers
maintain it with caution.
The intelligent and wise
maintain it with apparent foolishness.
The widely learned and strong in memory
maintain it with apparent shallowness.
This is what is called suppressing and reducing."
The Book of Songs says:
"Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended."
3.31 The Duke of Zhōu occupied the Son of Heaven's position for seven years,
during which ten common scholars presented gifts and met him as teacher.
Twelve met him as friends,
forty-nine from poor alleys and humble huts were received first,
a hundred who timely offered good counsel,
a thousand who taught scholars,
and ten thousand who served at court.
King Chéng enfeoffed Bó Qín in Lǔ,
and the Duke of Zhōu admonished him, saying:
"Go now!
Do not be arrogant towards scholars because of the state of Lǔ.
I am the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
and the uncle of King Chéng,
and I also assist the Son of Heaven.
My position in the world is not insignificant.
Yet, I would interrupt my bath three times to receive guests,
and spit out food three times to attend to visitors,
still fearing to lose the scholars of the world.
I have heard that moral conduct and generosity,
upheld with respect,
bring honor.
Vast and extensive lands,
upheld with frugality,
bring peace.
High rank and prosperity,
upheld with humility,
bring nobility.
A large population and strong army,
upheld with caution,
bring victory.
Intelligence and wisdom,
upheld with apparent simplicity,
bring excellence.
Broad knowledge and strong memory,
upheld with modesty,
bring wisdom.
These six qualities
are all virtues of humility.
To be honored as the Son of Heaven,
and to possess the wealth of the four seas,
comes from this virtue.
Those who lost the world and perished due to lack of humility
were Jié and Zhòu.
Can one not be cautious?
Thus, the Yì Jīng has a principle:
on a grand scale, it can protect the world;
on a moderate scale, it can protect the state and family;
on a personal scale, it can protect oneself.
This refers to humility.
The way of Heaven diminishes the full and supplements the humble;
the way of Earth transforms the full and flows to the humble;
spirits and gods harm the full and bless the humble;
the way of humans dislikes the full and favors the humble.
Therefore, when a garment is completed, a lapel must be left unfinished;
when a palace is completed, a corner must be left unfinished;
when a house is completed, a crude addition must be made—
to show incompleteness,
for such is the way of Heaven.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Humility brings success;
the nobleman has a fortunate end.'
The Shī Jīng says:
'Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended.'
Take this admonition to heart!
Do not be arrogant towards scholars because of the state of Lǔ."
3.32 The tradition says:
Zǐlù, in splendid attire, went to see Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Yóu, why so ostentatious?
In the past, the Jiāng River at its source in Wèn,
when it first emerges,
is not enough to float a wine cup.
But when it reaches the ford of the Jiāng,
without a boat,
without avoiding the wind,
it cannot be crossed.
Is it not because of the multitude of its tributaries?
Now, your clothes are so splendid,
your countenance so full of pride—
who in the world can surpass you?"
Zǐlù hurried out,
changed his clothes, and returned,
appearing humble and respectful.
Confucius said:
"Yóu, remember this.
Let me tell you:
Those cautious in speech are not boastful;
those cautious in action are not self-promoting.
To show off knowledge and pose as superior is the way of a petty person.
Thus, the nobleman knows what he knows
and does not know what he does not know—
this is the essence of speech.
Can do what he can do,
and cannot do what he cannot do—
this is the essence of action.
With the essence of speech comes wisdom;
with the essence of action comes benevolence.
Having both wisdom and benevolence,
what more is needed?
The Shī Jīng says:
'Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended.'"
3.33 The nobleman does not value actions that are merely difficult for the sake of difficulty,
does not value theories that are merely clever for the sake of cleverness,
does not value fame that is merely widespread for the sake of fame,
but values only what is appropriate.
Carrying a stone and drowning oneself in a river
is an action difficult to perform,
and Shēntú Dí could do it.
The nobleman does not value it
because it is not in accordance with ritual and righteousness.
That mountains and abysses are level,
that heaven and earth are comparable,
that Qí and Qín are connected,
that sound enters the ear
and comes out the mouth,
that a hook has beard,
that an egg has feathers—
these are theories difficult to uphold,
and Dèng Xī and Huì Shī could do it.
The nobleman does not value them
because they are not in accordance with ritual and righteousness.
Dào Zhí was notorious,
his fame like the sun and moon,
passed down endlessly alongside Shùn and Yǔ.
The nobleman does not value him
because it is not in accordance with ritual and righteousness.
Thus, the nobleman does not value actions that are merely difficult for the sake of difficulty,
does not value theories that are merely clever for the sake of cleverness,
does not value fame that is merely widespread for the sake of fame,
but values only what is appropriate.
The Shī Jīng says:
"Not contentious, not hasty,
not too hard, not too soft."
3.34 Bóyí and Shūqí would not look at evil sights with their eyes,
would not listen to evil sounds with their ears.
They would not serve a ruler who was not their own,
nor employ people who were not their own.
Where tyrannical governance prevailed,
or where unruly people resided,
they could not bear to live.
To think of living with villagers
was like wearing court robes and court cap
while sitting in mud and charcoal.
Thus, those who heard of the character of Bóyí
became incorruptible if greedy,
and resolute if cowardly.
As for Liǔxià Huì, it was not so.
He was not ashamed to serve a corrupt ruler,
nor did he decline a minor office.
In advancement, he did not hide his worth,
but always followed the right path.
In poverty and distress, he did not grieve;
neglected and forgotten, he did not complain.
Living with villagers,
he was so congenial he could not bear to leave.
Even if others were half-naked or fully exposed by my side,
how could they defile me?
Thus, those who heard of the character of Liǔxià Huì
became broad-minded if narrow,
and generous if mean.
As for Confucius leaving Lǔ,
he departed slowly and reluctantly.
He left when it was time to leave,
and stayed when it was time to stay—
such is the way of leaving one's native land.
Bóyí
was the sage of purity.
Liǔxià Huì
was the sage of harmony.
Confucius
was the sage of the mean.
The Shī Jīng says:
"Not contentious, not hasty,
not too hard, not too soft."
This refers to the mean, harmony, and penetration.
3.35 The king's
graded taxes and regulated affairs,
one-tenth from the fields,
inspections at passes and markets without levies,
mountains, forests, marshes, and weirs,
accessible in season without prohibition.
Assess the land to determine the soil.
Govern the way to secure tribute,
so all things come in multitude,
without stagnation,
circulating and exchanging.
Those nearby do not hide their abilities,
those afar do not resent their toil.
Even remote and backward states
all come to serve and live in peace and joy.
This is called the king's
graded taxes and regulated affairs.
The Shī Jīng says:
"His governance is gentle and ample,
and all blessings gather around him."
3.36 Xúnqīng and Línwǔjūn debated military affairs before King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
The king said:
"May I ask about the essentials of warfare?"
Línwǔjūn said:
"The essentials of warfare
are to secure favorable timing from above,
gain advantageous terrain from below,
move after the enemy,
yet arrive before them.
These are the essentials of warfare."
Xúnqīng said:
"Not so.
The essentials of warfare
lie solely in winning the affection of the officers and people.
If the six horses are not in harmony,
even Zàofǔ cannot travel far.
If the bow and arrows are not adjusted,
even Yì cannot hit subtle targets.
If the officers and people are not affectionate and attached,
even Tāng and Wǔ could not achieve victory in battle.
From this perspective,
the key lies solely in winning the affection of the officers and people."
Línwǔjūn said:
"Not so.
What warfare employs
is change and adaptation.
What it values
is strategy and deception.
Those skilled in its use are like a fleeing hare,
none know where they will emerge.
Sūn and Wú used this to be invincible under heaven.
From this perspective,
how can one only achieve victory after winning the affection of the officers and people?"
Xúnqīng said:
"Not so.
What you, my lord, speak of
is the warfare of feudal lords,
the business of strategists.
What I speak of
is the warfare of benevolent men,
the enterprise of sage kings.
Those who can be deceived
must be negligent and lazy.
Between ruler and minister, high and low,
there is clearly a disunity of virtue.
For Zhí to deceive Jié,
there might still be skill or clumsiness.
For Jié to deceive Yáo,
is like stirring boiling water with a finger,
throwing an egg at a stone,
carrying feathers into a fierce fire -
upon entering, one is scorched.
How could he be deceived?
Moreover, with whom would a tyrannical state come?
Those who come with him must have deceived their people.
The people's affection for me
is fragrant like pepper and orchids,
joyful like father and son.
They look upon their superiors
as upon venomous bees and scorpions.
By human nature,
even Jié or Zhí would hardly do what they most detest
to harm those they most love?
This is like making a man's children and grandchildren harm their own parents.
They would first perceive the error,
how could they be deceived?
Furthermore, the troops of a benevolent man,
when gathered form ranks,
when dispersed form columns.
Extended, they are like the long blade of Mòyé -
whatever touches it is severed.
Sharp, they are like the sharp edge of Mòyé -
whatever opposes it crumbles.
In circular formation, they are like mountains that cannot be moved;
in square formation, like bedrock that cannot be uprooted.
Whatever touches them breaks horns and joints and retreats;
how could they be deceived?
The Book of Songs says:
'King Wǔ set forth his banners,
reverently grasping his axe,
like a blazing fire,
then none dared oppose us.'
This describes the troops of Tāng and Wǔ."
King Xiàochéng rose from his mat, looked up and said:
"Although I am not clever,
I wish to follow the master's way of warfare."
3.37 A man who has received the mandate stands
with robes and cap adjusted,
dignified, so people look upon him and trust him.
Next,
hearing his words, they trust him.
Next,
seeing his actions, they trust him.
If after seeing his actions,
the multitude still does not trust him,
this is the lowest.
The Book of Songs says:
"Be cautious in your speech,
lest people say they cannot trust you."
3.38 In ancient times, one could know the world without leaving the door,
see the way of heaven without looking through the window,
not because the eyes could see a thousand miles ahead,
nor the ears hear a thousand miles away,
but because one measured it
by one's own feelings.
If one dislikes hunger and cold,
then one knows the world desires food and clothing.
If one dislikes toil and hardship,
then one knows the world desires peace and ease.
If one dislikes decline and poverty,
then one knows the world desires wealth and sufficiency.
Knowing these three things,
the sage king can set the world right without leaving his mat.
Therefore, the way of the gentleman
is simply loyalty and reciprocity.
To suffer hunger and thirst, distress the vital energy,
endure cold and heat, trouble the skin and flesh -
these four are the great harms to the people.
If these harms are not removed,
they cannot be taught and governed.
If the four limbs are not covered,
there will be few benevolent men.
If the five viscera are empty,
there will be no established scholars.
Therefore, in the laws of the former kings,
the Son of Heaven personally plowed,
the queen and consorts personally silkwormed,
worrying about clothing and food before all under heaven.
The Book of Songs says:
"What have our parents done?"
"My heart is grieved,
that this man has no lower garment."
4.1 When Zhòu instituted the punishment of the roasting pillar,
Prince Bǐgān said:
"If the ruler is tyrannical and one does not remonstrate,
that is not loyalty.
If one fears death and does not speak,
that is not courage.
Seeing error, one remonstrates immediately;
if not heeded, one dies -
this is the ultimate loyalty."
Thereupon he remonstrated,
and for three days did not leave the court.
Zhòu imprisoned and killed him.
The Book of Songs says:
"Great Heaven is unjust,
for I am truly innocent."
4.2 Jié made a pool of wine
large enough to sail boats,
with a lees mound high enough to see ten lǐ;
at one drumbeat, three thousand people drank like cattle.
Guān Lóngpáng came forward and admonished:
"The rulers of old
personally practiced ritual and righteousness,
loved the people and conserved resources,
therefore the state was secure and their lives long.
Now you use resources as if inexhaustible,
kill people as if fearing not to surpass others.
If you do not change,
Heaven's calamity will surely descend,
and punishment will certainly come.
Please change your ways."
He stood and would not leave the court.
Jié imprisoned and killed him.
The gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"It is Heaven's mandate."
The Book of Songs says:
"Great Heaven is unjust,
for I am truly innocent."
4.3 There is the greatly loyal,
the secondarily loyal,
the inferiorly loyal,
and the national traitor.
To cover the ruler with the Way and transform him
is called great loyalty.
To harmonize the ruler with virtue and assist him
is called secondary loyalty.
To remonstrate against the ruler's errors and incur his resentment
is called inferior loyalty.
To have no regard for the public way and righteous principles,
flattering and agreeing to maintain salary and nurture connections
is called being a national traitor.
Like the Duke of Zhōu towards King Chéng,
this can be called great loyalty.
Like Guǎn Zhòng towards Duke Huán,
this can be called secondary loyalty.
Like Wǔ Zǐxū towards Fūchāi,
this can be called inferior loyalty.
Like Cáo Chùlóng towards Zhòu,
this can be called being a national traitor.
These are all deeds of ministers,
demonstrating the effects of good and ill fortune, worthiness and unworthiness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Not only do they not fulfill their duties,
but they are the king's burden."
4.4 Duke Āi inquired about selecting personnel.
Confucius said:
"Do not select the aggressive,
do not select the glib,
do not select the slanderous.
The aggressive tend to be arrogant.
The glib tend to be sycophantic.
The slanderous tend to be deceitful.
Thus, a bow must first be adjusted,
then one may seek its strength.
A horse must first be tamed,
then one may seek its excellence.
A scholar must first be trustworthy and sincere,
then one may seek his knowledge.
If a scholar is untrustworthy yet highly knowledgeable,
he is like a jackal or wolf,
with whom it is difficult to get close personally."
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"To add wings to a tiger,
is that not perilous?"
The "Shī" says:
"Not in their duties do they abide,
only the king's burdens they provide."
This speaks of their failure to reverently perform their duties,
thereby harming their lord.
4.5 Duke Huán of Qí privately discussed with Guǎn Zhòng about attacking Jǔ,
yet the people of the state came to know of it.
Duke Huán said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I only spoke of this to you, Father Zhòng,
yet the people of the state know of it. Why?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Perhaps there is a sage in the state?
Where is Dōngguō Yá now?"
Duke Huán looked and said:
"Here he is."
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"Did you speak of it?"
Dōngguō Yá said:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"How did you know?"
He replied:
"I have heard that a nobleman has three countenances,
thus I knew."
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"What are the three countenances?"
He replied:
"Joyful and loving delight,
is the countenance of bells and drums.
Sorrowful and grieving worry,
is the countenance of mourning garments.
Fierce and resolute intensity,
is the countenance of arms and armor.
Thus I knew."
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"How did you know it was Jǔ?"
He replied:
"You pointed facing southeast,
your mouth open and uncovered,
your tongue raised and not lowered,
thus I knew it was Jǔ."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
The "Shī" says:
"Others have thoughts in their hearts,
I can measure them." Dōngguō Xiānshēng said:
"The eyes
are the symbols of the heart.
Speech
indicates actions.
The wise, regarding others,
do not necessarily seek knowledge before understanding.
Observe their appearance and demeanor,
examine their spirit and will,
determine acceptance or rejection,
and human feelings are fully revealed."
The "Shī" says:
"Others have thoughts in their hearts,
I can measure them."
4.6 Now, having strong armor and sharp weapons
is insufficient to deploy against enemies and defeat foes;
having excellent bows and well-adjusted arrows
is insufficient to shoot far and hit minute targets;
this is equivalent to having no weapons.
Having people but not enough to strengthen and employ against formidable enemies
is equivalent to having no people.
Thus, a thousand lǐ of solid rock
does not count as having land,
and a million ignorant people
do not count as having people.
The "Shī" says:
"In the south is the Winnowing Basket,
but it cannot winnow.
In the north is the Dipper,
but it cannot ladle wine."
4.7 The "Zhuàn" says:
Shùn played the five-stringed zither,
singing the poem of the "South Wind,"
and the world was well-governed.
Duke Píng of Zhōu never lacked wine before him,
bells and stone chimes never left their hangings,
yet the realm was also well-governed.
A commoner with a hundred acres and one house,
toils without rest,
has nowhere to transfer his duties.
For one person to govern the entire world,
with days to spare and governance lacking,
this is achieved by having others do it.
To hold the power of employing others,
yet be unable to control the masses below,
means the one in position is not the right person.
The "Shī" says:
"In the south is the Winnowing Basket,
but it cannot winnow.
In the north is the Dipper,
but it cannot ladle wine."
This speaks of having a position without its proper functions.
4.8 Duke Huán of Qí attacked the Shānróng,
his route passed through Yān,
and the lord of Yān escorted him beyond the border.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"When feudal lords escort each other,
is it customary to go beyond the border?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Only for the Son of Heaven is it not beyond the border."
Duke Huán said:
"Then the lord of Yān, out of fear, has breached etiquette.
I cannot allow Yān to breach etiquette."
Thereupon, he ceded the territory where the lord of Yān had reached to him.
The feudal lords heard of this and all paid homage to Qí.
The "Shī" says:
"Quietly reverent in your position,
love what is upright and honest.
The spirits, hearing this,
will grant you great blessings."
4.9 The "Sháo" dance using shields and axes,
is not the ultimate music.
Shùn taking two daughters as wives,
is not the ultimate ritual.
Enfeoffing nineteen sons of Huángdì,
is not the ultimate righteousness.
Weeping while going to the fields,
does not fully fulfill the mandate.
Judging by human standards,
it is acceptable.
Measuring by the standards of law,
it is not yet sufficient.
The "Lǐ" says:
"Major rituals number three hundred,
minor rituals three thousand."
The "Shī" says:
"Quietly reverent in your position,
align with the upright and honest.
The spirits, hearing this,
will bestow goodness upon you."
4.10 Ritual is
the ultimate means of governance and distinction,
the foundation of a strong state,
the way to assert authority,
the system for achieving merit and fame.
Kings and dukes follow it,
thereby unifying the world.
Not following it,
leads to the downfall of the state.
Hence, strong armor and sharp weapons are not enough to be considered martial,
high walls and deep moats are not enough to be considered secure,
harsh decrees and numerous punishments are not enough to be considered authoritative.
Following the proper way leads to success,
not following it leads to failure.
In the past, the Chǔ people used alligator hide, rhinoceros, and wild ox hides for armor,
hard as metal and stone,
coiled like giant serpents,
fierce as bees and scorpions,
light, sharp, sturdy, and swift,
swift as a whirlwind.
Yet their army was nearly destroyed at Chuíshā,
Tángzǐ died,
Zhuāng Qiāo fled,
and Chǔ was divided into three or four parts.
Was this due to a lack of strong armor and sharp weapons?
It was because the way they were governed was not the proper way.
They used the Rǔ and Huái rivers as natural barriers,
the Jiāng and Hàn rivers as moats,
fortified with Fāngchéng,
bounded by Dènglín,
yet the Qín army reached Yānyǐng,
capturing it as easily as shaking dry leaves.
Was this due to a lack of strong defenses and natural barriers?
It was because the way they were governed was not the proper way.
Zhòu killed Bǐgān and imprisoned Jīzǐ,
created the punishment of the heated pillar,
killed indiscriminately at any time,
causing his subordinates to grieve and resent,
none hoping to preserve their lives,
yet when the Zhōu army arrived, his orders were not followed by those around him.
Is this due to the lack of strict decrees and numerous punishments?
It is because the methods used to govern are not in accordance with the proper way.
If one clarifies the way and distributes resources equitably,
sincerely cares for the people and employs them seasonally,
then the response from below to above will be as swift as an echo or a shadow.
Should anyone disobey orders,
then await them with punishment. Thus, punishing one person brings submission throughout the world,
and those below do not blame those above,
knowing the fault lies with themselves.
Therefore, punishments diminish while authority flows smoothly,
for no other reason
than following this way.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"From east to west,
from south to north,
none think not to submit."
Thus, those nearby sing praises,
while those from afar hasten to come,
and even remote, secluded countries all eagerly serve and find peace and joy,
like infants returning to a loving mother.
Why is this?
Because benevolent punishments and righteousness are established,
teaching is sincere and care is deep,
and rituals and music interact harmoniously.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Rituals are fully measured,
laughter and talk are fully appropriate."
4.11 A ruler governs with ritual, distributing it
equally and without bias.
Ministers serve their ruler with ritual,
loyal and obedient without slack.
Fathers are lenient, kind, and courteous,
sons are respectful, loving, and reverent.
Elder brothers are affectionate and friendly,
younger brothers are respectful, yielding, and not negligent.
Husbands are illuminating and discerning,
wives are gentle, obedient, and compliant.
If one acts not in accordance with the way,
they become fearful and self-composed.
This is the complete way;
if only one part is established, there is chaos,
if all are established, there is order.
May I ask how to achieve all?
The answer is to examine ritual.
In the past, the ancient kings examined ritual to benefit the world,
thus their virtue reached heaven and earth,
and their actions were always appropriate.
The noble person is respectful without distress,
reverent without rigidity,
poor yet not constrained,
wealthy yet not arrogant,
adapting to change without exhaustion,
all through examining ritual.
Thus, the noble person regards ritual
with reverence and ease.
In handling affairs,
they are consistent and without error.
In dealing with people,
they are generous, seldom resentful, and not partial.
In demeanor,
they are cultivated and not perilous.
In responding to change,
they are quick and adept without burden.
With officials and skilled individuals,
they do not compete in ability
but utilize their achievements.
With heaven, earth, and all things,
they do not oppose their nature but carefully manage their abundance.
In serving superiors,
they are loyal and obedient without slack.
In directing subordinates,
they are equal and without bias.
In social interactions,
they associate by category with righteousness.
In their local community,
they are accommodating yet not disorderly.
Thus, in obscurity, they have fame;
in prominence, they have achievements.
Benevolence and righteousness cover the world without exhaustion,
enlightening heaven and earth,
managing myriad changes without doubt.
With balanced vitality and broad will,
their righteous actions fill heaven and earth,
reaching the pinnacle of benevolence and wisdom.
This is what is called the ancient kings' examination of ritual.
If so,
then the elderly are at peace,
the young are cherished,
friends trust each other,
like infants returning to a loving mother.
It is said:
Benevolent punishments and righteousness are established,
teaching is sincere and care is deep,
and rituals and music interact harmoniously.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Rituals are fully measured,
laughter and talk are fully appropriate."
4.12 Yànzǐ was sent to Lǔ on a mission,
ascending the hall quickly and kneeling when presenting the jade.
Zǐgòng found it strange
and asked Confucius:
"Does Yànzǐ understand ritual?
Now Yànzǐ has come to Lǔ on a mission,
ascending the hall quickly and kneeling when presenting the jade.
Why?"
Confucius said:
"There must be a reason.
Wait until he sees me;
I will ask him."
Soon Yànzǐ arrived,
and Confucius inquired.
Yànzǐ replied:
"The ritual for ascending the hall
requires the ruler to take one step,
the minister two.
Now the ruler moves swiftly;
dare I not hurry?
The ruler presents the gift humbly;
dare I not kneel?"
Confucius said:
"Excellent!
There is ritual within ritual.
Cì (Zǐgòng) is seldom on missions;
how could he fully understand ritual!"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Rituals are fully measured,
laughter and talk are fully appropriate."
This refers to Yànzǐ.
4.13 In ancient times, eight families shared the well-field system.
A square lǐ constituted one jǐng.
Three hundred bù wide
and three hundred bù long made one lǐ,
with nine hundred mǔ of land.
One bù wide
and one hundred bù long made one mǔ.
One hundred bù wide
and one hundred bù long made one hundred mǔ.
Eight families formed a neighborhood,
each receiving one hundred mǔ.
Surplus laborers each received twenty-five mǔ.
Each family contributed ten mǔ for public land,
with the remaining twenty mǔ used for huts,
each family getting two and a half mǔ.
The eight families protected each other,
taking turns on guard duty,
caring for each other in illness,
helping in times of trouble,
lending to each other,
sharing meals,
consulting on marriages,
dividing fishing and hunting gains,
and practicing benevolence and kindness,
so the people lived in harmony and friendship.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"In the fields are huts,
on the borders are melons."
Now it is not so.
People are grouped into fives,
watching for each other's crimes,
reporting each other's punishments,
creating grudges and enmity,
leading to mutual harm,
damaging harmonious hearts,
undermining benevolence and kindness,
harming moral transformation.
Those in harmony are few,
while those seeking ruin are many,
and the way of benevolence is extinguished.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"How can they be good?
They will all drown together."
4.14 The Son of Heaven does not speak of abundance or scarcity,
feudal lords do not speak of advantage or harm,
great officers do not speak of gain or loss,
scholars do not speak of trading wealth,
nor do they trade on the road.
Thus, families with carriage horses do not rely on poultry and pig profits,
those who cut ice do not seek cattle and sheep income,
rulers of a thousand chariots do not trade goods,
chief ministers do not manage currency distributions,
great officers do not cultivate gardens,
officials in charge of stores do not covet market profits,
so the poor have joy,
and orphans and widows have means to sustain themselves.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"There a leftover sheaf,
here a stray ear of grain,
benefit for the widow."
4.15 If a ruler desires skilled archers
who hit distant, tiny targets,
he offers noble titles and heavy rewards to attract them.
Internally, he does not favor his own kin;
externally, he does neglect those from afar.
Those who can hit the target are selected.
Is this not called the great way?
Even a sage cannot change it.
Now, to govern the state and control the people,
harmonize the upper and lower ranks,
internally secure the cities,
externally resist calamities,
in order prevails over others,
and others cannot prevail over it;
in chaos, danger, decline, and ruin can be expected to arrive swiftly.
Yet, in seeking ministers and chancellors for support, one does not act with such impartiality,
but only employs those who are flattering, close, and aligned with oneself.
Is this not considered a fault?
Thus, those who possess the altars of soil and grain,
all desire stability,
yet soon face peril.
All wish to preserve it,
yet soon face ruin.
In ancient times, there were over a thousand states,
now not even a few tens remain.
What is the reason for this?
None have not failed in this regard.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler may show favoritism in granting gold, stones, pearls, and jade,
but not in bestowing official positions and responsibilities.
Why is that?
It is said:
Fundamentally, it does no good to those favored.
If the ruler employs those incapable,
that is a benighted ruler.
If ministers take on tasks they cannot handle,
that is deceitful ministers.
With a benighted ruler above,
and deceitful ministers below,
ruin is not far off.
This is a path harmful to all.
Thus, only an enlightened ruler can truly cherish what he loves,
while a benighted ruler inevitably endangers what he loves.
Now, King Wén did not lack flattering and close associates,
yet he transcendentally elevated Tàigōng from among the boatmen and employed him.
Was it out of personal favor?
If considered as kin?
Then he was of a different clan. As an old acquaintance?
They had never met before.
For his good looks?
Tàigōng was seventy-two years old,
frail and with teeth fallen out.
Yet he was employed because
King Wén wished to establish noble principles,
to make illustrious his reputation,
to uniformly govern the world,
and to benefit the Central States,
but could not do it alone;
thus he elevated this man and used him.
Noble principles were indeed established,
his illustrious reputation indeed made clear,
and he uniformly governed the world.
He established seventy-one states,
with the Jī clan alone occupying fifty-two.
The descendants of Zhōu,
if not insane or deluded,
all became prominent lords of the world.
This is called being able to cherish what one loves.
Therefore,
only an enlightened ruler can cherish what he loves,
while a benighted ruler inevitably endangers what he loves—
this refers to that.
The "Greater Odes" say:
"He left his grandson plans,
to secure and assist his son."
The "Lesser Odes" say:
"Death and mourning may come any day,
we have little chance to meet again."
This refers to endangering what one loves.
4.16 Do not inform one who asks improperly;
do not question one who informs improperly.
Do not debate with one who has a contentious air.
Only if they come by the proper way,
then engage with them.
If not by the proper way,
then avoid them.
Thus, only after they are ritually respectful can one discuss the methods of the Way;
only after their words are compliant can one discuss the principles of the Way;
only after their expression shows accord can one discuss the ultimate of the Way.
Therefore, to speak with one not yet ready to be spoken to is called blindness;
not to speak with one ready to be spoken to is called concealment.
The noble person is not blind, speaking cautiously
in proper sequence.
The "Odes" say:
"He was not proud nor tardy,
so the Son of Heaven gave to him."
This means he must first connect with our intent before we give.
4.17 A son covering up for his parents,
cannot be rectified by righteousness.
A ruler punishing the unrighteous,
cannot be accepted through benevolence.
Though it may violate benevolence and harm righteousness,
the law lies within it.
The "Odes" say:
"Leisurely and at ease,
this too is acceptable."
4.18 Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What does a king value most?"
He replied:
"He values Heaven."
Duke Huán looked up and gazed at the sky.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The Heaven referred to
is not the vast blue sky.
A king takes the common people as Heaven.
If the people support him, there is stability;
if they assist him, there is strength;
if they oppose him, there is peril;
if they betray him, there is ruin."
The "Odes" say:
"The people are not good,
blaming each other from one side."
When the people all reside on one side
and resent their superiors,
it is unheard of for the state not to perish.
4.19 A skilled charioteer does not forget his horses.
A skilled archer does not forget his bow.
A skilled ruler does not forget his subordinates.
Sincerely care for and benefit them,
and within the four seas,
all will be as one family.
Without care yet seeking benefit,
a son may kill his father—
how much more so the world?
The "Odes" say:
"The people are not good,
blaming each other from one side."
4.20 Outwardly, they bring trouble to the clan;
inwardly, they cause worry in the village.
The "Odes" say:
"Like southern barbarians and Máo tribes,
they are my cause for worry."
Such is the conduct of petty persons.
4.21 There are rulers they cannot serve,
yet they expect loyalty from ministers.
There are fathers they cannot serve,
yet they expect filial piety from sons.
There are elder brothers they cannot respect,
yet they expect obedience from younger brothers.
The "Odes" say:
"Receiving rank without yielding,
until it reaches oneself, it is lost."
This means they can understand others,
but cannot understand themselves.
4.22 The fools of the present age,
adorn heretical doctrines,
embellish deceitful words,
to bring chaos to the world,
deceiving and confusing the masses of fools,
making them muddled and unaware of where right and wrong, order and disorder lie—
these are Fàn Jū, Wèi Móu, Tián Wén, Zhuāng Zhōu, Shèn Dào,
Tián Pián, Mò Dí, Sòng Xíng, Dèng Xī, Huì Shī, and their like.
These ten masters
all follow what is wrong and glorify it,
with mixed and broad knowledge,
yet they do not emulate antiquity,
nor model themselves on the former kings,
but according to past precedents create their theories,
striving to be skillful on their own,
their ways meeting no acceptance,
yet people follow them.
Thus it is said that the skillful theories of these ten masters
are all insufficient to align with the great Way,
beautify customs,
and govern the social order.
However, their positions each have their reasons,
their words all have their logic,
enough to deceive and confuse the masses of fools,
and disrupt simplicity and honesty—
this is the crime of these ten masters.
As for unifying strategies,
consolidating categories,
aligning words and deeds,
gathering the heroes of the world
to instruct them in the great Way,
teach them ultimate compliance,
in the secluded spaces,
on the mats and couches,
clearly the tools of the sage kings are present,
abundantly the trends of a peaceful age converge—
the skillful theorists cannot enter,
the ten masters cannot approach.
Without even a place to stick an awl,
yet kings and dukes cannot contend with them in reputation—
these are the sages who have not yet attained their ambitions,
such as Zhòngní.
Shùn and Yǔ are also such.
What then should the benevolent person strive for?
Above, emulate the systems of Shùn and Yǔ;
below, follow the righteousness of Zhòngní;
to strive to silence the theories of the ten masters.
When it is thus,
the benevolent person's task is complete,
the harms of the world are eliminated,
and the traces of the sage are made evident.
The Book of Songs says:
"Thick falls the snow,
but when the sun appears, it melts away."
4.23 The noble person, when broad-minded, reveres Heaven and follows the Way;
when cautious, fears righteousness and practices restraint;
when wise, is clear and discerning and classifies things appropriately;
when simple, is upright and sincere and follows the law;
when joyful, is harmonious and orderly;
when worried, is calm and withdraws;
when successful, is tranquil and tolerant;
when in hardship, is frugal and careful.
The petty person, when broad-minded, becomes arrogant and violent;
when cautious, becomes excessive and biased;
when clever, seizes and steals and schemes;
when foolish, becomes venomous and treacherous and causes chaos;
when joyful, becomes frivolous and hasty;
when worried, becomes broken and fearful;
when successful, becomes proud and partial;
when in hardship, becomes abandoned and burdened.
Their bodily movements share the same rhythm as beasts,
their violent speech is no different from barbarians,
abroad they bring trouble to their clan,
at home they cause worry to their village.
The Book of Songs says:
"Like the barbarians of Mán and Máo,
thus I am filled with worry."
4.24 The Tradition says:
Love arising from genuine feeling is called benevolence;
moderating love according to principle is called righteousness.
Expressing love with respect and caution is called ritual;
adorning ritual is called demeanor.
The beauty of ritual and demeanor
is sufficient to bring order.
Therefore, their words can serve as a guide for the people,
and the people follow these words.
Their actions can serve as a model for the people,
and the people follow these actions.
Written on bamboo slips,
passed down in records,
for ten thousand generations, sons and grandsons follow without ceasing.
Following them brings order,
losing them brings chaos.
Following them brings life,
losing them brings death.
Now, those whose bodily movements share the same rhythm as beasts,
whose violent speech is no different from barbarians,
chaotic and without the Way,
these are condemned by enlightened kings and sage rulers.
The Book of Songs says:
"Like the barbarians of Mán and Máo,
thus I am filled with worry."
4.25 A guest advised Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:
"Tāng with seventy lǐ,
King Wén with a hundred lǐ,
both united the world,
and unified the realm.
Now, Sūnzǐ here
is a worthy of the world;
if you lend him the power of a hundred lǐ,
I privately think it would be disadvantageous to you.
What do you think?"
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to dismiss Sūnzǐ.
Sūnzǐ left and went to Zhào,
where he was made a high minister.
The guest again advised Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:
"In the past, Yī Yǐn left Xià for Yīn,
and Yīn became king while Xià perished.
Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ and entered Qí,
and Lǔ weakened while Qí strengthened.
From this, we see that
where the worthy are,
their ruler is never not good,
and their state is never not secure.
Now, Sūnzǐ is a worthy of the world;
why dismiss him and let him leave?"
Chūnshēn Jūn again said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to invite Sūnzǐ back.
Sūnzǐ then feigned delight and declined, saying:
"A common saying goes:
'The leper pities the king.'
This is an irreverent saying.
Nevertheless,
it must be carefully considered.
It refers not to those who are robbed and killed or die, but to the rulers themselves.
When a ruler is young and unrestrained,
lacking methods and laws to recognize treachery,
then ministers seize absolute power to scheme for personal gain,
and to prevent execution against themselves.
Thus, they abandon the virtuous and elder and set up the weak and young,
discard the upright and employ the unworthy.
Therefore, the record of the Spring and Autumn Annals
says:
'King Chǔ's son Wéi was on a mission to Zhèng,
but before leaving the border,
heard the king was ill,
returned to inquire about the illness,
then used his cap strings to strangle the king and kill him,
and thus made himself king.
Cuī Zhù of Qí had a beautiful wife,
and Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her.
Cuī Zhù led his faction to attack Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng begged to share the state with him.
Cuī Zhù refused.
Duke Zhuāng wanted to stab himself in the temple,
but Cuī Zhù refused.
Duke Zhuāng fled,
climbed over the outer wall,
was shot in the thigh,
and was then killed,
and his brother Duke Jǐng was set up.'
In recent times, we have seen:
Lì Duì controlling Zhào,
starved the lord father at Shāqiū,
and killed him after a hundred days.
Nào Chǐ controlling Qí,
pulled out King Mǐn's tendons and hung them in the temple,
and killed him overnight.
Now, leprosy, though it involves ulcers, abscesses, and sores,
compared to ancient times,
does not reach strangling the neck or shooting the thigh;
compared to recent times,
does not reach pulling out tendons or starving to death.
The rulers who are robbed and killed or die,
their mental toil and worry,
their physical pain and suffering,
must be worse than leprosy.
From this perspective,
even if the leper pities the king,
it is acceptable."
Thereupon, he composed a poem, saying:
"They know not how to wear jade and pearls,
nor distinguish coarse cloth from brocade.
Lǘ Jū and Zǐ Dū find no matchmakers,
while Mó Mǔ and Lì Fù are delighted in.
They take blindness for sight,
deafness for hearing.
Wrong for right,
misfortune for good fortune.
Alas, O Heaven above,
how can I be the same as they!"
The Book of Songs says:
"God is very changeable,
do not bring ruin upon yourself."
4.26 The hide of the strange beast of the southern Miáo is like that of dogs and sheep,
but giving it to a person is like giving a deadly poison.
This is due to clinging to the old, indulging in one's nature, and being accustomed to habits that change one's character.
The madman bites himself,
forgetting it is not grass or grain,
eats earth and forgets it is not fine grain.
Thus, the madman of Chǔ speaks the Chǔ language,
the madman of Qí speaks the Qí language,
habit makes it so.
Habit affects people subtly yet evidently,
deeply and firmly,
permeating the sinews and bones,
stronger than glue and lacquer.
Therefore, the noble person is devoted to learning.
The Book of Songs says:
"Having seen the noble person,
his virtuous words are very firm."
4.27 Mèngzǐ said:
Benevolence
is the human heart.
Righteousness
is the human path.
To abandon the path and not follow it,
to let the heart stray and not seek it—
if a person's chickens or dogs are lost,
they know to seek them.
But if the heart is lost and they do not seek it,
is their heart not even as good as chickens or dogs?
They do not know the analogy, and that is extreme.
How lamentable!
In the end, they must perish.
Therefore, the way of learning and inquiry has no other purpose,
but to seek the lost heart.
The Book of Songs says:
"Keep it in the heart's core,
never forgetting it for a day."
4.28 Though the Way is near,
without walking, one does not reach it.
Though affairs are small,
without doing, they are not accomplished.
Those who often have many idle days
will not go far beyond others.
A skillful bow in one's hand,
with horn layered, sinews applied, and the blend of glue and lacquer,
can become a treasure for a ruler of ten thousand chariots.
And yet, with that same hand, one cannot sell even a few coins' worth.
People of the same talent and equal ability may differ ten-thousandfold in nobility and baseness,
because of the dedication and focus of their minds.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"What is hidden in the heart,
how can it be forgotten any day?"
4.29 The *Tradition* says:
Sincerely hating evil,
one knows the root of punishment.
Sincerely loving goodness,
one knows the root of respect.
Only sincerity can move the spirits.
Reaching the hearts of the people,
knowing the roots of punishment and respect,
then one is awe-inspiring without anger,
trustworthy without speaking.
Sincerity is the master of virtue.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"When bells are struck in the palace,
their sound is heard outside."
4.30 Confucius met a guest.
After the guest left,
Yán Yuān said:
"Is the guest benevolent?"
Confucius said:
"Resentful is his heart,
sharp is his mouth;
whether he is benevolent, I do not know.
It is the gathering of words." Yán Yuān's countenance changed with unease,
and he said:
"A fine jade measuring a foot,
even buried under ten ren of earth,
cannot hide its light.
A fine pearl measuring an inch,
even submerged under a hundred ren of water,
cannot conceal its luster.
As for form,
it is the body; expression, the heart;
how shallow they are!
If warmth and goodness are within,
they show in the brows and lashes.
If flaws and blemishes are within,
the brows and lashes cannot conceal them."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"When bells are struck in the palace,
their sound is heard outside."
4.31 Falsity and deceit cannot long endure,
emptiness cannot be maintained,
rotten wood cannot be carved,
and without genuine feeling, one cannot last.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"When bells and drums are in the palace,
their sound is heard outside."
This means that what is within will surely manifest without.
4.32 The so-called mediocre person
cannot speak good words with their mouth,
cannot understand the laws of the former kings with their heart,
acts without knowing what to pursue,
stops and stands without knowing what to settle on,
daily chooses among things without knowing what is valuable,
does not know to select worthy and good individuals to entrust themselves to,
flows along with things,
not knowing where to return,
the five organs lack governance,
the heart follows and decays,
never to turn back.
Therefore, in action, they face physical danger,
in stillness, their reputation is dishonored.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"This person has no goodness,
their virtue is inconstant."
4.33 A guest came to see the Duke of Zhōu,
who responded at the gate, saying:
"What instruction do you have for Dàn?"
The guest said:
"If outside, speak of outside matters;
if inside, speak of inside matters.
Shall I enter or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Please enter."
The guest said:
"Standing, speak of righteousness;
sitting, speak of benevolence.
Shall I sit or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Please sit."
The guest said:
"Speaking quickly, it is indistinct;
speaking slowly, it is not heard.
Shall I speak or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu assented:
"Dàn has been remiss."
The next day, he raised an army and punished Guǎn and Cài.
Thus, the guest was skilled in speechless persuasion,
and the Duke of Zhōu was skilled in hearing speechless words.
One may say the Duke of Zhōu could listen to subtle words.
Therefore, the gentleman's admonitions are subtle,
and his rescue of others in urgency is gentle.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"How dare I fear the journey?
I fear I cannot hasten."
5.1 Zǐxià asked:
"Why is 'Guān Jū' the beginning of the 'Airs of the States'?"
Confucius said:
"'Guān Jū' is the ultimate!
The person of 'Guān Jū'
looks up to heaven,
looks down to earth,
mysterious and obscure,
where virtue is stored;
bustling and seething,
where the Way is practiced;
like the divine dragon's transformations,
with elegant patterns.
Great is the Way of 'Guān Jū'!
It is what all things depend on,
what all living beings hang their lives upon.
The Hé and Luò rivers produced the *Book* and *Chart*,
the qílín and phoenix roamed the suburbs.
Without following the Way of 'Guān Jū',
how could the matters of 'Guān Jū' come to be?
The texts of the Six Classics
all urgently discuss and归结,
largely drawn from 'Guān Jū'.
The matters of 'Guān Jū' are truly great!
Vast and supportive,
from east to west,
from south to north,
none do not submit in thought.
You should strive for it,
think and submit to it.
Between heaven and earth,
among all living people,
the source of the kingly way
lies not beyond this."
Zǐxià sighed deeply and said:
"Great is 'Guān Jū',
it is the foundation of heaven and earth."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"With bells and drums, delight her."
5.2 Confucius embraced the heart of a sage,
wandered in the realm of morality,
roamed freely in the formless land,
leaned on heavenly principles,
observed human feelings,
clarified beginnings and ends,
knew gains and losses.
Thus, he promoted benevolence and righteousness,
despised power and profit,
to sustain and nurture them.
At that time, the Zhōu house was declining,
the kingly way was cut off,
the feudal lords governed by force,
the strong plundered the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
the common people had no peace,
with no one to uphold order,
rituals and righteousness were abandoned and ruined,
human relationships were not properly managed.
Thereupon, Confucius went from east to west,
from south to north,
crawling on all fours to save them.
5.3 In the governance of a true king,
the worthy and capable are promoted without waiting for their turn,
the unworthy are dismissed without a moment's delay,
the arch-villains are executed without waiting for instruction,
the mediocre are transformed without waiting for administration.
If ranks are not yet fixed,
then there is the order of Zhāo and Mù.
Even the sons and grandsons of dukes, ministers, and great officers,
if their conduct violates rituals and righteousness,
are relegated to commoners.
As for the people who have fallen,
shepherd and test them.
Even the sons and grandsons of commoners,
if they accumulate learning
and correct their personal conduct,
and are capable in rituals and righteousness,
are promoted to officers and great officers.
Respect and await them;
if they are stable, nurture them;
if unstable, discard them.
The restless people,
the ruler gathers and supports them,
employs them according to their talent,
provides them with official positions, clothing, and food,
so the king's coverage leaves none behind.
Those whose talent and conduct oppose the times
are put to death without pardon,
which is called heaven's punishment.
This is the governance of a true king.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"If a person has no dignity,
why not die?"
5.4 The ruler is
the source of the people.
If the source is clear, the flow is clear;
if the source is turbid, the flow is turbid.
Therefore, one who possesses the altars of soil and grain,
if they cannot love their people,
yet seeks for the people to be close to them and love them,
cannot obtain it.
If the people are not close and do not love,
yet seeks for them to be used by oneself,
to die for oneself,
cannot obtain it.
If the people are not used,
do not die,
yet seeks for the troops to be strong,
the city walls to be firm,
cannot obtain it.
If the troops are not strong,
the city walls not firm,
yet desires not to face danger, diminishment, and destruction,
cannot obtain it.
The circumstances of danger, diminishment, and destruction,
all accumulate from this,
and to seek to hear of peace and joy,
is it not difficult?
This is to live in vain.
Alas!
Those who live in vain do not await the time and perish.
Therefore, if a ruler desires strength, firmness, peace, and joy,
nothing is better than turning to oneself.
If one wishes to attach the subordinates and unify the people,
then nothing is better than attending to governance.
If one wishes to cultivate governance and beautify customs,
then nothing is better than seeking the right person.
That person,
born in the present age,
yet aspires to the ancient age.
Though the kings and dukes of the world do not favor it,
this person alone favors it.
Though the people do not act for it,
this person alone acts for it.
Even when acting for it leads to hardship,
this person still acts for it,
without a moment's negligence.
Clearly and uniquely understanding how the former kings encountered it,
how they lost it,
knowing the safety and danger, good and bad of the state,
as if distinguishing white from black,
then this is the person.
If a ruler desires strength, firmness, peace, and joy,
then nothing is better than working with this person,
employing them greatly,
then the world becomes one,
the feudal lords become ministers.
Employing them modestly,
then authority extends to neighboring states.
None can resist it.
Like Yīn's use of Yī Yǐ,
Zhōu's encounter with Tài Gōng,
one may say they were greatly employed.
Qí's use of Guǎn Zhòng,
Chǔ's use of Sūn Shū'áo,
may be considered modest employment.
Great employment is like that,
modest employment is like this.
Therefore it is said:
Pure and one becomes king,
mixed and one becomes hegemon,
without unity, one perishes.
The "Shī" says:
"The four states have no governance,
they do not use their good."
Not using their good ministers and not perishing,
has never happened.
5.5 Zào Fù,
is the world's expert charioteer,
without chariot and horse, he has no means to show his ability.
Yì,
is the world's expert archer,
