without bow and arrow, he has no means to show his skill.
That great Ru,
harmonizes and unifies the world,
without a hundred lǐ of land, he has no means to show his achievement.
If the chariot is sturdy and the horse selected but cannot reach a thousand lǐ,
then it is not Zào Fù.
If the bow is tuned and the arrow straight but cannot shoot far and hit the minute,
then it is not Yì.
Using a hundred lǐ of land but cannot harmonize and unify the world and control the four barbarians,
then it is not a great Ru.
That great Ru,
even if dwelling in poor alleys and humble rooms,
without land enough to stick an awl,
kings and dukes cannot contend with him for fame.
Using a hundred lǐ of land,
then a state of a thousand lǐ cannot contend with him for victory.
Whipping the violent states,
unifying and aligning the world,
none can overturn it,
this is the achievement of the great Ru. His words have categories,
his actions have ritual,
his undertakings have no regret,
his upholding standards and responding to change are perfectly fitting,
moving with the times,
rising and falling with the age,
in a thousand actions and ten thousand changes,
his Way is one,
this is the standard of the great Ru.
Therefore, there are the vulgar person,
the vulgar Ru,
the refined Ru,
and the great Ru.
Ears not hearing learning,
actions without correct righteousness,
confusedly considering wealth and profit as supreme,
this is the vulgar person.
With wide sleeves and broad belt,
roughly imitating the former kings yet sufficient to confuse the age,
methods erroneous and learning mixed,
entirely unaware of modeling on later kings to unify institutions,
unaware of exalting ritual righteousness and reducing the "Shī" and "Shū",
his clothing, cap, speech, and actions are already identical with the common customs,
yet unaware of their faults.
In speech and discussion, already no different from Lǎo Zǐ and Mò Zǐ,
yet unaware of the distinction.
This is the vulgar Ru.
Modeling on the former kings,
unifying institutions,
speech and actions having great standards,
yet his clarity cannot aid where the laws and teachings do not reach,
where hearing and sight have not arrived,
knowing what is known,
not knowing what is unknown,
inwardly not deceiving himself,
outwardly not deceiving others,
thereby respecting the worthy and revering laws,
and not daring to be negligent or arrogant.
This is the refined Ru.
Modeling on the former kings, following ritual righteousness,
using the shallow to grasp the broad,
using the one to manage the ten thousand.
If there is the category of benevolence and righteousness,
even among birds and beasts, it is like distinguishing black and white.
Strange things and bizarre changes,
never before heard or seen,
suddenly arising in one place,
then he raises the guiding category to respond to it,
without doubt,
takes the law and measures it,
seamlessly as if tallying tally and tally.
This is the great Ru.
Therefore, if a ruler uses the vulgar person,
then a state of ten thousand chariots perishes.
If using the vulgar Ru,
then a state of ten thousand chariots survives.
If using the refined Ru,
then a state of a thousand lǐ is secure.
If using the great Ru,
then a hundred lǐ of land lasts long,
and after three years,
the world becomes one,
the feudal lords become ministers.
Using a state of ten thousand chariots, then actions and halts are settled
within a single morning.
The "Shī" says:
"Zhōu, though an old state,
its mandate is renewed."
King Wén may also be called a great Ru.
5.6 King Chéng of Chǔ was reading in the hall,
while Lún Biǎn was below,
rose and asked:
"May I ask what book Your Majesty is reading?"
King Chéng said:
"The books of the former sages."
Lún Biǎn said:
"This is truly the dregs of the former sage kings.
Not the essence."
King Chéng said:
"How do you say that?"
Lún Biǎn said:
"By my wheel-making, I say it.
Using compasses to make circles,
squares to make angles,
this can be handed down to sons and grandsons.
But joining three pieces of wood into one,
responding to the mind,
moving with the body,
that cannot be transmitted.
Thus, all that is transmitted is truly the dregs."
Therefore, the methods of Táng and Yú can be examined.
But their enlightenment of the human mind cannot be reached.
The "Shī" says:
"The workings of high heaven,
are without sound, without smell."
Who can reach it?
5.7 Confucius learned to play the zither from Master Xiāngzǐ but did not progress.
Master Xiāngzǐ said:
"You may advance now."
Confucius replied:
"I have mastered the melody,
but not the technique yet."
After some time,
he said:
"You may advance now."
Confucius said:
"I have mastered the technique,
but not the meaning yet."
After some time,
he said again:
"You may advance now."
Confucius said:
"I have perceived the composer,
but not his essence yet."
After some time,
he said:
"Gazing distantly,
vast and majestic,
this music must have been composed by him.
Silent in thought,
solemn and reflective,
to rule the world,
and receive homage from feudal lords -
could this be none other than King Wén?"
Master Xiāngzǐ rose from his mat and bowed twice, saying:
"Excellent!
I believe this is indeed King Wén's composition."
Thus through King Wén's music,
Confucius understood King Wén's character.
Master Xiāngzǐ asked:
"May I ask how you knew this was King Wén's composition?"
Confucius replied:
"Well.
The benevolent prefer grandeur,
the harmonious prefer elegance,
the wise prefer subtlety,
and the earnest prefer beauty.
Thus I knew it was King Wén's composition."
The Tradition says:
He who comprehends the root through hearing the branches -
is a sage.
5.8 When Zhòu was ruler,
he exhausted the people's strength,
imposed cruel decrees
upon the common people,
and inflicted harsh punishments
upon his ministers.
His subordinates distrusted him,
the people hated and resented him,
so the world rebelled and wished to serve King Wén instead -
this was Zhòu's own doing.
Though honored as Son of Heaven,
and possessing all under heaven,
when Zhōu's army arrived, none around him would obey his orders -
how tragic!
At that time,
even wishing to be a commoner
was impossible.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven appointed the Yin heir,
yet he failed to rule the four quarters."
5.9 Though the five colors are bright,
they sometimes fade.
Luxuriant trees
sometimes shed their leaves.
All things have growth and decay,
none remains constant.
Thus the way of the Three Sovereigns
cycles and begins anew,
exhaustion leads to returning to the root -
not merely for the sake of change,
but to stop evil and support the weak,
correct errors and eliminate wrongs,
harmonize yin and yang,
and accord with what suits all things.
The Book of Songs says:
"Diligent is our king,
governing the four quarters."
5.10 Ritual embodies the form of heaven and earth,
and provides regulation according to human feelings. Teachers are those who correct ritual.
Without ritual,
how can one rectify oneself?
Without teachers,
how can one know what is proper in ritual?
Following what ritual prescribes
means feelings are at peace with ritual.
Saying what the teacher says
means knowledge follows the teacher.
When feelings accept ritual
and knowledge follows the teacher,
this is the way of the gentleman.
When words accord with principles
and actions accord with reason,
the world will be orderly.
The Book of Songs says:
"Without knowledge or awareness,
following Heaven's rule."
5.11 If superiors do not know filial piety,
the people will not know to return to fundamentals.
If rulers do not respect elders,
the people will not value kinship.
If ancestral sacrifices lack reverence,
and mountains and rivers are neglected in season,
the people will have nothing to revere.
Punishing without teaching,
the people will not understand encouragement.
Thus when gentlemen cultivate themselves and practice filial piety,
the people will not rebel.
When reverence and filial piety reach below,
the people will know kindness and love.
When likes and dislikes are made clear to the people,
those below will respond to their superiors like shadow and echo.
This is the essential method to
govern the world,
stabilize the realm,
and make all surnames submit -
what enlightened kings and sage rulers cannot abandon for a moment.
The Book of Songs says:
"King Chéng's sincerity
is a model for the world.
Ever speaking of filial thought,
filial thought is the rule."
5.12 During King Chéng's time,
three rice seedlings grew through a mulberry tree,
producing a single ear,
large enough to nearly fill a cart,
long enough to fill a box.
King Chéng asked Duke Zhōu:
"What is this thing?"
Duke Zhōu replied:
"Three seedlings producing one ear
suggests the world will likely become unified."
Within about three years,
envoys from Yuècháng came through nine translations,
presenting white pheasants to Duke Zhōu:
"The road is long,
mountains and rivers deep and obscure.
Fearing our messengers might not reach you,
we came through repeated translations."
Duke Zhōu asked:
"For what am I granted this gift?"
The interpreter said:
"I received orders from our country's elders:
'For long, heaven has sent no violent storms or torrential rains,
the seas have shown no waves or flooding -
three years it has been thus.
Does the Middle Kingdom perhaps have a sage?
Why not go and pay homage?'
Thus we have come."
Duke Zhōu then respectfully sought the reason for their coming.
The Book of Songs says:
"For ten thousand years,
will there not be support?"
5.13 The pleasure of climbing high and overlooking depths,
of seeing far -
towers and pavilions cannot match the height seen from hills.
The pleasure of viewing broadly
on open plains -
ponds and pools cannot match the breadth seen from rivers and marshes.
Laboring the mind and toiling in thought,
indulging desires to the extreme,
wasting wealth and injuring feelings,
destroying reputation and shortening life -
how sorrowful and damaging!
When poor rulers act contrary to this way, they trouble the people.
The Book of Songs says:
"God is unpredictable,
and the common people are exhausted."
5.14 The Rú is soft.
Rú means yielding,
an unchanging method.
Through thousands of actions and myriad changes,
its way never exhausts -
such are the Six Classics.
As for the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
the order among friends -
these are what the Rú carefully uphold,
daily polishing without cease.
Though dwelling in poor alleys and humble huts,
with insufficient food inside
and inadequate clothing outside,
without land enough to stick an awl -
their clear understanding can sustain the world.
Greatly employed above others,
they become material for kings and dukes;
modestly employed in office,
they become ministers to the altars of soil and grain.
Though living in cliffs and caves, kings and marquises cannot contend with their reputation -
why?
Because the transformation of benevolence and righteousness remains.
If kings would listen to their words
and trust their actions,
then the laws of Yáo and Shùn could be seen, and odes of praise could be heard.
The Book of Songs says:
"The ancients had a saying:
Consult the grass and firewood gatherers."
This illustrates the importance of seeking broad counsel.
5.15 The tradition states:
The Son of Heaven dwells beneath vast mansions,
within curtains and canopies,
upon felt cushions,
wearing embroidered slippers,
his gaze not extending beyond the threshold,
yet comprehending all under heaven effortlessly,
because he has worthy attendants.
Thus, seeing alone is not as clear as seeing with the multitude;
hearing alone is not as sharp as hearing with the multitude;
deliberating alone is not as skillful as deliberating with the multitude.
Therefore, the enlightened king causes worthy ministers
to converge and advance together,
thereby connecting with fairness and attracting reclusive scholars.
The Book of Songs says:
"The ancients had a saying:
Consult the grass and firewood gatherers."
This is what it means.
5.16 Heaven established its height,
and the sun and moon bring brightness.
Earth established its thickness,
and mountains and hills bring renown.
The ruler establishes the Way,
and all affairs attain order.
Since the decline and collapse of the Zhōu,
the Kingly Way has been abandoned and not revived,
ritual and righteousness severed and not continued.
During the Qín era,
they rejected ritual and righteousness,
discarded the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
neglected antiquity,
greatly destroyed the sagely Way,
indulged in recklessness and deceit,
made greed for profit the custom,
and promoted hunting as culture,
leading to great chaos under heaven.
Then armies rose and fires ignited,
people were exposed and homeless,
and the populace became accustomed to invasion, plunder, and mutual seizure,
far removed from the glorious achievements of the sage kings for so long,
they had never witnessed the path of benevolence and righteousness,
nor experienced the influence of ritual and music.
Hence, they became boorish, stubborn, and ill-mannered,
while solemn respect daily diminished,
declining to the point of intimidation by might,
recklessly becoming sycophants,
not avoiding disaster and peril,
this is why they were difficult to govern.
Humans have six emotions:
the eyes desire to see beautiful colors,
the ears desire to hear harmonious music,
the nose desires to smell fragrances,
the mouth desires to taste sweet flavors,
the body and limbs desire comfort without toil,
and clothing desires to be embroidered, light, and warm.
These six
are the six emotions of the people.
Neglecting them leads to chaos,
following them leads to harmony.
Therefore, when the sage kings taught their people,
they necessarily regulated these emotions with ritual,
and controlled their desires with righteousness.
Righteousness is simple yet complete,
ritual is easy yet lawful,
not far from human emotions,
so the people followed commands swiftly.
Confucius, knowing the Way is easy to practice, said:
"The Book of Songs states:
'Enlightening the people is very easy.'
These are not empty words."
5.17 The nature of a cocoon is to become silk,
but without a woman worker boiling it in hot water,
drawing out its threads,
it does not become silk.
The nature of an egg is to become a chick,
but without a good hen brooding and nurturing it,
over many days,
it does not become a chick.
Human nature is good,
but without an enlightened king or sage ruler to support,
and guide it with the Way,
it does not become that of a noble person.
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitude,
their nature is not constant,
all have a beginning,
but few can maintain it to the end."
This means only an enlightened king or sage ruler can make them so.
5.18 One whose wisdom is like a fountainhead,
and whose conduct can serve as a model,
is a teacher of others.
One whose wisdom can sharpen others,
and whose conduct can assist and support,
is a friend of others.
One who adheres to laws and duties,
and dares not do wrong,
is an official of others.
One who seeks immediate pleasure,
and responds with quick obedience,
is a servant of others.
Thus, the superior ruler employs teachers as aides,
the middling ruler employs friends as aides,
the inferior ruler employs officials as aides,
and the ruler facing peril and ruin employs servants as aides.
It is said:
"In deep and broad waters, the fish are large;
under an enlightened ruler, the ministers are wise."
Mutual observation and shared aspirations
must come from within.
Thus, those with the same brightness see each other,
those with the same sound hear each other,
those with the same will follow each other,
for none but the worthy can employ the worthy.
Therefore, the assistants and attendants,
those appointed and employed,
hold the key to survival or demise,
and the crux of gain or loss.
Can one not be cautious?
The Book of Songs says:
"If your virtue is not bright,
there will be none behind or beside you;
if your virtue is not enlightened,
you will have no companions or ministers."
5.19 In the past, Yǔ ruled Xià and became king,
while Jié ruled Xià and brought its ruin.
Tāng ruled Yīn and became king,
while Zhòu ruled Yīn and brought its ruin.
Thus, there is no eternally secure state,
nor people inherently easy to govern;
obtaining the worthy leads to prosperity,
while having the unworthy leads to ruin.
From ancient times to the present,
this has never been otherwise.
A clear mirror is for reflecting form,
the past is for understanding the present.
To know the reasons for the peril and ruin of the past,
yet not follow the ways that ensured safety and survival,
is no different from walking backward while trying to catch up with those ahead.
A common saying goes:
"If you do not know how to be an official,
look at accomplished affairs."
Some say:
"If the front carriage overturns and the rear carriage does not take warning,
the rear carriage will also overturn."
Thus, what caused Xià's ruin was practiced by Yīn,
and what caused Yīn's ruin was practiced by Zhōu.
Therefore, Yīn could take warning from Xià,
and Zhōu could take warning from Yīn.
The Book of Songs says:
"The mirror of Yīn is not far;
it is in the age of the Xià sovereign."
5.20 The tradition states:
An arrogant and excessive ruler has few loyal followers,
a person of empty promises rarely keeps faith.
Thus, a tree that fills the hand has no branches as thick as arms,
and the waters of a small marsh have no fish that can swallow boats.
Shallow roots lead to short branches and leaves,
a severed trunk leads to withered branches and leaves.
The Book of Songs says:
"The branches and leaves are unharmed,
but the root is already destroyed."
Fortune and misfortune come from oneself.
5.21 When waters are deep and vast,
dragons and fish are born there.
When mountains and forests are lush,
birds and beasts gather there.
When ritual and righteousness are cultivated and clear,
noble persons are drawn there.
Thus, when ritual reaches the individual, conduct is cultivated;
when ritual reaches the state, governance is clear.
If one can support oneself with ritual,
a noble reputation naturally spreads,
all under heaven submit,
orders are carried out and prohibitions heeded,
and the tasks of a king are complete.
The Book of Songs says:
"With upright virtue,
all states submit to it."
This is what it means.
5.22 Confucius said:
The art of persuasion
requires dignity to establish it,
sincerity to handle it,
firmness to maintain it,
analogies and references to illustrate it,
division and clarity to explain it,
joy and fragrance to convey it,
treasuring it, valuing it,
honoring it, revering it;
if so, persuasion will always be effective.
This is called being able to honor what is honorable.
As for theories without categories,
actions without form,
and words without substance,
the noble person is cautious of them.
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not lightly change your words,
do not say 'it is merely so'."
5.23 When the common people have no lack of food within,
and no suffering from cold without,
then they can be taught and guided with ritual and righteousness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Present them to the ancestral grandparents,
to harmonize all rituals."
When all rituals are harmonized, all intentions are fulfilled;
when all intentions are fulfilled, yin and yang are balanced;
when yin and yang are balanced, cold and heat are regulated;
when cold and heat are regulated, the three lights are clear;
when the three lights are clear, wind and rain are timely;
when wind and rain are timely, all living beings are tranquil.
Thus, the Way of Heaven is attained.
Therefore, one does not leave the door yet knows the world;
one does not peer through the window yet sees the Way of Heaven.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only this sage,
can see a hundred miles ahead."
"Oh, brilliant royal troops,
nourish and bide your time in obscurity."
This speaks of mutual nourishment reaching to obscurity.
5.24 Heaven has four seasons—
spring, summer, autumn, winter—
wind, rain, frost, dew—
all are teachings.
When clarity and brightness reside in one's person,
one's spirit and will are like the divine;
when desires are about to arise,
there must be an opening beforehand;
when Heaven sends timely rain,
mountains and rivers produce clouds.
The Book of Songs says:
"High are the sacred mountains,
soaring to the heavens.
The sacred mountains send down spirits,
giving birth to Fǔ and Shēn.
It is Shēn and Fǔ
who are the pillars of Zhōu.
They guard the four states,
and proclaim throughout the four quarters."
This is the virtue of King Wén and King Wǔ.
5.25 The kings of the three dynasties
always first established their good reputation.
The Book of Songs says:
"Brilliant Son of Heaven,
your good fame is unceasing.
You display your civil virtue,
harmonizing these four states."
This is the virtue of King Tài.
5.26 Indigo has blue,
and silk borrows from it to become bluer than indigo.
Earth has yellow,
and silk borrows from it to become yellower than earth.
Indigo blue and earth yellow
can still be borrowed.
How much more so
can benevolence and righteousness be borrowed?
In the Eastern Sea, there is a fish called flounder,
which swims side by side;
without mutual cooperation, they cannot proceed.
In the North, there is an animal called lóu,
which alternates eating and watching;
without mutual cooperation, they cannot be full.
In the South, there is a bird called jiān,
which flies wing to wing;
without mutual cooperation, they cannot rise.
In the West, there is an animal called jué,
with front legs like a rat's,
and hind legs like a rabbit's;
when it finds sweet grass, it must carry it to give to qióngqióngjùxū;
its nature is not inherently that of qióngqióngjùxū,
but it does so for the sake of borrowing.
If even birds, beasts, and fish borrow from each other,
how much more should the lord of ten thousand chariots?
If he alone does not know to borrow the heroes and talented scholars of the world to be his companions,
is that not a fault?
Therefore it is said:
When brightness supports brightness,
they ascend to heaven.
When brightness supports darkness,
it returns to the person.
When two blind men support each other,
if they do not injure themselves on walls or trees,
or fall into wells
or traps,
it is their fortune.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only those who are disobedient,
go to gather filth."
This is walking in darkness.
5.27 Blessings arise from non-action,
while calamities arise from excessive desires.
Knowing contentment,
then wealth follows.
When virtue suits ruling others,
then honor follows.
Thus, those who value rank but disdain virtue,
even if they become the Son of Heaven,
are not honored.
Those who covet things and do not know when to stop,
even if they possess the world,
are not wealthy.
What the land produces does not increase,
what mountains and marshes yield is finite;
harboring an insatiable heart while seeking things that do not increase,
clinging to a hundredfold desire while seeking finite wealth—
this is why Jié and Zhòu lost their positions.
The Book of Songs says:
"The great wind has its path,
greedy men ruin their kind."
5.28 Duke Āi asked Zǐxià:
"Must one learn before one can bring peace to the state and protect the people?"
Zǐxià said:
"There has never been one who could bring peace to the state and protect the people without learning."
Duke Āi said:
"Then did the Five Emperors have teachers?"
Zǐxià said:
"I have heard that Huángdì studied with Dàfén,
Zhuānxū studied with Lùtú,
Emperor Kù studied with Chìsōngzǐ,
Yáo studied with Wùchéngzǐ Fù,
Shùn studied with Yǐnshòu,
Yǔ studied with Xīwángguó,
Tāng studied with Dàihū Xiàng,
King Wén studied with Xīchóuzǐ Sī,
King Wǔ studied with Tàigōng,
Zhōugōng studied with Guóshū,
and Zhòngní studied with Lǎodān.
These eleven sages,
had they not encountered these teachers,
could not have made their achievements known to the world,
nor could their names have been passed down to later generations."
The Book of Songs says:
"Without error, without forgetfulness,
follow the old statutes."
5.29 Virtue—
it encompasses the vastness of heaven and earth,
matches the brightness of sun and moon,
stands through the cycle of the four seasons,
presides over the interaction of yin and yang.
Cold and heat cannot shake it,
the four seasons cannot transform it.
Gathered in the great yin, it is not damp;
dispersed in the great yang, it is not withered.
Fresh, pure, clear, and bright, it is complete;
stern, majestic, resolute, and swift, it is divine.
The most essential and wondrous thing between heaven and earth
is virtue.
Who but the sage can attain this!
The Book of Songs says:
"Virtue is light as a hair,
yet few can lift it."
5.30 As in a year of drought,
the grass does not flourish.
But when Heaven suddenly raises clouds,
and rain falls abundantly,
then all things without exception revive.
It is not that people lack benevolence and righteousness rooted in their hearts,
but kingly governance is suppressed and cannot be seen.
Depressed and unable to emerge,
the sage king is over there in his straw sandals.
Though he does not look beyond his gate,
the world follows him;
when he leads, the world harmonizes.
How can one here respond to this?
The Book of Songs says:
"As in that year of drought,
the grass did not flourish."
5.31 What is the Way?
It is said:
What the ruler follows.
What is a ruler?
It is said:
He is the multitude,
he who removes harm for all things under heaven
is called a ruler.
What is a king?
It is said:
He is the one who goes.
When all under heaven go to him, he is called a king.
It is said:
Those who excel at nurturing life,
are thus revered by others.
Those who excel at governing people through debate,
are thus pacified by others.
Those who excel at establishing prominence in others,
are thus befriended by others.
Those who excel at embellishing others,
are thus delighted by others.
When these four essentials are all present,
the world turns to them.
When not even one of the four essentials exists,
the world abandons them.
Those to whom the world turns are called kings,
those whom the world abandons are called ruined.
Hence it is said: if the Way exists, the state exists;
if the Way perishes, the state perishes.
To reduce artisans and merchants,
increase farmers,
guard against thieves and robbers,
and eliminate the treacherous and evil,
these are the means to nurture and sustain them.
The Son of Heaven and the Three Dukes,
the feudal lords and their single chancellor,
the grand masters holding official positions,
the scholars preserving their duties,
all without exception govern and manage,
this is the means to debate and govern them.
Determine rank based on virtue,
assign office according to ability,
appoint the worthy as the Three Dukes,
appoint the worthy as feudal lords,
the next level as grand masters,
this is the means to embellish them.
Thus from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
none fail to acclaim their abilities,
attain their intentions,
and find joy and peace in their tasks,
this is what is shared by all.
As for layering colors to form patterns,
accumulating flavors to prepare delicacies,
these are what the sage uses to distinguish the worthy from the foolish,
and clarify the noble and the base.
Therefore, when the Way is attained, blessings flow to all living beings,
and fortune returns to the kings and dukes.
Blessings flowing to all living beings brings peace and harmony below,
fortune returning to the kings and dukes brings honor and glory above.
The common people all cherish peace and harmony in their hearts,
and delight in supporting their superiors,
this is called good governance below and communication above.
Good governance below and communication above
is the reason why songs of praise arise.
The Book of Songs says:
"Blessings descend abundant and vast,
Dignified and solemn the rites.
When drunk and sated,
Fortune and prosperity come in return."
5.32 The sage nurtures one nature to control the vital energy,
holds to one destiny to moderate flavors,
comprehensively governs the world,
not neglecting even the small,
preserving his essence and spirit,
to replenish his center,
such a person is called a scholar.
5.33 Scholars at court seek emolument,
thus they enter but do not leave.
Scholars in the mountains and forests seek fame,
thus they go but do not return.
To enter and also be able to leave,
to go and also be able to return,
moving freely with constancy,
is sageliness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Not contentious, not hasty,
Not rigid, not soft."
This speaks of attaining the mean.
5.34 Confucius was sitting in attendance with Jìsūn,
when Jìsūn's steward Tōng said:
"The ruler sends someone to borrow a horse,
should we give it to him?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that when a ruler takes from his minister, it is called taking,
not called borrowing."
Jìsūn understood,
informed steward Tōng,
saying:
"From now on,
when the ruler takes something, call it taking,
do not say borrow."
Confucius corrected the words about borrowing a horse,
and the principle between ruler and minister was established.
The Analects says:
"It is indeed necessary to rectify names."
The Book of Songs says:
"The gentleman does not lightly utter words."
6.1 Bǐgān remonstrated and died.
Jīzǐ said:
"To speak knowing it will not be used,
is foolish.
To sacrifice one's life to expose the ruler's faults,
is disloyal.
Both are unacceptable,
yet he still did it,
there is no greater inauspiciousness."
Then he loosened his hair and pretended madness before leaving.
The gentleman heard of this and said:
"How arduous for Jīzǐ!
He exhausted his essence and spirit,
spent his loyalty and love.
Seeing Bǐgān's affair, he preserved his own life,
the pinnacle of benevolence and wisdom."
The Book of Songs says:
"There is a saying among people,
No wise man is without folly."
6.2 Duke Huán of Qí went to see a minor official,
but after three visits still could not meet him.
His attendants said:
"That minor official is a lowly servant of the state.
You have gone three times and still cannot see him,
you can stop now."
Duke Huán said:
"Alas!
What kind of talk is this?
I have heard that
a scholar in common cloth,
if he does not desire wealth and honor,
will not demean himself before the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
The ruler of ten thousand chariots,
if he does not love benevolence and righteousness,
will not demean himself before a scholar in common cloth.
Even if the master does not desire wealth and honor, that is acceptable,
but if I do not love benevolence and righteousness, that is unacceptable."
After five visits, he finally met him.
When the feudal lords of the world heard of this,
they said Duke Huán even humbled himself before a scholar in common cloth,
how much more would he do for a ruler of a state?
Thereupon they came to pay homage one after another,
with none failing to arrive.
The reason Duke Huán was able to nine times assemble the feudal lords,
and once rectify the world,
was this.
The Book of Songs says:
"With upright virtue and conduct,
the four states submit to him."
6.3 Reward the diligent and punish the indolent,
then the people will not be negligent.
Listen broadly and see clearly,
then the world will turn to you.
Then clarify their duties and responsibilities,
examine their work and achievements,
compare their official capabilities,
all without exception follow the law,
then the public way is reached and private gates are blocked,
public righteousness is established and private affairs cease.
Thus the substantial and sincere are advanced,
and the flattering and sycophantic are stopped,
the greedy and cruel are dismissed,
and the honest and principled arise.
The Zhou system says:
"Those who act ahead of time—death without pardon.
Those who fail to act in time—death without pardon."
People become accustomed to affairs and thereby adapt,
the employment of people in tasks,
is like the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth which cannot be interchanged.
Therefore it is said:
when duties are divided, the people are not negligent;
when ranks are fixed, order is not chaotic;
when listening broadly and seeing clearly, all affairs are not滞留.
Thus all the numerous officials below,
none fail to cultivate themselves,
and only then dare to settle into office.
Only after achieving capability dare they accept their positions.
Petty men change their hearts,
the common people change their customs,
and all kinds of treacherous and wicked return to honesty.
This is the ultimate in governance and education,
beyond which nothing can be added.
The Book of Songs says:
"Great plans determine the mandate,
Far-reaching strategies are timely announced.
Respectful and cautious in dignity and demeanor,
They are the model for the people."
6.4 Zǐlù governed Pú for three years,
Confucius passed through,
and upon entering the borders praised it,
saying:
"Excellent!
Yóu! You are reverent and respectful, and trustworthy."
Entering the city,
he said:
"Excellent!
Yóu! You are loyal and trustworthy, and generous."
Arriving at the courtyard,
he said:
"Excellent!
Yóu indeed! Discerning and decisive in judgment."
Zǐgòng, holding the reins, asked:
"Master, you have not witnessed Yóu's
governance, yet praise him thrice—
may I hear the reason?"
Confucius replied:
"I have observed his governance. Entering his territory,
the fields are fully cultivated,
and weeds thoroughly cleared.
This shows reverence and trustworthiness,
hence his people exert their strength.
Entering his town,
the walls and houses are well-maintained,
and trees lush.
This reflects loyalty, trust, and magnanimity,
so his people are not negligent.
In his courtyard,
it is very orderly,
thus demonstrating discernment and decisiveness, and the people are not disturbed."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Rise early and retire late,
sweep and clean the courtyard."
6.5 In ancient times, there were appointed commoners.
Those among the people who could respect elders, pity orphans,
choose yielding over contention, and labor diligently in affairs
were commended to their ruler,
after which they could ride in adorned carriages with paired horses.
Those not appointed were forbidden to ride them;
unauthorized use of adorned carriages or paired horses
incurred punishment.
Thus, even if people had surplus wealth and luxuries,
without ritual righteousness, merit, or virtue,
these were of no use.
Therefore, all promoted benevolence and righteousness while disdaining wealth and profit.
Disdaining wealth and profit prevented contention;
without contention, the strong would not oppress the weak,
nor the many abuse the few.
This is how the ruler modeled laws and punishments,
and the people did not break the law.
When people do not break the law,
chaos thereby ceases.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Steady your people,
carefully observe your lordly duties,
to guard against the unforeseen."
6.6 In debates under heaven,
there are three ultimate points and five victories,
yet rhetoric is placed below.
The debater distinguishes different categories,
preventing mutual harm,
orders divergent views,
preventing contradiction,
conveys public understanding,
clarifies intentions,
enabling others to foresee,
not seeking to confuse.
Thus, the victor does not lose his stance,
the defeated gains what he sought,
so debate is worth observing.
Using elaborate language to deceive,
ornate words to contradict,
numerous analogies to shift meaning,
alienating others from their own intent—
then clever arguments lead to harm.
Failing to clarify meaning is called obscurity;
avoiding intent and self is called evasion;
subtle insinuations causing missteps are called shifting;
employing fallacious arguments is called recklessness.
These four are not to be done,
so principles can be clearly seen.
Obscurity, evasion, shifting, and recklessness—
contentious words compete until ceasing,
inevitably harming one's character as a noble person,
hence the noble person avoids them.
The *Analects* say:
"The noble person, in speech,
is never reckless."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Do not be careless in speech,
do not say it's reckless."
6.7 I tell you,
to win others' hearts:
do not be arrogant due to high status;
do not obscure others with intelligence and wisdom;
do not bully others with bravery and might;
do not deceive others with quick wit and agility.
If incapable, then learn;
if ignorant, then ask.
Even if knowledgeable, be humble—
then it is true wisdom.
Before a ruler, observe the duties of a subject;
outside one's village, observe the rites of elder and younger;
before elders, observe the conduct of a disciple;
with peers, observe the ways of friendship;
with the young and lowly, practice guidance and generosity.
Thus, there is none not loved,
none not respected,
no contention with others,
vast as heaven and earth embracing all things.
Thus,
the old are content,
the young are cherished,
friends are trusted.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Kind to friends,
to the common people and youth,
descendants continuous,
all people follow."
6.8 The benevolent necessarily respect others.
Respecting others has its way:
towards the worthy, love and respect them;
towards the unworthy, keep distant yet respect them.
The respect is the same,
the feelings differ.
As for loyalty, trustworthiness, integrity, and harmlessness,
in all interactions, it should be so—
this is the essence of benevolence.
With benevolence as essence,
righteousness as principle,
every word can be a model for others.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Without error or harm,
rarely not taken as a rule."
6.9 The Master said:
"To love thinking without learning,
even if knowledgeable, it is not broad.
To learn but neglect self-cultivation,
even if learned, it is not respected.
Without sincerity to establish oneself,
even if established, it does not last.
Sincerity not yet evident but fond of speech,
even if spoken, it is not believed.
Fine talent,
yet unaware of the noble person's way,
ignoring small matters to harm greater ones—
disaster will surely reach oneself."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"How can they be good?
Together they will drown."
6.10 The people, wearied, think of ease;
under tyranny, they think of benevolence;
in peril of punishment, they think of safety;
with state chaos, they think of heaven.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"They have no strength,
to think of the vast heavens."
6.11 The questioner asked:
"In ancient times, those who understood the Way were called Xiānshēng—
why?"
It means "first awakened."
Those unaware of the Way and methods
are blind to gain and loss.
Not knowing the causes of chaos,
they are dazed as if drunk. Thus, rulers include the first-awakened,
the later-awakened,
and the unawakened.
Once, King Zhuāng of Chǔ, though his plans were fitting,
sat with a worried expression.
Shēngōng Wūchén asked:
'Why is the king worried?'
King Zhuāng said:
'I hear that among feudal lords' virtues,
those who can select teachers become kings;
those who can choose friends become hegemons;
those who associate with inferiors perish.
With my lack of virtue,
none of my ministers' counsel surpasses me—
hence my worry.'
King Zhuāng's virtue suited ruling people,
his awed the feudal lords,
yet he was daily fearful,
seeking wise aides—
this is the first-awakened.
Once, Duke Zhāo of Sòng fled exile,
telling his charioteer:
'I know why I fell.'
The charioteer asked:
'Why?'
Duke Zhāo said:
'Dressed in finery, standing,
attended by dozens of servants,
all called me majestic.
In speech and action,
with hundreds of courtiers,
all called me sage.
I saw no faults inside or out—
thus I fell.'
Thereupon, he changed conduct,
embraced righteousness and practiced the Way,
and within two years, his virtue was renowned in Sòng.
The people welcomed and restored him,
posthumously named Zhāo.
This is the later-awakened.
Long ago, Lord Jìngguō left the city walls,
and said to his charioteer:
"I am thirsty and wish to drink."
The charioteer presented clear wine.
He said:
"I am hungry and wish to eat."
The charioteer presented dried meat and millet provisions.
He said:
"How is it that you are so prepared?"
The charioteer said:
"I have stored these for a long time."
He said:
"Why did you store them?"
The charioteer said:
"For when you, my lord, would flee and suffer hunger and thirst on the road."
He said:
"You knew that I was about to flee?"
The charioteer said:
"Indeed."
He said:
"Why did you not remonstrate with me?"
The charioteer said:
"You, my lord, delight in flattering words and detest straightforward advice.
I wished to offer remonstration,
but feared I would perish before the city's fall,
and therefore did not remonstrate."
Lord Jìngguō changed countenance and angrily said:
"The reason for my flight—
what truly is it?"
The charioteer shifted his words, saying:
"The reason for your flight, my lord,
is because you are too virtuous."
He said:
"That a virtuous man should flee rather than preserve himself—
why is that?"
The charioteer said:
"The world lacks virtue, and you alone are virtuous,
therefore you fled."
Leaning on the carriage rail, he sighed, saying:
"Alas!
Is this how one who loses virtuous men ends up?"
Thereupon, his body wearied and strength dissipated,
he lay down with his head on the charioteer's knee.
The charioteer stealthily replaced it with a preparation,
and slipped away.
His body died in the wilderness,
eaten by tigers and wolves.
This is the case of one who does not awaken.
Thus, those who awaken early
become hegemons in their time,
as King Zhuāng of Chǔ was.
Those who awaken later,
return after three years,
as Duke Zhāo of Sòng was.
Those who do not awaken,
die in the wilderness,
eaten by tigers and wolves,
as Lord Jìngguō was."
There are those who awaken early,
those who awaken later,
and those who do not awaken.
The Book of Songs says:
"To plausible words they respond;
to admonitions they are as if drunk."
6.12 Tián Cháng assassinated Duke Jiǎn,
then made a pact with the people of the state, saying:
"Those who do not pledge will die along with their families."
Shí Tuō said:
"In ancient times, those who served their lord
died for their lord's affairs.
To abandon one's lord to preserve one's parents
is not loyalty.
To abandon one's parents to die for one's lord's affairs
is not filial piety.
I, Tuō, cannot do either.
Yet not pledging would mean the death of my parents,
while following others to pledge
is to betray my lord.
Alas!
Born in a chaotic age, one cannot act rightly;
coerced by violent men,
one cannot preserve righteousness.
How sorrowful!"
Thereupon he came forward to pledge and save his parents,
then withdrew and fell on his sword to die for his lord.
Those who heard of it said:
"A true gentleman!
He accepted his fate."
The Book of Songs says:
"There is a saying among people:
In advance and retreat, it's all precarious."
This refers to Master Shí.
6.13 The Book of Changes says:
"Beset by rocks,
resting on thorns,
entering his house,
he does not see his wife.
Inauspicious."
This speaks of being beset and not resting on worthy men.
Long ago, Duke Mù of Qín was beset at Xiáo,
but quickly relied on Five Rams Grandee,
Jiǎn Shū, and Gōngsūn Yǒu to become a minor hegemon.
Duke Wén of Jìn was beset by the Lí clan,
but quickly relied on Jiù Fàn,
Zhào Cuī, and Jièzǐ Tuī to become ruler.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè was beset at Kuàijī,
but quickly relied on Fàn Lǐ and Grandee Zhǒng to become hegemon in the southern states.
Duke Huán of Qí was beset at Chángsháo,
but quickly relied on Guǎn Zhòng, Níng Qī, and Xí Péng to rectify the world.
These all were beset but knew to quickly rely on worthy men.
To be beset and not know to quickly rely on worthy men, yet not perish—
this has never happened.
The Book of Songs says:
"When men are lost,
the state is stricken."
This speaks of having no good men.
6.14 Mencius spoke to King Xuān of Qí but pleased him not.
Chúnyú Kūn was in attendance.
Mencius said:
"Today I spoke to your lord,
and your lord was not pleased.
Might it be that he does not recognize goodness as goodness?"
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"It is you, Master, who truly lack goodness.
Long ago, Hù Bā played the se and hidden fish emerged to listen;
Bó Yá played the qin and six horses lifted their heads from feeding.
Even fish and horses know goodness as goodness,
how much more so should a ruler?"
Mencius said:
"When thunder and lightning arise,
they split bamboo and break trees,
shaking heaven and earth,
yet cannot make the deaf suddenly hear.
The brightness of sun and moon
illuminates all under heaven,
yet cannot make the blind suddenly see.
Such is your lord now."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Not so.
Long ago, Yī Fēng gave birth to Gāo Shāng,
and the people of Qí became fond of singing.
When the wife of Qǐ Liáng wept in sorrow,
people sang of it.
No sound is too faint not to be heard,
no action too hidden not to take form.
If you, Master, were truly worthy,
yet while dwelling in Lǔ, Lǔ's territory diminished—
why is that?"
Mencius said:
"If worthies are not employed,
how can diminution be avoided?
Fish that swallow boats do not dwell in hidden marshes;
men of measure do not dwell in corrupt ages.
Plants inevitably wither at winter's solstice—
I too have met my time.
The Book of Songs says:
'Not before me,
not after me.'
Have I not encountered an age of withering?"
6.15 Confucius said:
"That which one can discuss all day without tiring—
is it not learning?
One's physical form is not worth admiring,
one's courage and strength are not worth fearing,
one's clan name is not worth praising,
one's ancestors are not worth mentioning—
yet what can make one known throughout the four quarters
and illustrious among the feudal lords—
is it not learning?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Without error, without forgetfulness,
follow the old statutes."
This speaks of learning.
6.16 The Master said:
"Without knowing fate,
one has no means to become a gentleman."
This means that what heaven gives birth to
all possess hearts of humaneness, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and compliance with goodness.
Not knowing what heaven mandates in birth
means lacking hearts of humaneness, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and compliance with goodness.
Lacking hearts of humaneness, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and compliance with goodness
makes one a petty person.
Therefore it is said:
"Without knowing fate,
one has no means to become a gentleman."
The Minor Odes say:
"Heaven protects and sustains you,
making it very firm."
This means that heaven, through humaneness, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom,
protects and sustains people with great firmness.
The "Dàyǎ" says:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitudes of people,
endowing them with substance and principles.
The people uphold the constant norms,
and love this virtuous excellence."
This speaks of the people upholding virtue to emulate Heaven.
If one does not know how to emulate Heaven,
how can one become a gentleman?
6.17 A true king must establish overseers,
appointing two for each region,
to observe from afar and govern the masses.
When the people in distant regions suffer from hunger and cold without clothing or food,
have legal disputes without their injustices being redressed,
or miss worthy individuals without recommending them,
they report to the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven receives their ruler at court,
he greets them with a bow and invites them forward, saying:
"Alas,
could it be that my governance and teachings have failed to reach you?
How is it that there are those suffering from hunger and cold without clothing or food,
those with legal disputes without their injustices being redressed,
and those missing worthy individuals without recommending them?"
Then the ruler withdraws and consults with his ministers and high officials.
When the people in distant regions hear of this,
they all say:
"Truly, he is the Son of Heaven!
Though we dwell in remote places,
he sees us as if we were near;
though we reside in obscurity,
he perceives us with clarity.
How can we deceive him?"
Thus, the overseers serve to open
the four eyes
and connect the four ears.
The "Shī" says:
"Whether the states are well or ill governed,
Zhòng Shānfǔ makes it clear."
This expresses that meaning.
6.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng bared his shoulder,
holding a ceremonial banner in his left hand,
and a ritual knife in his right,
advancing to address King Zhuāng,
saying:
"I, the unworthy one, have incompetent border ministers
who have provoked your great offense,
causing the ruler of your great state to trouble himself
and come so far in humiliation."
King Zhuāng replied:
"A gentleman does not command his ministers
to exchange words lightly,
thus allowing me, the unworthy, to behold your jade-like countenance,
and humbly arrive here."
King Zhuāng accepted the token,
and with a wave of his hand, ordered the Chǔ army to retreat seven lǐ.
General Zǐchóng remonstrated, saying:
"Between Nányǐng and Zhèng,
the distance is several thousand lǐ;
several officers have died,
and hundreds of soldiers have perished.
Now that we have conquered but do not possess it,
are we not wasting the efforts of our people and ministers?"
King Zhuāng said:
"I have heard that in ancient times, if the sheath is not pierced,
and the leather is not moth-eaten,
one does not venture out to the four directions.
Thus, a gentleman values ritual and despises wealth,
seeking the people,
not their land.
If one is told to desist but does not relent,
it is inauspicious.
If I were to establish myself in the world through inauspicious means,
disaster would befall me;
what gain would there be?"
Soon after,
the forces of Jìn coming to rescue Zhèng arrived,
saying:
"We request battle."
King Zhuāng agreed.
General Zǐchóng again remonstrated, saying:
"Jìn
is a powerful state,
with short supply lines and sharp troops,
while the Chǔ army is weary and exhausted.
My lord, you should not agree."
King Zhuāng said:
"It cannot be.
If I avoid the strong
and intimidate the weak,
then I, the unworthy, have no way to establish myself in the world."
So he turned his army to confront the Jìn invaders.
King Zhuāng took up the drumstick and beat the drum himself;
the Jìn army was utterly defeated,
and the fleeing soldiers fought for boats, with fingers piled up enough to be scooped.
King Zhuāng said:
"Alas!
If our two rulers are not on good terms,
what crime have the common people committed!"
He then withdrew the Chǔ army to let the Jìn invaders escape.
The "Shī" says:
"He does not swallow the soft,
nor spit out the hard."
6.19 A gentleman esteems others' virtues
and praises others' merits,
but this is not flattery.
Speaking uprightly and acting directly,
pointing out others' faults,
is not slander or fault-finding.
Yielding and compliant,
firm and resolute,
moving with all things in circulation,
his virtue does not stray outward.
The "Shī" says:
"He does not swallow the soft,
nor spit out the hard,
does not bully the widowed or orphaned,
nor fears the strong and oppressive."
6.20 Duke Líng of Wèi rose after a daytime nap,
his spirit and energy much declined,
and sent a messenger galloping to summon the warrior Gōngsūn Yuān.
On the way, he met the messenger Bǔ Shāng.
Bǔ Shāng asked:
"Why are you in such a hurry?"
The messenger replied:
"The duke rose from a daytime nap
and ordered me to summon the warrior Gōngsūn Yuān."
Zǐxià said:
"If not Yuān himself,
would someone as brave as Yuān suffice?"
The driver said:
"Yes."
Zǐxià said:
"Take me back with you."
Upon arrival,
the duke said:
"I sent you to summon a warrior;
why have you brought a scholar?"
The messenger said:
"The messenger said:
'If not Yuān himself,
would someone as brave as Yuān suffice?'
I said:
'Yes.'
So I brought him along."
The duke said:
"Very well,
invite the master up.
Quickly summon Gōngsūn Yuān."
When he arrived,
he entered with a sword in hand, shouting loudly,
saying:
"Shāng, come down!
I'll preserve your head."
Zǐxià turned and rebuked him sharply,
saying:
"Halt!
Sheathe your sword.
I will discuss courage with you."
Thereupon, the duke ordered him to sheathe his sword and come forward.
Zǐxià said:
"Come!
I once accompanied you following our lord westward to meet Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào.
Jiǎnzǐ met our lord with disheveled hair and a spear in hand.
I, from behind the thirteen rows of attendants,
hurried forward and said:
'When feudal lords meet,
it is improper not to wear court attire.
If you do not wear court attire,
I, the messenger Bǔ Shāng, will stain your robes with the blood from my neck.'
Who made him change into court attire to meet our lord?
Was it you or I?"
Yuān said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià said:
"In courage, you are not as good as me by one measure.
Again, I accompanied you following our lord east to Ē,
where we encountered the ruler of Qí seated on double-layered mats.
Our lord sat on a single mat.
I, from behind the thirteen rows of attendants,
hurried forward and said:
'By ritual,
when feudal lords meet,
they should not face each other with disparity in status.'
Who lifted one of the mats and removed it?
Was it you or I?"
Yuān said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià said:
"In courage, you are not as good as me by two measures.
Again, I accompanied you with our lord in the hunting park,
when two assailants charged shoulder-to-shoulder after our lord.
Who drew a spear, dismounted to fight them off, and returned?
Was it you or I?"
Yuān said:
"It was you."
Zǐxià said:
"Your courage falls short of mine in three aspects.
What is valued in a scholar-official is
to restrain mighty powers above,
yet not dare to be arrogant toward commoners below,
to establish integrity outwardly so that enemies do not invade or harass,
and to prevent harm internally so that the ruler is not endangered.
These are the strengths of scholar-officials
and what gentlemen highly value.
As for using strengths to cover shortcomings,
using numbers to oppress the few,
bullying innocent people,
and establishing authority in the alleys—
these are the most poisonous traits of scholar-officials,
what gentlemen deeply detest,
and what the masses would eradicate.
The Book of Songs says:
'If a person has no dignity,
what else is there but death?'
How then can one discuss courage before a ruler!"
Thereupon, Duke Líng rose from his mat, pressed his hands together, and said:
"Although I am not clever,
I wish to follow your courage, sir."
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not bully the widowed and orphaned,
do not fear the strong and powerful."
This refers to you, sir.
6.21 When Confucius was traveling,
Jiǎnzǐ intended to kill Yánghǔ,
and Confucius resembled him,
so armored soldiers surrounded Confucius's residence.
Zǐlù was enraged,
branding a halberd and about to charge down.
Confucius stopped him, saying:
"Yóu!
How lacking in the magnanimity of benevolence and righteousness you are!
Not studying the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
not discussing rites and music—
these are my faults.
But if I am not Yánghǔ yet am mistaken for him,
that is not my fault.
It is fate! I
will sing, and you join in."
Zǐlù sang,
Confucius harmonized with him,
and after three rounds, the siege was lifted.
The Book of Songs says:
"Come to wander, come to sing."
This illustrates the harmony of great virtue acting effortlessly.
6.22 The Book of Songs says:
"A joyful and approachable gentleman
is the parent of the people."
How is a gentleman the parent of the people?
It is said:
A gentleman
is dignified in appearance yet unrestrained in action,
frugal in personal life yet generous in giving,
so the unworthy cannot match him.
He exhausts his efforts for himself
but is lenient with others,
thus one can serve him with one's whole life.
He loves deeply without seizing,
gives generously without boasting.
Seeing others' goodness,
he joyfully delights in it;
seeing others' faults,
he cautiously covers them up,
bearing their errors while包容 them.
He gives clothes of the finest,
and provides food in abundance.
His laws are easy for inferiors to follow,
his affairs few and easy to manage.
Thus he stands centered and becomes the parent of the people.
He builds cities for them to dwell in,
allocates fields for their sustenance,
establishes schools for their education,
making them know kinship and respect.
Kinship and respect mean wearing the coarsest mourning for a father for three years,
and likewise for a ruler—this is what it means to be the parent of the people.
6.23 Serving a violent and powerful state is difficult;
making such a state serve us is easy.
Serving it with treasures and valuables
depletes the treasures without securing the alliance.
Making treaties and oaths
leads to agreements that are broken unpredictably.
Ceding a state's strong chariots as bribes
results in settled cessions but insatiable desires.
The more compliantly one serves,
the more aggressively it invades,
inevitably leading to exhausted treasures and a conquered state.
Even with Yáo on the left and Shùn on the right,
none can avoid this outcome by such means.
Thus, without the way of a sage,
relying on cleverness, flattery, and fearful servitude,
one cannot preserve the state or secure oneself.
Hence, an enlightened ruler does not follow this path.
He must cultivate rites to unify the court,
rectify laws to unify the officials,
and balance governance to unify the people.
Then ritual principles and rhythms harmonize the court,
rules and measures correct the officials,
and loyalty, trust, love, and benefit pacify the people.
He would not commit one unjust act
or kill one innocent person
even to gain the world.
Thus, those nearby compete to be close, and those afar wish to come.
Upper and lower are of one mind,
the three armies united in strength.
Their reputation is enough to inspire awe,
their power sufficient to unify them.
Then with a mere gesture or command,
violent states all hasten to serve,
like infants returning to a loving mother.
Why?
Because benevolence is manifested and righteousness established,
teaching sincere and love profound.
Thus the Book of Songs says:
"The king's plans are truly sincere,
the Xú region has come."
6.24 A brave warrior's single shout makes the three armies retreat—
such is the sincerity of a scholar-official.
Long ago, Chǔ's Xióng Qúzǐ was walking at night
and saw a recumbent stone, mistaking it for a crouching tiger.
He bent his bow and shot at it,
embedding the metal and sinking the feathers.
Looking down,
he realized it was a stone.
The stone split open for him—
how much more so with people?
To initiate without response,
to act without support,
must stem from incompleteness within.
Those who rectify the world without leaving their mat
seek it within themselves.
Confucius said:
"If one's person is upright,
orders are unnecessary for action;
if one's person is not upright,
even orders are not followed."
The reason former kings could command and have all within the seas come as guests
was the utmost sincerity of their virtue,
manifested outwardly in their demeanor.
The Book of Songs says:
"The king's plans are truly sincere,
the Xú region has come."
6.25 Long ago, when Zhào Jiǎnzǐ died and had not yet been buried,
Zhōngmóu rebelled against him.
Five days after the burial,
Xiāngzǐ raised an army to attack it.
Before the encirclement was complete,
a hundred feet of the city wall collapsed on its own.
Xiāngzǐ sounded the gongs to retreat.
A military officer remonstrated:
"You are punishing Zhōngmóu's crime, and the wall collapses—
this is heaven aiding us.
Why retreat?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"I heard from Shūxiàng:
'A gentleman does not take advantage of others in profit,
nor corner them in danger.'"
He waited for the city to be repaired before attacking.
Hearing of his righteousness, Zhōngmóu requested to surrender,
saying:
"Excellent!
This is what Xiāngzǐ stands for."
The Book of Songs says:
"The king's plans are truly sincere,
the Xú region has come."
6.26 There are three types of authority.
There is the authority of the Dàodé,
the authority of violent surveillance,
and the authority of reckless arrogance.
These three must be carefully examined.
What is the authority of the Dàodé?
It is said:
When rites and music are cultivated,
roles and duties are clear,
actions are timely,
and love and benefit are regulated.
Thus,
the people honor such a ruler as an emperor,
cherish him as parents,
and fear him as divine.
Hence, rewards are unused yet the people are motivated,
punishments unapplied yet authority prevails.
This is the authority of the Dàodé.
What is the authority of violent surveillance?
It is said:
When rites and music are not cultivated,
Yet its prohibitions against wrongdoing are violent,
its executions of the disobedient are excessively meticulous,
its punishments are severe yet trustworthy,
its killings are fierce and inevitable,
darkly like being struck by thunder,
like being crushed by a wall.
The common people, when coerced, become fearful;
when neglected, they become arrogant toward their superiors;
when restrained, they gather;
when they hear of distance, they scatter.
If not coerced by the threat of punishment,
or intimidated by executions,
there would be no way to control them.
This is the authority of tyrannical scrutiny.
What is called the authority of reckless arrogance?
It is said:
Without a heart that loves people,
without deeds that benefit people,
yet daily engaging in ways that disrupt people.
When the common people clamor in protest,
they are then subjected to punishment and torture.
It does not harmonize with people's hearts,
it goes against the natural order,
thus floods and droughts occur untimely,
and grain harvests fail to rise.
The common people are afflicted above by the woes of violence and chaos,
and below by the exhaustion of clothing and food supplies,
grieving and sorrowful with nowhere to plead their case,
forming cliques in frustration and dispersing from their rulers,
leading to collapse and ruin,
which can be expected to happen imminently.
This is the authority of reckless arrogance.
Now, the authority of virtue and morality
achieves widespread strength.
The authority of tyrannical scrutiny
leads to danger and weakness.
The authority of reckless arrogance
results in destruction and extinction.
Thus, though the names of authority are the same, the outcomes of fortune and misfortune are vastly different.
Therefore, it must be carefully examined.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Heaven is swift in its wrath,
it heavily sends down calamities,
afflicting us with famine,
so the people all flee into exile."
6.27 Duke Píng of Jìn was enjoying himself on the river and said,
"How can I obtain worthy scholars to enjoy this with me!"
The boatman Hé Xū knelt and replied,
"It is only that my lord does not truly favor scholars.
Pearls come from the rivers and seas,
jade comes from the Kūnlún Mountains,
and they arrive without feet—
this is because of my lord's favor.
Scholars have feet but do not come,
likely because my lord lacks the intent to favor scholars.
Do not worry about the absence of scholars."
Duke Píng said,
"I have a thousand guests to the left of my gate,
and a thousand to the right.
If the morning meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes by evening;
if the evening meal is insufficient,
I collect market taxes by morning.
Can I be said not to favor scholars?"
Hé Xū replied,
"The swan soars a thousand miles in one flight,
relying only on its six primary feathers.
The feathers on its back,
the down on its belly—
add a handful,
and its flight does not become higher;
remove a handful,
and its flight does not become lower.
Now, my lord's guests, a thousand to the left and right of the gate,
may include those six primary feathers among them.
But are they all just back feathers and belly down?"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Though counselors are many,
the plans do not come to fruition."
7.1 King Xuān of Qí said to Tián Guò,
"I hear that Confucians mourn their parents for three years,
and mourn their ruler for three years.
Who is more important, the ruler or the father?"
Guò replied,
"Perhaps the father is more important."
The king angrily
said,
"Then why do scholars leave their parents to serve the ruler?"
He replied,
"Without the ruler's land, there is no place to settle my parents;
without the ruler's stipend, there is no means to support my parents;
without the ruler's rank, there is no way to honor and glorify my parents.
What is received from the ruler
is given to the parents.
Thus, all service to the ruler
is for the sake of the parents."
King Xuān was silent and had no response.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The king's affairs are never done,
no leisure to care for my father."
7.2 The King of Zhào sent an envoy to Chǔ.
While playing the sè, he dispatched him, saying,
"Be careful not to misspeak my words."
The envoy received the command,
prostrated and did not rise, saying,
"My king, your sè playing has never been as sorrowful as today."
The king said,
"Indeed, the sè was just being tuned."
The envoy said,
"If it is tuned, then the bridges can be marked."
The king said,
"No.
The weather has dryness and dampness,
the strings have looseness and tightness,
the bridges have shifts and changes—
they cannot be marked."
The envoy said,
"Allow me to use this as a metaphor.
Chǔ is over a thousand lǐ from Zhào,
and there will also be changes, both auspicious and inauspicious.
If inauspicious, we mourn;
if auspicious, we congratulate—
just as the bridges have shifts,
they cannot be marked.
Thus, when an enlightened king sends an envoy,
he must be careful in his selection,
and once sent,
entrust him with trust in his heart,
not just with words."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The messengers are quick,
but each fears not fulfilling his duty."
This laments the difficulty of governing from above.
7.3 In Qí, there were recluses, Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shí Jūn.
When Chancellor Cáo was the prime minister of Qí,
a guest said to Kuì Shēng,
"Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shí Jūn
are worthies of the age.
They live in seclusion in the deep mountains,
never stooping or lowering their aspirations to seek office.
I have heard that you, sir, have access to Chancellor Cáo,
and I hope you will pave the way for them.
In my village, there was a mother who was friendly with a neighbor.
The daughter-in-law was suspected of stealing meat,
and her mother-in-law drove her away.
Resentful, she told the village mother,
who said,
'Go peacefully.
I will now have your mother-in-law call you back.'
She then bundled hemp and asked for fire at the exiled daughter-in-law's home, saying,
'My dogs fought over meat and killed each other;
I need fire to cook it.'
The mother-in-law then immediately sent someone to bring the daughter-in-law back.
Thus, the village mother was no skilled persuader,
and bundling hemp to ask for fire
was not the way to retrieve a daughter-in-law,
yet things can resonate with each other,
and actions can be fitting.
Why not pave the way for them?"
Kuì Shēng said,
"I fear I am not capable,
but I will do my best to 'bundle hemp and ask for fire' for Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shí Jūn."
Thereupon, he visited Chancellor Cáo and said,
"In my village, there was one who remarried three days after her husband's death,
and one who never remarried in her lifetime.
If you were to choose a wife for yourself,
which would you choose?"
The chancellor said,
"I would choose the one who never remarried."
Kuì Shēng said,
"In Qí, there are recluses Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shí Jūn,
worthies of the age.
They live in seclusion in the deep mountains,
never stooping or lowering their aspirations to seek office.
When the chancellor chooses a wife,
he wants one who does not remarry;
in selecting ministers, why not choose those who do not serve?"
Thereupon, Chancellor Cáo, through Kuì Shēng, sent silk and a comfortable carriage to welcome Dōngguō Xiānshēng and Liáng Shí Jūn,
and treated them as honored guests.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Having seen the noble man,
my heart is at ease."
7.4 Confucius said:
"In the past, the Duke of Zhōu served King Wén.
In action, he did not act arbitrarily;
in affairs, he did not act on his own;
his demeanor was as if he could not bear the weight of his clothes;
his words were as if they could not leave his mouth;
when holding something in front,
he was so cautious as if fearing to lose it—
he can be said to have been a filial son."
King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
the Duke of Zhōu inherited the legacy of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
occupied the Son of Heaven's position,
administered the Son of Heaven's governance,
quelled the rebellions of the barbarian tribes,
punished the crimes of Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū,
held King Chéng in his arms while receiving the feudal lords in audience,
making decisions on punishments and rewards,
without consulting anyone,
his might shook heaven and earth,
frightening all within the seas,
he can be said to have been capable in military affairs.
When King Chéng came of age,
the Duke of Zhōu returned the governance to him,
facing north and serving him as a minister,
acting only after seeking permission,
without any boastful demeanor,
he can be said to have been capable as a minister.
Thus, one person
was able to change three times,
in order to respond to the times.
The Book of Songs says:
"To the left, to the left,
the nobleman is suited for it;
to the right, to the right,
the nobleman possesses it."
7.5 The Tradition says:
Birds with beautiful feathers and hooked beaks
are feared by other birds.
Fish with wide mouths and hanging bellies
are feared by other fish.
People with sharp tongues and eloquent words
are feared by others.
Therefore, the nobleman avoids three points:
he avoids the tip of the scholar's pen,
he avoids the tip of the warrior's spear,
he avoids the tip of the debater's tongue.
The Book of Songs says:
"My friend is respectful!
Slanderous words are on the rise."
7.6 Confucius was trapped between Chén and Cài,
sitting on a mat of three classics,
for seven days without eating,
having only wild vegetable soup without rice,
his disciples showing signs of hunger,
yet he continued reading the Book of Documents and practicing rituals and music without cease.
Zǐlù came forward to admonish him, saying:
"Those who do good,
heaven rewards with blessings.
Those who do evil,
heaven rewards with harm.
Now, Master, you have accumulated virtue and practiced benevolence,
doing good for a long time.
Could it be that you still have some misconduct,
why do you live in such obscurity?"
Confucius said:
"Come here, Yóu!
You are a petty person,
who has not studied the theories.
Stay,
and I will tell you.
Do you think the wise are without fault?
Then why did Prince Bǐgān have his heart cut out and die?
Do you think the righteous are listened to?
Then why was Wǔ Zǐxū's eyes gouged out and hung at the eastern gate of Wú?
Do you think the incorruptible are employed?
Then why did Bóyí and Shūqí starve on Shǒuyáng Mountain?
Do you think the loyal are employed?
Then why was Bào Shū not employed?
Lord Yè Gōngzǐgāo never held office his whole life,
Bào Jiāo hugged a tree and wept,
and Zǐtuī climbed a mountain and was burned?
Thus, there are many noblemen with broad learning and deep strategies
who do not encounter the right time.
How could I, Qiū, be the only one?
Being worthy or unworthy is a matter of talent.
Encountering the right time or not is a matter of timing.
Now, without the right time,
how can the worthy be employed?
Thus, Yú Shùn plowed on the south side of Lìshān,
and was made the Son of Heaven,
because he encountered Yáo.
Fù Yuè carried soil and built walls,
and was made a high official,
because he encountered Wǔ Dīng.
Yī Yǐn was originally a servant of the Yǒushēn clan,
carrying tripods and handling utensils to season flavors,
and was made prime minister,
because he encountered Tāng.
Lǚ Wàng at fifty,
sold food at Jíjīn,
at seventy,
he slaughtered animals at Zhāogē,
at ninety, he became the teacher of the Son of Heaven,
because he encountered King Wén.
Guǎn Yíwú was bound and in a prison cart,
and was made Uncle,
because he encountered Duke Huán of Qí.
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for the price of five sheepskins,
herded cattle for the Earl of Qín,
and was elevated to high official,
because he encountered Duke Mù of Qín.
Yú Qiū was famous throughout the land,
was made Prime Minister,
and yielded to Sūnshū Áo,
because he encountered King Zhuāng of Chǔ.
Wǔ Zǐxū had many achievements earlier,
but was executed later,
not because his wisdom waxed and waned,
but because he first encountered Hé Lǘ,
and later encountered Fū Chāi.
When a fine horse is exhausted pulling a salt cart,
it is not without form and appearance,
but no one recognizes it.
If a fine horse does not meet Bó Lè,
how can it display its thousand-mile hooves?
Zàofǔ would also have no means to drive a thousand miles.
When orchids and angelica grow in dense forests,
deep in the mountains,
people do not see them, so they are not fragrant.
Scholars do not study merely to attain success.
They study to avoid being distressed in poverty,
and not to lose their will in worry,
to foresee the beginnings of fortune and misfortune,
and to have no confusion in their hearts.
Thus, the sage lives in seclusion and reflects deeply,
hearing and seeing alone.
Shùn was also a worthy sage,
facing south and governing the world,
only because he encountered Yáo.
Had Shùn lived in the time of Jié and Zhòu,
he would have been fortunate to avoid punishment and execution,
merely by doing good,
what position could he have held?
Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān,
at that time,
was it that Guān Lóngpáng lacked wisdom,
and Prince Bǐgān lacked intelligence?
It was because they did not encounter the right time.
Thus, the nobleman devotes himself to learning,
cultivates his person, rectifies his conduct, and awaits his time.
Do not be confused about this."
The Book of Songs says:
"The crane cries in the nine-fold marsh,
its voice is heard in heaven."
7.7 Zēngzǐ said:
"Those who, once gone, cannot return are our parents.
What, once reached, cannot be increased is age.
Therefore, when a filial son wishes to provide,
his parents may not wait.
A tree wishes to be straight,
but time may not wait.
Thus, to sacrifice an ox at the grave
is not as good as offering a chicken or pig while the parents are alive.
Thus, when I once served as an official in Qí,
my salary was no more than a zhōng or fǔ,
yet I was still joyful and happy,
not because I thought it abundant,
but because I was glad to be able to support my parents.
After they passed away,
I traveled south to Chǔ,
and obtained a high position there,
with a hall nine ren high,
rafters three arm-spans thick,
and a hundred carriages with turning wheels,
yet I still faced north and wept,
not because I thought it lowly,
but because I grieved that I could no longer support my parents."
Thus, if the family is poor and the parents old, one does not choose the office but serves.
As for those who are true to their own aspirations
but stint their parents,
they are not filial.
The Book of Songs says:
"There is a mother to offer the sacrifice."
7.8 Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào had a minister named Zhōu Shě,
who stood at the gate for three days and three nights.
Jiǎnzǐ sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"What matter do you wish to see me about?"
Zhōu Shě replied:
"I wish to be a straightforward minister,
with ink and brush in hand, holding tablets,
following behind my lord,
overseeing my lord's errors and recording them,
so there is a record each day,
an accomplishment each month,
and an effect each year."
Jiǎnzǐ was pleased, and when he stayed, he stayed with him,
when he went out, he went out with him.
Not long after,
Zhōu Shě died.
Jiǎnzǐ mourned as if for a son.
Later, when drinking with his officials at the Hóngbō Tower,
in the midst of wine,
Jiǎnzǐ wept.
The officials all rushed out,
saying:
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"The high officials are all without fault.
In the past, I had Zhōu Shě who once said,
stating:
'The skin of a thousand sheep is not as good as the armpit fur of one fox;
the yes-men of the masses are not as good as the outspokenness of one scholar.'
In the past, King Zhòu of Shāng perished due to his silence,
while King Wǔ prospered because of his forthright speech.
Now since the death of Zhōu Shě,
I have never heard of my faults.
My downfall is not far off.
This is why I, the ruler, weep."
7.9 The "Zhuàn" says:
Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Yànzǐ:
"What is the worry in governing a state?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"The worry lies in the altar rats."
Duke Jǐng said:
"What are altar rats?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Altar rats come out to steal outside,
and return to shelter at the altar.
If you flood them out, you fear damaging the wall;
if you smoke them out, you fear burning the wood.
This is the harm of such rats.
Now, your attendants,
when outside, sell your favor to seek profit,
and when inside, take shelter with you,
escaping punishment for disrupting the law,
and you further protect and nurture them all.
This is the harm of altar rats."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Alas,
how can this be!"
"There was a man who sold wine of excellent quality,
and hung a very long sign,
yet the wine turned sour without selling.
He asked his neighbor the reason.
The neighbor said:
'Your dog is very fierce,
and when someone comes with a container to buy,
the dog always rushes to bite them,
so the wine turns sour without selling.'
When a scholar wishes to advise the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
the officials in power rush to bite him,
they are the state's vicious dogs.
The attendants are the altar rats,
the officials in power are the vicious dogs,
these are the great worries of the state."
The "Shī" says:
"Look at that central forest,
all are firewood and kindling."
This means the court is full of petty men.
7.10 In the past, Sīchéng Zǐhǎn was chancellor of Sòng,
and said to the ruler of Sòng:
"The safety and danger of the state,
the order and chaos among the people,
lie in the ruler's exercise of rewards and punishments.
Bestowing ranks, emoluments, and rewards,
these are what the people like,
you should administer them yourself.
Killings, executions, and penalties,
these are what the people dislike,
I request to take charge of them."
The ruler of Sòng said:
"Good.
I will take the credit for the good,
and you bear the blame for the bad,
I know I will not be laughed at by the feudal lords."
The people knew that the power of life and death lay solely with Zǐhǎn,
the high ministers drew close to him,
the common people feared him.
Within less than a year,
Zǐhǎn then ousted the ruler of Sòng and monopolized the government.
Therefore, the "Lǎozǐ" says:
"The fish should not leave the deep;
the sharp weapons of the state should not be shown to others."
The "Shī" says:
"Why do you make me act,
without consulting me?"
7.11 During the time of Duke Yì of Wèi,
there was a minister named Hóng Yǎn,
who was sent on a mission.
Before he returned,
the Dí people attacked Wèi.
Thereupon, Duke Yì wanted to raise an army to meet them.
His people all said:
"What you value and give rank and emolument to
are the cranes.
What you love
are the palace maidens.
Let the cranes and palace maidens do the fighting.
How can we fight!"
So they dispersed and all left.
The Dí people arrived,
attacked Duke Yì at Yíngzé,
and killed him.
They ate all his flesh,
only leaving his liver.
When Hóng Yǎn arrived,
he reported his mission to the liver.
After finishing his report,
he cried out to heaven and wailed.
When his grief subsided,
he said:
"As for a minister like me,
I alone should die."
Thereupon, he cut open his own belly,
removed his internal organs,
placed Duke Yì's liver inside,
and then died.
Duke Huán heard of this,
and said:
"Wèi's downfall
was due to its lack of virtue.
Now with a minister like this,
it must be preserved."
So he reestablished Wèi at Chǔqiū.
As for Hóng Yǎn,
he can be called a loyal scholar.
He gave his life to aid his ruler,
not only aiding his ruler,
but also causing Wèi's ancestral temple to be reestablished,
with sacrifices unceasing,
he can be said to have achieved great merit.
The "Shī" says:
"All around there is abundance,
I alone dwell in sorrow.
