People all have ease,
I alone dare not rest."
7.12 Sūnshū Áo met the old man of Húqiū.
The old man of Húqiū said:
"I have heard
that a person with three advantages must have three troubles;
do you know this?"
Sūnshū Áo, startled, changed expression and said:
"I am not clever,
how could I know this?
May I ask what are the three advantages?
What are the three troubles?"
The old man of Húqiū said:
"Those with high rank,
others envy them.
Those with great office,
the ruler dislikes them.
Those with ample salary,
resentment gathers to them.
This is what it means."
Sūnshū Áo said:
"Not so.
The higher my rank,
the lower my aspirations.
The greater my office,
the more cautious my heart.
The more ample my salary,
the broader my charity.
Can this avoid trouble?"
The old man of Húqiū said:
"Excellent words!
Even Yáo and Shùn would find it hard to achieve this."
The "Shī" says:
"The mild and respectful man,
as if perched on a tree.
Anxious and careful,
as if overlooking a valley."
7.13 Confucius said:
"An enlightened king has three fears.
First, being in a high position and fearing he does not hear of his faults;
second, achieving his aims and fearing arrogance;
third, hearing the perfect way of the world and fearing he cannot practice it.
In the past, King Gōujiàn of Yuè fought with Wú,
defeated them greatly,
and annexed the southern barbarians.
At that time,
the ruler stood facing south,
with three close ministers,
and five distant ministers,
and ordered the high officials:
'Those who hear of faults and do not report them to me will suffer the highest punishment.'
This is being in a high position and fearing he does not hear of his faults.
In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn fought with Chǔ,
defeated them greatly,
burned their grass,
and the fire did not cease for three days.
Duke Wén withdrew with a worried expression.
An attendant said:
'You have greatly defeated Chǔ yet look worried,
why?'
Duke Wén said:
'I have heard that only a sage can achieve victory through war and remain secure!
As for those who win by deceit,
they are never without danger,
this is why I worry.'
This is achieving his aims and fearing arrogance.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng, and stood facing south.
Duke Huán said:
'Having obtained these two gentlemen,
my eyes see more clearly,
my ears hear more acutely.
I dare not keep this benefit to myself alone,
but present it to my ancestors.'
This describes one who, having heard the perfect Way, fears being unable to practice it.
From the examples of Duke Huán, Duke Wén of Jìn, and King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
these three fears
are the concerns of enlightened rulers."
The Book of Songs says:
"Mild and reverent men,
as if perched on trees.
Anxious and careful,
as if overlooking valleys.
Trembling with fear,
as if treading on thin ice."
This describes the Great King's position above the people.
7.14 King Zhuāng of Chǔ hosted a banquet for his ministers.
As evening fell and the drinking reached its peak,
all attendants were drunk.
When the palace candles suddenly went out,
someone tugged at the queen's garment.
The queen grabbed and broke the tassel of his cap,
then said to the king:
"Just now when the candles extinguished,
someone pulled at my dress.
I've broken the tassel of his cap.
I request to quickly light the candles to identify the one with the broken tassel."
The king said:
"Stop!"
Immediately he issued a command:
"Today all who drink with me
must break their cap tassels,
or the celebration won't be complete."
Thus no minister retained an intact tassel,
and none could identify whose tassel the queen had broken.
Thereupon the king continued drinking joyfully with his ministers
until the banquet concluded.
Later when Wú raised troops to attack Chǔ,
there was a man who consistently fought in the vanguard,
five times breaking through enemy formations and repelling foes,
eventually capturing the enemy commander's head and presenting it to the king.
The king, surprised, asked him:
"I've never shown you special favor,
why are you so devoted to me?"
He replied:
"I am the one whose cap tassel was broken in the palace that night.
I should have died a bloody death then.
I've carried this debt for long,
with no chance to repay.
Now fortunate to be of service,
in duty I can still help my king crush Wú and strengthen Chǔ."
The Book of Songs says:
"Deep is that pool,
with reeds luxuriantly growing."
This speaks of how the great contains everything without exception.
7.15 The Tradition says:
Bó Qí was filial yet abandoned by his parent.
Duke Yīn was kind yet killed by his younger brother.
Shū Wǔ was virtuous yet slain by his elder brother.
Bǐ Gān was loyal yet executed by his ruler.
The Book of Songs says:
"I was careful, yet guilty of no crime."
7.16 When King Zhòu executed Prince Bǐ Gān,
Jīzǐ let his hair loose and feigned madness.
When Duke Líng of Chén killed Xiè Yě,
Dèng Yuán left Chén with his entire clan.
After these events,
Yīn was annexed by Zhōu,
Chén perished under Chǔ,
because they killed Bǐ Gān and Xiè Yě,
and lost Jīzǐ and Dèng Yuán.
When King Zhāo of Yān obtained Guō Wěi's service, Zōu Yǎn and Yuè Yì came from Qí and Wèi,
enabling Yān to raise troops with Zhào to attack Qí,
forcing King Mǐn to take refuge in Jǔ.
Yān's territory and population
were not equal to Qí's.
Yet the reason Yān achieved such success
was through obtaining capable men.
Thus no state enjoys perpetual security,
no people are inherently easy to govern.
Those who obtain worthy men prosper,
those who lose them perish.
From ancient times to present,
this has never been otherwise.
The clear mirror
serves to reflect form.
The past
serves to understand the present.
Knowing what caused danger and destruction in antiquity,
yet not striving to follow what brought security and preservation,
is no different from running backward while hoping to catch up with those ahead.
Tài Gōng understood this,
therefore he honored Wēizǐ's descendants and built a monument at Bǐ Gān's tomb.
When even sages treat worthy men's posterity
with such generosity,
how much more should we value contemporary talents?
The Book of Songs says:
"Great Heaven is too cruel,
I was careful, yet guilty of no crime."
7.17 Sòng Yù gained audience with King Xiāng of Chǔ through his friend's recommendation,
yet the king treated him no differently from others,
so he reproached his friend.
His friend said:
"Ginger and cinnamon grow from the earth,
but don't derive their pungency from the earth.
A woman marries through a matchmaker,
but doesn't become intimate through the matchmaker.
Your service to the king hasn't succeeded,
why blame me?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Not so.
Once Qí had a swift hare
that could run five hundred lǐ in a day.
If you merely pointed where to look,
even the best hound couldn't catch the dust of that swift hare.
But if unleashed with loosened reins,
even the Dōngguō rabbit couldn't escape.
Now when you recommended me,
did you unleash me with trailing traces?
Or merely point where to look?"
The Book of Songs says:
"When about to be comfortable and happy,
you abandon and cast me away."
7.18 Sòng Yān, chancellor of Qí, was dismissed from office.
Returning dejected to his residence,
he summoned his gatekeeper Chén Ráo and twenty-five others,
saying:
"Is there any among you gentlemen who would follow me to another state?"
Chén Ráo and the others all knelt without responding.
Sòng Yān said:
"How lamentable!
How easily scholars are obtained, yet how difficult to employ!"
Ráo replied:
"It's not that scholars are easily obtained yet hard to employ,
but that you, sir, cannot employ them.
Your inability to employ them
creates resentment in them.
This means you fault others for your own failures."
Sòng Yān asked:
"What does 'faulting others for one's own failures' mean?"
Chén Ráo said:
"Your scholars lack even three pecks of grain,
while your geese and ducks have surplus grain,
this is your first fault.
The pears and chestnuts from your orchard
are thrown about by palace women for amusement,
yet your scholars never taste one,
this is your second fault.
Silks and satins,
gorgeous in your hall,
fray in the wind,
yet your scholars never get even trimmings,
this is your third fault.
Moreover, wealth
is what you, sir, consider light,
while death
is what scholars consider heavy.
You cannot give what you consider light,
yet expect scholars to devote what they consider heavy -
this is like keeping a leaden knife
but expecting to use it as a Gānjiàng sword -
is this not difficult?"
Sòng Yān showed shame on his face,
retreated respectfully from his mat and said:
"This is Yān's fault."
The Book of Songs says:
"Some are given wine,
others not even gruel."
7.19 The Tradition says:
Those skilled in governance
follow what is proper to human nature,
conform to the sequence of yīn and yáng,
comprehend the principles connecting root and branch,
and harmonize the relationship between Heaven and humanity.
Thus the cosmic breath nurtures all, and living things flourish beautifully.
Those ignorant of governance
make emotions oppress nature,
let yīn override yáng,
cause branches to oppose the root,
and make humanity deceive Heaven.
The breath becomes stifled and untrustworthy,
depressed and unexpressed.
Thus disasters arise,
strange phenomena occur,
all living beings suffer,
and the year's harvest fails.
Therefore their actions injure virtue,
their inaction brings no salvation.
So what should be relaxed they tense,
what should be urgent they ignore,
daily opposing principle while believing they govern.
The Book of Songs says:
"When all is destroyed and damaged,
none knows their own faults."
7.20 During the time of Marquis Wén of Wèi,
Zǐ Zhì held office but incurred offense,
so he left and traveled north.
He said to Lord Jiǎn:
"From now on,
I will no longer cultivate virtue in others."
Lord Jiǎn asked:
"Why is that?"
Zhì replied:
"Half of the scholars I nurtured in the hall,
half of the grand officers I nurtured in the court,
and half of the border people I nurtured
now have the hall scholars intimidating me with laws,
the border people threatening me with weapons.
That is why I won't cultivate virtue in people anymore."
Lord Jiǎn said:
"Alas!
Your words are mistaken.
If you plant peach and plum trees in spring,
you get shade under them in summer,
and eat their fruit in autumn.
If you plant thistles in spring,
you cannot pick their leaves in summer,
and get their thorns in autumn.
From this perspective,
it depends on what you plant.
Now what you planted,
were not the right people.
Thus, a gentleman first selects and then plants."
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not push the great cart,
only dust will rise darkly."
7.21 The upright follow the Way in action,
speak according to reason,
are fair and impartial,
do not indulge desires in safety,
nor act rashly in danger.
Once Duke Xiàn of Wèi fled,
and upon returning reached the outskirts,
planned to distribute fiefs to his followers before entering.
Grand Historian Liǔ Zhuāng said:
"If all guarded the altars of state,
then who would harness and follow?
If all followed,
then who would guard the altars?
If you return with partiality,
would that not be improper?"
So he did not distribute them.
Liǔ Zhuāng was upright.
Once the Wèi grand officer Shǐ Yú was ill and near death,
told his son:
"I often spoke of Qú Bóyù's worth but couldn't advance him,
and of Mí Zǐxiá's incompetence but couldn't remove him.
As a minister, living I couldn't promote the worthy and dismiss the incompetent,
dead I don't deserve the main hall for funeral;
placing my coffin in a room suffices."
The lord of Wèi asked the reason.
The son reported his father's words.
The lord promptly summoned Qú Bóyù and honored him,
dismissed Mí Zǐxiá,
moved the coffin to the main hall,
completed the rites before leaving.
Advising with his life,
and with his corpse after death,
he can be called upright.
The Book of Songs says:
"Reverently fulfill your duties,
love this uprightness."
7.22 Confucius was leisurely at home,
with Zǐgòng sitting in attendance,
who asked about the way of being humble.
Confucius said:
"Excellent!
Your question.
To be humble,
is like the earth, isn't it?"
Zǐgòng didn't understand.
Confucius said:
"The earth,
when dug, yields sweet springs;
planted, produces the five grains;
grasses and trees grow on it;
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles thrive there.
The living stand on it,
the dead enter it;
much merit without speaking,
its rewards never cease.
Thus it is said:
One who can be humble,
is surely like the earth?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Though I am not clever,
I will practice this teaching."
The Book of Songs says:
"In ritual, no error."
7.23 The Tradition says:
Nán Jiǎzǐ passed by Chéng Běn,
who cooked a snakehead fish for him.
Nán Jiǎzǐ said:
"I hear gentlemen do not eat snakehead fish."
Běnzǐ said:
"That's why gentlemen don't eat it,
what has that to do with me?"
Jiǎzǐ said:
"Comparing high broadens virtue,
comparing low narrows conduct.
Comparing with the good
is a step to self-advancement.
Comparing with the bad
is a source of self-degradation.
Moreover, doesn't the Book of Songs say:
'The high mountain I look up to,
the great path I travel.'
How dare I compare myself to a gentleman?
I only aspire to emulate them."
7.24 Zǐgòng asked about great ministers.
The Master said:
"Qí had Bào Shū,
Zhèng had Zǐ Pí."
Zǐgòng said:
"No.
Qí had Guǎn Zhòng,
Zhèng had Dōnglǐ Zǐchǎn."
Confucius said:
"Chǎn was recommended."
Zǐgòng said:
"Then recommending the worthy is better than being worthy."
The Master said:
"Knowing the worthy is wisdom;
promoting the worthy is benevolence;
introducing the worthy is righteousness.
With these three qualities,
what more is needed?"
7.25 Confucius was wandering on Jǐng Mountain,
with Zǐlù, Zǐgòng, and Yán Yuān following.
Confucius said:
"A gentleman climbing high must compose;
young ones, if willing,
speak your aspirations.
I will enlighten you."
Zǐlù said:
"I wish to wield a long halberd, charge through three armies,
with a nursing tigress behind,
enemies ahead,
leaping like a mantis, fierce like a dragon,
advancing to save the troubles of two states."
Confucius said:
"A warrior indeed!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Two states locked in conflict,
warriors arrayed in formation,
dust darkening the sky,
I, without a foot of weapon,
nor a peck of grain,
would resolve the difficulties of both states.
Those who use me survive,
those who don't perish."
Confucius said:
"A debater indeed!"
Yán Huí remained silent.
Confucius said:
"Huí, why no aspiration?"
Yán Yuān said:
"The two have spoken,
so I dare not."
Confucius said:
"Different,
each has their own matter.
Speak your wish,
I will enlighten you."
Yán Yuān said:
"I wish to minister to a small state.
The ruler governs with the Way,
ministers transform with virtue,
ruler and minister united in heart,
internal and external in harmony.
The various feudal lords,
all follow righteousness and turn to our influence,
the strong hasten to advance,
the aged support each other to come.
Teaching extends to the common people,
virtue reaches the four barbarians,
all laying down arms,
converging at the four gates like spokes.
All under heaven attain eternal peace,
from flying insects to crawling creatures,
each joyful in its nature.
Promoting the worthy and employing the able,
each undertaking their duties."
Thus the ruler rests in tranquility above,
while ministers harmonize below,
ruling effortlessly through non-action,
their every movement aligned with the Way,
composed and adhering to ritual.
Those who speak of benevolence and righteousness are rewarded,
while those who advocate warfare are put to death.
Then how could Zǐlù advance to rescue?
What difficulty would Zǐgòng have to resolve?"
Confucius said:
"What a sagely scholar!
When great men emerge,
petty men hide away.
When sages arise,
the worthy withdraw.
If Yán Huí were to hold governance,
how could Zǐlù and Zǐgòng display their abilities!"
The Book of Songs says:
"Thick falls the snow,
but sunlight melts it away."
7.26 Once when Confucius was playing the sè,
Zēngzǐ and Zǐgòng stood listening by the side door.
When the melody ended,
Zēngzǐ said:
"Alas!
Our master's music seems to contain the ambition of a greedy wolf,
and the conduct of one depraved and wicked—
how exceedingly does he pursue profit without benevolence?"
Zǐgòng agreed with this,
but without responding, entered.
Noticing Zǐgòng's expression of one about to remonstrate over a fault,
and his demeanor of facing a difficult matter,
the master set aside his sè and waited.
Zǐgòng then reported Zēngzǐ's words.
The master said:
"Alas!
That Shēn [Zēngzǐ],
is a worthy man of the world,
well-versed in understanding music.
Just now as I played the sè,
a mouse came out wandering,
a wildcat appeared in the room,
moving stealthily along the beam,
approaching then hiding,
squinting and arching its back,
seeking but failing to catch it.
I expressed this pursuit through the music of my sè.
For Shēn to think me greedy, wicked, and depraved—
is that not fitting!"
The Book of Songs says:
"When bells are struck in the palace,
their sound is heard outside."
7.27 As for being a father,
one must embrace the love of kindness and benevolence
to nurture his children.
Provide for their food and drink,
to preserve their bodies whole.
When they reach understanding,
dwell solemnly and speak correctly
to guide them first.
When they tie their hair [come of age],
entrust them to enlightened teachers to complete their skills.
At nineteen, they show their aspirations;
invite guests to cap them,
fulfilling their intent fully.
When their blood is calm and pure,
arrange marriages to settle them,
sincerely receiving parental instruction
without any doubt.
Do not scold a capped son,
nor whip a haired child;
listen to their subtle admonitions,
and not let them worry.
This is the way of being a father.
The Book of Songs says:
"My father begot me,
my mother nurtured me.
They stroked me, reared me,
raised me, educated me,
cared for me, looked after me,
in and out, they held me to their bosom."
8.1 King Gōujiàn of Yuè sent Lián Jī to present gifts to the King of Jīng.
A minister of the King of Jīng said:
"Yuè
is a country of barbarians.
I request to deceive their envoy."
The King of Jīng said:
"The King of Yuè
is a worthy man,
and his envoy is also worthy;
you must be cautious."
The minister went out to meet Lián Jī,
saying:
"If you wear a cap, you may see us according to custom.
Without a cap, you cannot see us."
Lián Jī said:
"Now Yuè was also enfeoffed by the Zhōu court,
though not situated among the great states,
but residing by rivers and seas,
keeping company with turtles and fish,
tattooing and cutting hair before settling.
Now coming to your superior state,
you insist that capped, we see by custom;
uncapped, we cannot see.
If so,
then when your state's envoys go to Yuè,
they too must be tattooed, have noses cut, hair shorn to see by custom—
is that acceptable?"
Hearing this, the King of Jīng,
threw on his robes and came out to apologize.
Confucius said:
"Missioned to the four quarters,
not disgracing the sovereign's command—
such may be called a scholar."
8.2 The reason people desire wealth, honor, peace, and glory,
being praised by others,
is for their own sake.
And hating poverty, low status, danger, and disgrace,
being slandered by others,
is also for their own sake.
But what is precious in the self?
Nothing more precious than qì.
People live when they have qì,
and die when they lose it.
This qì is not gold, silk, pearls, or jade,
that can be sought from others.
It is not silk cloth or the five grains,
that can be bought in the market.
It resides in our own selves—
we cannot but be careful of it.
The Book of Songs says:
"Wise and discerning,
they preserve their persons."
8.3 When the Wú people attacked Chǔ,
King Zhāo fled the state,
and a butcher named Yuè followed in his train.
When King Zhāo returned to the state,
he rewarded his followers.
Reaching Yuè,
Yuè declined, saying:
"When the lord lost the state,
what I lost was butchery.
When the lord returned to the state,
I too returned to my butchery.
My livelihood is already ample—
what reward is there to receive?"
He refused the command.
The lord pressed him,
and Yuè said:
"The lord's loss of the state
was not my fault,
so I dared not accept punishment.
The lord's return to the state
was not my achievement,
so I dare not accept reward.
When the Wú army entered Yǐng,
I feared the invaders and avoided trouble.
Now the lord has returned—
what service have I rendered?"
The lord said:
"If you won't accept, at least come see me."
Yuè replied:
"By the laws of Chǔ,
if a merchant wishes to see the ruler,
he must present great offerings or valuable pledges
before gaining audience.
Now my wisdom could not save the state,
my integrity did not die for the lord,
my courage could not resist the invaders—
to see you thus
would violate state law."
So he refused the command
and went into the valleys.
King Zhāo said to Sīmǎ Zǐqī:
"There is a man here
who lives most humbly,
yet speaks most nobly.
Find him for me.
I wish to be as brothers,
and ask him to be among the three lords."
Sīmǎ Zǐqī left his chariot and went seeking him on foot,
for five days and five nights,
until he found him,
saying:
"Not to save the state in peril
is unbenevolent.
Not to obey the lord's command
is unloyal.
To reject wealth and honor above,
embracing poverty and hardship below—
surely this is mistaken.
Now the lord wishes to be as brothers,
asks you to be among the three lords—
why do you not heed him?"
Shuō said:
"I know that the position of the Three Dukes is more honored than a butcher's stall.
I know that a salary of ten thousand zhōng is wealthier than the profits from slaughtering sheep.
Now, to see the benefits of rank and salary,
yet forget the rites of declining and accepting,
is not what I have heard to be right."
Thereupon, he declined the position of the Three Dukes,
and returned to his butcher's stall.
A gentleman heard of this and said:
"How extreme!
Such is the action of Butcher Yang.
He restrains himself and endures poverty while residing in his state."
Shuō said:
"What is called poverty?
I declined with propriety and thus ended my service to the state."
The gentleman said:
"To be in the depths and not rescue others from peril,
to see King Zhāo's virtue decline in Wú,
and to cherish one's treasure and cut off all traces,
thereby harming the state,
is to desire solely to preserve oneself.
This is being generous to oneself but stingy to the ruler,
narrow-minded and not a savior of the age."
"What then can be called saving the age?"
He said:
"Like Shēn Bó and Zhòng Shānfǔ,
they can be called saviors of the age.
In the past, when the virtue of Zhōu greatly declined,
and the Way was abandoned under King Lì,
Shēn Bó and Zhòng Shānfǔ assisted King Xuān,
brought order out of chaos and restored it to correctness,
causing the world to somewhat revive,
and the ancestral temples to flourish again.
Shēn Bó and Zhòng Shānfǔ then harmoniously guided the world,
corrected and remedied errors and faults,
promoted virtuous teachings,
raised up neglected scholars,
and all within the seas uniformly followed their influence.
Thus, the common people fervently sang of King Xuān's virtue.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The whole land of Zhōu rejoiced,
for it had a good bulwark.'
It also says:
'Whether the state is well or ill,
Zhòng Shānfǔ understands it.
He is both intelligent and wise,
thus preserving his person.
Day and night, he never slackens,
in serving the one man.'
Thus can one be called a savior of the age."
8.4 Cuī Zhù of Qí murdered Duke Zhuāng.
Jīng Kuàiruì was returning from a mission to Jìn,
and his servant said:
"Cuī Zhù has murdered Duke Zhuāng,
what will you do?"
Xíng Kuàikuì said:
"Drive on.
I will enter and die to repay my lord."
His servant said:
"The lord's lack of virtue
is known to all the neighboring feudal lords.
For you, sir, to die for him,
is it not misguided?"
Jīng Kuàiruì said:
"Well said.
Had you spoken earlier,
I could have remonstrated.
If my remonstrance was not heeded,
I could have left.
Now, I have neither remonstrated,
nor have I left.
I have heard that
he who eats another's food
should die for his affairs.
Since I have eaten the food of a disorderly lord,
how can I seek a well-ruled lord to die for?"
Thereupon, he drove his chariot in and died.
His servant said:
"If one has a disorderly lord,
one must still die for him.
I have a well-ruled master,
can I not die for him?"
Then, he tied the reins and cut his throat in the chariot.
A gentleman heard of this,
and said:
"Jīng Kuàiruì can be said to have upheld his integrity and died for righteousness.
As for the servant, there was no need for him to die;
it was like eating and drinking and encountering poison."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Day and night, he never slackens,
in serving the one man."
This refers to Master Jīng.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Not constant in his virtue,
he may incur disgrace."
This refers to the servant.
8.5 To remonstrate with deference and straightforwardness
is the best way.
To be blunt
is next.
To criticize and remonstrate is the lowest.
To be cowardly leads to death.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"He does not devour even the soft."
8.6 Sòng Wàn fought with Duke Zhuāng,
and was captured by Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng, having been defeated, housed him in the palace,
and after several months,
then sent him back.
He returned to become a high official in Sòng.
Sòng Wàn was gambling with Duke Mǐn,
and women were all by their side.
Wàn said:
"How extreme
is the goodness of the Marquis of Lǔ,
the beauty of the Marquis of Lǔ!
Among the feudal lords under heaven, the one fit to be ruler
is only the Marquis of Lǔ."
Duke Mǐn, proud before these women,
was jealous of his words,
and turned to say:
"You captive,
how can you know the beauty or ugliness of the Marquis of Lǔ?"
Sòng Wàn became angry,
struck Duke Mǐn and broke his neck.
Qiú Mù heard that the lord had been murdered,
hurried and arrived,
encountered him at the gate,
and brandishing his sword, shouted at him.
Wàn swung his arm and struck Qiú Mù,
shattered his head,
and his teeth stuck on the door leaf.
Qiú Mù can be said to have feared no strong opponent.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Only Zhòng Shānfǔ
does not devour even the soft,
nor spit out the hard."
8.7 What is permissible to the lord,
but not to the father,
a filial son does not do.
What is permissible to the father,
but not to the lord,
a gentleman also does not do.
Thus, the lord cannot be disregarded,
nor can the parent be disregarded.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"A joyful and courteous gentleman,
is a model for all directions."
8.8 When the Yellow Emperor ascended the throne,
he bestowed blessings, receiving the Mandate of Heaven,
unified the Way and cultivated virtue,
acting only with benevolence,
so that the world was peaceful and harmonious,
yet he had not seen the phoenix,
and only pondered its image.
Rising early in the morning after a night's sleep,
he summoned Tiān Lǎo and asked him:
"What is the image of the phoenix like?"
Tiān Lǎo replied:
"The image of the phoenix
has the front of a swan and the rear of a qilin,
a snake's neck and a fish's tail,
a dragon's pattern and a turtle's body,
a swallow's jaw and a chicken's beak,
it bears virtue and carries benevolence,
embraces the mean and holds righteousness.
Its small sound is like metal,
its large sound is like a drum.
It stretches its neck and spreads its wings,
with five colors brilliantly displayed.
Its movements stir the eight winds,
its breath responds to seasonal rains.
It eats with substance,
drinks with decorum.
When it goes, it marks the beginning of culture,
when it comes, it signifies the completion of excellence.
Only the phoenix can communicate with heavenly blessings,
respond to earthly spirits,
harmonize the five notes,
and encompass the nine virtues.
When the world has the Way,
if it obtains one aspect of the phoenix's image,
then the phoenix passes by.
If it obtains two aspects of the phoenix's image,
then the phoenix hovers over it.
If it obtains three aspects of the phoenix's image,
then the phoenix gathers there.
If it obtains four aspects of the phoenix's image,
then the phoenix descends in spring and autumn.
If it obtains five aspects of the phoenix's image,
then the phoenix dwells there for life."
The Yellow Emperor said:
"Alas,
truly so!
How dare I aspire to this!"
Thereupon, the Yellow Emperor donned yellow robes,
wore a yellow crown,
and fasted in the palace.
The phoenix then came, obscuring the sun.
The Yellow Emperor descended to the eastern steps,
facing west,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"The August Heaven bestows blessings,
I dare not decline the mandate!"
The phoenix then settled in the Emperor's eastern domain,
perched on the Emperor's parasol tree,
fed on the Emperor's bamboo fruits,
and never departed throughout his lifetime.
The Book of Songs says:
"The phoenixes fly,
rustling their wings,
and come to rest together."
8.9 Wénhóu of Wèi had a son named Jī,
and a younger son named Sù.
Sù, though younger, was established as heir.
Jī was enfeoffed in Zhōngshān,
and for three years there was no communication between them.
His tutor Zhào Cāngtáng said:
"A father may forget his son,
but a son should not forget his father.
Why not send an envoy?"
Jī said:
"I wish to,
but have no one to send."
Cāngtáng said:
"I beg to be sent as envoy."
Jī said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon he inquired about the ruler's preferences and delights.
It was said:
"The ruler favors northern dogs,
and delights in morning wild geese."
So he sought northern dogs and morning wild geese to bring along.
When Cāngtáng arrived,
he said:
"The lord of the northern borderland Zhōngshān,
has northern dogs and morning wild geese,
and sends Cāngtáng to bow twice and present them."
Wénhóu said:
"Jī knows I favor northern dogs,
and delight in morning wild geese."
Then he received the envoy.
Wénhóu said:
"Is Jī well?"
Cāngtáng assented but did not answer.
Three times he was asked and three times he did not answer.
Wénhóu said:
"Why do you not answer?"
Cāngtáng said:
"I have heard that feudal lords do not address their ruler by name.
Since you have granted him this humble city,
making him a minor state's lord,
if you ask using his name,
I dare not answer."
Wénhóu said:
"Is the lord of Zhōngshān well?"
Cāngtáng said:
"When I came,
he bowed in farewell at the outskirts."
Wénhóu said:
"How tall is the lord of Zhōngshān now?"
Cāngtáng said:
"In ritual,
one must compare people to their peers; when asking about feudal lords,
compare them to feudal lords.
At a feudal lord's court,
those standing aside are all subjects,
with none to compare him to.
However, the robes you bestowed are nearly outgrown."
Wénhóu said:
"What does the lord of Zhōngshān delight in?"
He replied:
"He delights in the Book of Songs."
Wénhóu said:
"Which parts of the Book of Songs does he delight in?"
He said:
"He delights in 'Shǔ Lí' and 'Chén Fēng'."
Wénhóu said:
"What is 'Shǔ Lí' about?"
He replied:
"The millet sways lush,
the sorghum sprouts.
My steps drag slow,
my heart wavers unsteady.
Those who know me say my heart grieves;
those who know me not ask what I seek.
Vast, vast the blue sky,
who has brought this upon me!"
Wénhóu said:
"Does he resent it?"
He said:
"He dares not resent,
but longs for the times."
Wénhóu said:
"What does 'Chén Fēng' say?"
He replied:
"Swift flies the morning wind,
through the dense northern woods.
Not seeing my lord,
my heart grieves keenly.
What to do, what to do,
he forgets me so much."
Thereupon Wénhóu was greatly pleased,
saying:
"To know the son, look at the mother;
to know the ruler, look at his envoys.
If the lord of Zhōngshān were not worthy,
how could he get the worthy?"
So he deposed the crown prince Sù,
and summoned the lord of Zhōngshān to be his heir.
The Book of Songs says:
"The phoenixes fly,
rustling their wings,
and come to rest together.
Gracious king with many good men,
they are at the gentleman's service,
pleasing the Son of Heaven."
The gentleman says:
"Being an envoy is not merely about worn carriages and tired horses;
it also requires conveying sincerity and trust,
communicating intentions and wills,
clarifying likes and dislikes,
and only then can one be sent."
8.10 Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù,
and its people adhered to him.
Confucius said:
"Tell me how you governed it."
He replied:
"I, Bùqí, timely opened the granaries,
relieved the distressed and poor,
and supplemented shortages."
Confucius said:
"This makes the common people adhere,
but it's not enough."
He replied:
"I rewarded the capable,
recruited the virtuous and talented,
and dismissed the unworthy."
Confucius said:
"This makes the scholars adhere,
but it's not enough."
He replied:
"Three whom I served as father
could teach filial piety.
Five whom I served as elder brothers,
twelve whom I befriended,
and one whom I took as teacher."
Confucius said:
"Three served as father,
five served as elder brothers,
enough to teach fraternal duty.
Twelve befriended,
enough to remove obstructions and blindness.
One taken as teacher,
enough to ensure no missteps in planning,
and no failures in actions.
Pity that what Bùqí governed was small;
had it been greater,
his achievements would rival Yáo and Shùn."
The Book of Songs says:
"A joyful and approachable gentleman,
is the parent of the people."
Zǐjiàn resembles this.
8.11 Measure the land and settle to establish a state,
exalt kindness and broaden benefits to win the masses,
clarify likes and dislikes to rectify laws and standards,
lead the people in farming efforts,
establish schools and academies for education,
serve the aged and nurture orphans to transform the people,
promote the worthy and reward achievements to encourage goodness,
punish the treacherous and dismiss faults to disgrace evil,
practice charioteering and archery to prevent troubles,
prohibit wickedness and stop depravity to eliminate harm,
connect with the worthy and befriend allies to broaden wisdom,
honor kin and unite clans to increase strength.
The Book of Songs says:
"A joyful and approachable gentleman."
8.12 Jǐnggōng of Qí sent an envoy to Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ took him up a nine-tiered tower,
and said to the envoy:
"Does Qí have a tower like this?"
The envoy said:
"My lord has a seat for governing,
with earthen steps of three levels,
thatched roofs untrimmed,
and unhewn rafters,
yet still considers the builders laboring,
and the dwellers at ease.
How could my lord have a tower like this?"
Thereupon the King of Chǔ felt ashamed.
The envoy can be said to have not disgraced his lord's command,
and was capable of independent responses.
8.13 The Commentary says:
"I, the young son, have made you succeed Duke Shào."
One who receives a mandate must have it conferred in the name of his ancestor.
When Confucius became the Minister of Crime of Lǔ,
the mandate declared:
"The descendant of Fúfǔ, son of the Duke of Sòng,
namely, Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ,
is hereby appointed as Minister of Crime."
Confucius said:
"Fúfǔ diligently served his sovereign, a role I fear I cannot adequately fulfill."
The Duke said:
"Do not decline."
The Commentary says:
When a feudal lord is virtuous,
the Son of Heaven bestows gifts upon him.
The first bestowal is chariots and horses,
the second is clothing,
the third is tiger warriors,
the fourth is musical instruments,
the fifth is a raised pathway,
the sixth is a vermilion door,
the seventh is bows and arrows,
the eighth is axes of authority,
the ninth is black millet wine.
The Book of Songs says:
"I present you with a jade ladle,
and a jar of black millet wine."
8.14 Duke Jǐng of Qí said to Zǐgòng:
"Whom does the master study under?"
He replied:
"Zhòngní of Lǔ."
The Duke said:
"Is Zhòngní worthy?"
He said:
"A sage,
how could he merely be worthy!"
Duke Jǐng chuckled and laughed, saying:
"In what way is he a sage?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I do not know."
Duke Jǐng flushed with anger and changed countenance.
He said:
"At first you called him a sage,
now you say you do not know,
why is that?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I carry heaven upon my head all my life,
yet I do not know the height of heaven.
I tread upon the earth all my life,
yet I do not know the thickness of the earth.
As for my serving Zhòngní,
it is like being thirsty and holding a ladle,
going to the river or sea to drink from it;
when my belly is full and I leave,
how could I know the depth of the river or sea?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"Master, your praise,
is it not excessive?"
Zǐgòng said:
"How would I dare to speak excessively?
I only fear my words fall short.
My praising Zhòngní
is like using both hands to scoop up soil and add it to Mount Tài;
its futility is clear.
If I did not praise Zhòngní,
it would be like using both hands to scrape soil from Mount Tài;
its lack of harm is also clear."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Well said!
But is it truly so?
Well said!
But is it truly so?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Continuous and orderly,
unfathomable and unconquerable."
8.15 One grain not rising is called insufficiency,
two grains not rising is called hunger,
three grains not rising is called famine,
four grains not rising is called devastation,
five grains not rising is called great calamity.
The rites for a great calamity:
the ruler does not eat multiple dishes,
terraces and pavilions are not adorned,
roads are not maintained,
officials make up deficits but do not impose new measures,
prayers are offered to spirits but no sacrifices are made,
these are the rites for a great calamity.
The Book of Songs says:
"Our land is struck by great devastation."
This refers to that.
8.16 In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven enfeoffed feudal lords,
it was called a fief.
A lord of a hundred lǐ received thirty lǐ,
a lord of seventy lǐ received twenty lǐ,
a lord of fifty lǐ received ten lǐ.
Even if their descendants later committed crimes and
were deposed,
if there were worthy descendants, they would guard the land,
generation after generation sacrificing to the first lord who received the enfeoffment.
This is called reviving extinguished states and continuing severed lineages.
The Book of Documents says:
"Now I sacrifice to the former kings,
may your ancestors join in the sacrifice."
8.17 Mount Liáng collapsed,
the ruler of Jìn summoned his minister Bó Zōng.
On the way, he encountered a cart-puller,
whose cart blocked the road.
Bó Zōng ordered his attendant to dismount,
intending to whip the cart-puller.
The cart-puller said:
"Is the lord's hurry not for a distant matter?
To proceed without knowing the situation—
is that acceptable?" Bó Zōng was pleased,
and asked where he lived.
He said:
"I am from Jiàng."
Bó Zōng said:
"Have you heard anything?"
He said:
"Mount Liáng has collapsed,
blocking the river,
so that it has not flowed for three days;
that is why you are summoned."
Bó Zōng said:
"What should be done?"
He said:
"Heaven has mountains,
Heaven collapses them.
Heaven has rivers,
Heaven blocks them.
What will Bó Zōng do about it?"
Bó Zōng asked him privately.
He said:
"The lord should lead his officials in plain clothes to weep for it,
then sacrifice to it,
and the river will flow again."
Bó Zōng asked his name,
but he did not tell.
Bó Zōng arrived,
and the lord asked Bó Zōng.
He answered with the cart-puller's words.
Thereupon, the lord, in plain clothes, led his officials to weep for it,
then sacrificed to it,
and the river flowed again.
The lord asked Bó Zōng how he knew,
but Bó Zōng did not say he received it from the cart-puller,
falsely claiming he knew it himself.
Confucius heard of it and said:
"Will Bó Zōng not be without descendants!
He appropriated another's good idea."
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven sends down death and disorder,
destroying our established king."
It also says:
"Revere the majesty of Heaven,
and thus preserve yourself."
8.18 Duke Píng of Jìn sent Fàn Zhāo to observe the governance of Qí.
Duke Jǐng hosted a banquet for him.
Yànzǐ was present.
Fàn Zhāo hurriedly said:
"I wish to toast with the ruler's spare cup."
Duke Jǐng looked to his attendants and said:
"Pour from my cup and offer it to the guest."
Yànzǐ replied:
"Remove the cup."
Fàn Zhāo was displeased,
and began to dance.
He turned to the Grand Music Master and said:
"Play for me the music of Chéngzhōu,
I wish to dance."
The Grand Music Master replied:
"This blind servant is not familiar with it."
Fàn Zhāo rose and left.
Duke Jǐng said to Yànzǐ:
"Jìn is
a great state under heaven,
and sent Fàn Zhāo to observe Qí's governance;
now you have angered the envoy of a great state—
what shall we do?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Fàn Zhāo's character
is not crude and ignorant of rites;
he intended to test our lord,
so I deliberately did not comply."
Thereupon, Duke Jǐng summoned the Grand Music Master and asked:
"Fàn Zhāo asked you to play the music of Chéngzhōu,
why did you not play it?"
His reply matched Yànzǐ's.
Thereupon, Fàn Zhāo returned and reported to Duke Píng:
"Qí cannot be annexed.
I tested their lord,
and Yànzǐ knew it.
I challenged their music,
and the Grand Music Master knew it."
Confucius heard of it and said:
"Excellent, Yànzǐ!
Without leaving the space of the sacrificial vessels,
he repelled the enemy a thousand lǐ away."
The Book of Songs says:
"Truly he aids and orders the Zhōu people,
When he spreads his awe,
None are not awed and tremble."
8.19 What are the Three Dukes?
They are the Minister of Works,
Minister of War, and Minister of Education.
The Minister of War is in charge of heaven,
the Minister of Works is in charge of earth,
and the Minister of Education is in charge of people.
Thus when yīn and yáng are not harmonious,
the four seasons are not regulated,
the stars lose their proper courses,
and calamitous changes occur abnormally,
the Minister of War is held responsible.
When mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
streams and valleys cease to flow,
the five grains cannot be planted,
and plants and trees do not flourish,
the Minister of Works is held responsible.
When ruler and ministers are not upright,
human relations are not harmonious,
the state has many robbers and thieves,
and those below resent those above,
the Minister of Education is held responsible.
Thus the Three Dukes manage their duties,
worry about their responsibilities,
raise their arguments,
and clarify what is hidden -
this is the responsibility of the Three Dukes.
The Book of Songs says:
"Many are the officers,
And King Wén thereby rests in peace."
It also says:
"He brightly illumined the Zhōu people,
Orderly arranging those in position."
This speaks of each being competent in their office.
8.20 When a worthy ruler governs,
he is gentle, kind, and harmonious,
tolerant and loving,
his punishments are clear but sparing,
he delights in rewards and dislikes penalties.
He transforms customs and honors teaching,
preserves life and does not kill,
spreads kindness and bestows grace,
his benevolence is not partial in giving.
He does not seize the people's labor,
conscripted service does not exceed the season,
the hundred surnames can farm,
each family has harvests stored,
the people are not cold or hungry,
and food does not rot.
Artisans do not make useless things,
carved patterns are not sold in markets.
Axes enter the mountain forests according to the season.
The state has no unemployed scholars,
all are employed in the world.
The common people are joyful and abundant,
distant people from beyond the borders return to righteousness,
relying on interpreters while presenting gifts,
thus wind and rain are not violent.
The Lesser Odes says:
"Dense are the clouds,
Rising with gentle rain."
From this we clearly know that in great peace there are no raging winds or violent rains.
8.21 What was born yesterday?
What is accomplished today?
One must think of returning to simplicity,
one must think of managing one's livelihood.
Be cautious day by day,
complete like a metal wall.
The Book of Songs says:
"I daily go forward,
And monthly march on.
Rising early and retiring late,
Do not disgrace those who gave you birth."
8.22 Officials become negligent when they have achievements,
illness worsens after slight recovery,
calamity arises from laziness,
filial piety declines because of wife and children.
Examining these four things,
be as careful at the end as at the beginning.
The Book of Changes says:
"The little fox, after nearly crossing,
Wets its tail."
The Book of Songs says:
"There is nothing without a beginning,
But few things reach their end."
8.23 When Confucius was leisurely dwelling at home,
Zǐgòng lifted his gown's hem and came forward, saying:
"This disciple has served you for years,
my talent is exhausted and wisdom spent,
I've exerted myself in learning,
but cannot advance further.
I beg to take a rest from one thing."
Confucius said:
"Cì, from what do you wish to rest?"
He replied:
"Cì wishes to rest from serving rulers."
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'Morning and night, never slacken,
In serving the one man.'
To serve like this is not easy -
how can you rest from it!"
He said:
"Cì wishes to rest from serving his father."
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'The filial son never fails,
Forever he confers his pattern on your kind.'
To serve like this is not easy -
how can you rest from it!"
He said:
"Cì wishes to rest from serving his brothers."
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'Wife and children love and agree,
As when lute and zither harmonize.
Brothers then are friendly,
Happy and delightful.'
To serve like this is not easy -
how can you rest from it!"
He said:
"Cì wishes to rest from farming."
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'By day you gather the reeds,
By night you twist the ropes,
Hasten to mend the roof,
Then begin to sow the hundred grains.'
To serve like this is not easy -
how can you rest from it!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Does a gentleman also have rest?"
Confucius said:
"'Only when the coffin lid closes does the sowing stop,
Not knowing how easily time passes by.'
This refers to when a gentleman rests.
Thus learning never ceases,
only stopping when the coffin lid closes."
The Book of Songs says:
"Daily achievement, monthly progress."
This speaks of learners.
8.24 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Rǎn Yǒu:
"Are ordinary people sufficient as they are,
or must they learn before becoming gentlemen?"
Rǎn Yǒu replied:
"I have heard that
although there may be fine jade,
without carving and polishing it cannot become a vessel;
although one may have excellent natural qualities,
without learning one cannot become a gentleman."
The Duke said:
"How do we know this is so?"
Take Zǐlù -
he was a rustic from Biàn.
Zǐgòng -
he was a merchant from Wèi.
Both studied under Confucius,
and became renowned scholars throughout the world.
When feudal lords heard of them,
none failed to respect them.
When high ministers and officials heard of them,
none failed to cherish them.
This was because of their learning.
Formerly, Wú, Chǔ, Yān, and Dài
plotted to join forces and attack Qín.
Tiāo Gǔ,
son of a gatekeeper,
was sent by Qín as envoy to them,
whereupon he thwarted their plot
and stopped their troops.
When he returned to his country,
the King of Qín was greatly pleased
and appointed him as High Minister.
As for Bǎilǐ Xī,
he was a beggar from Qí,
driven out to western Qí
with no means to advance himself,
he sold himself for five sheepskins
to buy a cart with yoke.
When he met Duke Mù of Qín,
he was appointed chancellor,
and subsequently dominated the Western Róng.
Tàigōng Wàng in his youth was a son-in-law living with his wife's family,
in old age was sent away,
butchered oxen at Zhāogē,
hired himself out at Jíjīn,
fished at Pánxī,
until King Wén raised and employed him,
enfeoffing him in Qí.
Guǎn Zhòng personally shot Duke Huán,
yet he relinquished his desire for revenge,
established him as chancellor,
preserved what was perishing and restored what had been severed,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and unified and rectified the world.
These four men,
all once experienced lowliness, poverty, and humiliation,
yet their fame spread to later generations;
was this not due to the results of learning?
From this we observe,
a scholar must engage in learning,
only then can he become a nobleman.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Daily advancing, monthly progressing."
Thereupon, Duke Āi chuckled and laughed, saying:
"Although I am not clever,
I beg to follow the master's teachings."
8.25 Zēngzǐ committed a fault,
Zēng Xī took a staff and struck him.
He fell to the ground,
after a while he revived,
rose and said:
"Master, are you not unwell?"
The people of Lǔ praised Zēngzǐ's virtue,
and informed the Master of this.
The Master told his disciples:
"Shēn, come here."
"Have you not heard how Shùn in ancient times was a son?
For light whips he awaited the beating,
for heavy staffs he fled.
When sought to be employed,
he was never not at his side;
when sought to be killed,
he was never to be found.
Now you offered yourself to await violent anger,
standing erect without leaving;
are you not a subject of the sovereign?
To kill a subject of the Son of Heaven,
what would the crime be?"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Gentle and mild,
thus reaching harmony."
It also says:
"With a pleasant countenance and smiling,
not angry but instructing."
8.26 Duke Jǐng of Qí had a man make a bow,
which took three years to complete.
Duke Jǐng obtained the bow and shot,
but it could not penetrate three layers of armor.
Duke Jǐng was angry,
and was about to kill the bow-maker.
The bow-maker's wife went to see Duke Jǐng
and said:
"I am the daughter of a man of Cài,
and the wife of a bow-maker.
This bow,
from the south of Tài Shān,
uses the mulberry wood of Wū Hào,
the horn of a red ox,
the sinews of a Jīng River deer,
and the glue of river fish.
These four materials
are the finest in the world,
it should not penetrate so few layers.
Moreover, I have heard that Xī Gōng's chariot
cannot move by itself;
Mò Yé, though sharp,
cannot cut alone;
there must be something to wield them.
The way of shooting
is: the left hand as if resisting,
the right hand as if clinging to a branch,
the palm as if holding an egg,
the four fingers as if breaking a short stick,
the right hand releases it,
the left hand unaware;
this is indeed the way of shooting."
Duke Jǐng used this as a model and shot,
penetrating seven layers.
The Cài man's husband was immediately released.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"He loves what is upright."
8.27 In Qí, there was one who offended Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng was greatly enraged,
bound him and placed him in the court,
summoned his attendants to dismember him,
and declared that any who dared remonstrate would be executed.
Yànzǐ held his head with his left hand,
sharpened a knife with his right,
looked up and asked:
"In ancient times, when wise kings and sage lords
dismembered people,
from which limb did they begin?"
Duke Jǐng rose from his mat and said:
"Release him!
The fault lies with me."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"He loves what is upright."
8.28 The *Tradition* says:
When dwelling is regulated, the complexion is beautiful;
when eating and drinking are regulated, the breath is refined;
when speech is regulated, trust is heard;
when thoughts are regulated, success is achieved;
when will is regulated, it becomes full.
When these five are regulated,
then the spirit dwells therein.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Both harmonious and peaceful,
following my chime's sound."
8.29 Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Hú Juànzǐ:
"Is a worthy father sufficient to rely on?"
He replied:
"Not sufficient."
"Is a worthy son sufficient to rely on?"
He replied:
"Not sufficient."
"Is a worthy elder brother sufficient to rely on?"
He said:
"Not sufficient."
"Is a worthy younger brother sufficient to rely on?"
He replied:
"Not sufficient."
"Are worthy ministers sufficient to rely on?"
He replied:
"Not sufficient."
Marquis Wén changed countenance, flaring up in anger, saying:
"I asked you about these five,
why do you deem each one insufficient?"
He replied:
"No father was worthier than Yáo,
yet Dān Zhū was exiled.
No son was worthier than Shùn,
yet Gǔsǒu was obstinate.
No elder brother was worthier than Shùn,
yet Xiàng was arrogant.
No younger brother was worthier than the Duke of Zhōu,
yet Guǎn Shū was executed.
No minister was worthier than Tāng or Wǔ,
yet Jié and Zhòu were attacked.
To expect from others leads to failure;
to rely on others does not last.
If you, my lord, wish to govern well,
start with yourself.
How can one rely on others?"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Seek your own blessing."
8.30 Tāng composed the "Hù"
Hearing its gōng note,
makes people warm, kind, and broad-minded.
Hearing its shāng note,
makes people upright, incorruptible, and fond of righteousness.
Hearing its jué note,
makes people compassionate and loving benevolence.
Hearing its zhǐ note,
makes people joyful in nurturing and fond of giving.
Hearing its yǔ note,
makes people respectful and fond of propriety.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended."
8.31 Confucius said:
"The *Yì* places 'Tóng Rén' before 'Dà Yǒu',
followed by 'Qiān',
is this not appropriate?"
Thus, the way of heaven diminishes the full and benefits the humble;
the way of earth transforms the full and flows to the humble;
spirits and gods harm the full and bless the humble;
the way of humans dislikes the full and favors the humble.
Humility
means restraining affairs and reducing oneself.
The way to maintain fullness
is to restrain and reduce it;
this is the practice of the virtue of humility.
Those who follow it meet with good fortune,
those who oppose it meet with misfortune.
The Five Emperors have passed,
the Three Kings have declined,
but one who could practice the virtue of humility
was surely the Duke of Zhōu.
He was the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
the uncle of King Chéng,
acting as regent for seven years,
those whom he received with gifts and met as teachers numbered ten,
those whom he returned pledges to and met as friends numbered thirteen,
scholars from poor alleys and humble huts whom he first met numbered forty-nine,
those he regularly advanced for their goodness numbered a hundred,
those who served at court numbered a thousand,
his remonstrating ministers numbered five,
his assisting ministers numbered five,
his admonishing ministers numbered six,
he carried arms all the way to enfeoffment as a lord,
and the scholars of the same surname numbered a hundred.
Confucius said:
"If the Duke of Zhōu were taken as the standard for rewarding the world,
then those of the same clan would be many,
while those of different clans would be few."
Therefore, one who possesses virtuous conduct and tolerance yet maintains them with reverence is honored;
one who has vast lands yet preserves them with frugality is secure;
one who holds a high position and heavy salary yet maintains them with humility is noble;
one who has numerous people and strong soldiers yet guards them with caution is victorious;
one who is intelligent and wise yet preserves it with seeming foolishness is wise;
one who is widely learned and strong in memory yet maintains it with modesty does not overflow.
These six are all virtues of humility.
The Yì Jīng says:
"Humility brings success; the noble man carries it through to the end, which is auspicious."
To be able to end auspiciously in this way
is the way of the noble man.
As exalted as the Son of Heaven,
as rich as possessing all within the four seas,
yet if one's virtue is not humble,
it can lead to the loss of one's life,
as was the case with Jié and Zhòu.
How much more so for the common people?
Now, the Yì Jīng contains one way,
which, on a grand scale, is sufficient to govern the world,
on a medium scale, to bring peace to family and state,
and on a personal level, to protect oneself.
Is it not the virtue of humility?
The Shī Jīng says:
"Tāng descended without delay,
his sage-like reverence daily ascended."
8.32 In the past, Tián Zǐfāng went out
and saw an old horse on the road.
He sighed with deep feeling,
and asked the driver:
"What horse is this?"
The reply was:
"It is an old horse from the state's stables,
worn out and no longer of use,
so it was turned out to pasture."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"To use its strength when young
and discard it when old—
this is something a benevolent person would not do."
He paid with bolts of silk to redeem it.
Impoverished scholars heard of this
and knew where to turn their hearts.
The Shī Jīng says:
"Tāng descended without delay,
his sage-like reverence daily ascended."
8.33 Duke Zhuāng of Qí went out hunting,
and a mantis raised its leg as if to strike his chariot wheel.
He asked his driver:
"What insect is this?"
The driver replied:
"This is a mantis.
As an insect,
it knows only to advance and not to retreat,
not measuring its strength and lightly approaching the enemy."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"If it were a person, it would surely be a brave warrior of the world."
Thereupon, he turned his chariot to avoid it,
and brave warriors came to submit to him.
The Shī Jīng says:
"Tāng descended without delay."
8.34 Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Lǐ Kè:
"Do people incur hatred?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Yes.
The noble are hated by the humble,
the rich by the poor,
the wise by the foolish."
Marquis Wén said:
"Good.
If one practices these three things,
can one avoid being hated?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Yes.
I have heard that if the noble are humble towards the lowly,
then the masses will not hate them.
If the rich share with the poor,
then impoverished scholars will not hate them.
If the wise teach the foolish,
then the ignorant will not hate them."
Marquis Wén said:
"Excellent words!
Even Yáo and Shùn found such things difficult.
Although I am not clever,
I ask to abide by these words."
The Shī Jīng says:
"No leisure to rest."
8.35 There was a bird here
that built its nest on the tip of the reeds.
When the heavens sighed and the wind blew,
the reeds broke and the nest was destroyed.
Why?
Because what it relied on was weak.
The bees at the altar of Jì are not attacked,
and the rats at the altar of Shè are not smoked out,
not because the bees and rats are divine,
but because what they rely on is secure.
Therefore, the sage seeks worthy men to assist him.
The fish that can swallow a boat is large,
but if it drifts and loses water,
it can be controlled by ants,
because it has lost its support.
Hence it is said:
"If your virtue is not bright,
then there are none behind or beside you;
if your virtue is not bright,
it is because you have no ministers or high officials."
9.1 When Mèngzǐ was young and reciting,
his mother was weaving.
Mèngzǐ suddenly stopped,
then started again.
His mother knew he was distracted,
called him and asked:
"Why did you stop?"
He replied:
"I lost my place and found it again."
His mother took a knife and cut through her weaving,
using this to admonish him.
From then on,
Mèngzǐ was never distracted again.
When Mèngzǐ was young,
the eastern neighbor killed a pig.
Mèngzǐ asked his mother:
"Why did the eastern neighbor kill a pig?"
His mother said:
"To feed you."
Then she regretted her words,
saying:
"When I was pregnant with this child,
I would not sit if the mat was not straight,
nor eat if the cut was not proper—
this was prenatal education.
Now that he has understanding, to deceive him is to teach him dishonesty."
So she bought pork from the eastern neighbor to feed him,
to show she was not deceitful.
The Shī Jīng says:
"May your descendants be endless!"
This speaks of a worthy mother making her son worthy.
9.2 Tiánzǐ served as prime minister,
and after three years returned home on leave,
bringing a hundred yì of gold to present to his mother.
His mother said:
"How did you obtain this gold?"
He replied:
"It is from my salary."
His mother said:
"As prime minister for three years, have you not eaten?
To conduct official duties like this
is not what I desire.
A filial son in serving his parents
exhausts his efforts with sincerity;
unrighteous gains
do not enter his home.
As a son, one must
be filial.
You should take this away."
Tiánzǐ left in shame,
went to court and returned the gold,
then retreated and requested to be imprisoned.
The king admired his mother,
appreciated her righteousness,
pardoned Tiánzǐ's offense,
ordered him to resume his post as prime minister,
and bestowed the gold upon his mother.
The Shī Jīng says:
"May your descendants be endless!"
9.3 Confucius was traveling
and heard very sorrowful weeping.
Confucius said:
"Hurry, hurry!
There is a worthy person ahead."
When they arrived, it was Gāo Yú,
clad in coarse cloth and holding a sickle,
weeping by the roadside.
Confucius stepped down from his carriage to speak with him,
saying:
"You have no mourning,
why do you weep so sorrowfully?"
Gāo Yú said:
"I have three losses.
In my youth, I studied
and traveled around the various states,
thereby neglecting my parents—
this is the first loss.
I exalted my aspirations,
was selective in my service,
refusing to serve mediocre rulers,
and thus achieved nothing in my later years—
this is the second loss.
I had deep friendships but lightly broke them off,
Three losses have occurred. The tree desires stillness but the wind does not cease;
the son wishes to care for his parents but they do not await him;
that which passes and cannot be pursued is time;
that which departs and cannot be seen again are one's parents.
I beg to take my leave from here."
He stood withered and died.
Confucius said:
"Let my disciples take warning,
this is sufficient to understand."
Thereupon, thirteen disciples bade farewell and returned home to care for their parents.
9.4 Zǐlù said:
"Suppose there is a person here
who rises early and retires late,
with calloused hands and feet and a dark, weathered face,
cultivating the five grains to serve his parents,
yet he does not have the reputation of being filial.
Why is this?"
Confucius said:
"I suspect his demeanor lacks respect, perhaps?
His expression is not compliant, perhaps?
His speech is not humble, perhaps?
The ancients had a saying:
'Clothing and food,
you never come close to.'
You labor to serve your parents;
if you lack these three shortcomings,
why would you not have the reputation of being filial?
Perhaps those you befriend are not virtuous people?
Sit,
and I will tell you.
Even with the strength of a champion of the state,
one cannot lift oneself up.
It is not for lack of strength,
but because the circumstance is not favorable.
Therefore, the noble person at home is devotedly filial,
and abroad befriends the worthy.
How could they lack the reputation of being filial?"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"My parents are very near."
9.5 Bó Yá played the qín,
and Zhōng Zǐqī listened to him.
Just as he played
with his mind set on Tài Shān.
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How excellently you play the qín,
as lofty as Tài Shān!"
A short while later,
his mind was set on flowing water.
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How excellently you play the qín,
as vast as the rivers!"
After Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá broke his qín and severed the strings,
and never played the qín again for the rest of his life,
believing there was no one in the world worth playing for.
Not only is this so with the qín,
but also with the worthy.
If it is not their time,
then how can the worthy accomplish their achievements?
9.6 Qín attacked Wèi,
defeated it,
and the youngest son fled and could not be found.
A decree was issued in the state of Wèi:
"Whoever finds the young lord will be rewarded with a thousand jīn of gold;
whoever hides him will be punished with the extermination of ten clans."
The young lord's wet nurse fled with him.
Someone said to the wet nurse:
"The reward for finding the young lord is very great;
you, wet nurse, must know where the young lord is and should tell."
The wet nurse replied:
"I do not know his whereabouts.
Even if I knew,
if death comes, then death it is,
but I cannot speak.
To raise someone else's child,
and not be able to keep it secret but to speak of it,
is to betray one's superior and fear death.
I have heard that loyalty does not betray superiors,
and courage does not fear death.
Those who raise others' children do so to give them life,
not to ensure their death.
How can one, for the sake of profit and fear of execution,
abandon righteousness and act deceitfully?
I cannot live and let the young lord die alone."
Thereupon, she fled with the young lord into the marshes.
The Qín army saw them and shot at them;
the wet nurse shielded him with her body,
was hit by twelve arrows,
and thus did not let the young lord be hit.
The King of Qín heard of this,
feasted her with the Tàiláo sacrifice,
and enfeoffed her brother as a senior official.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be rolled away."
9.7 Zǐlù said:
"If others are good to me,
I am also good to them.
If others are not good to me,
I am not good to them."
Zǐgòng said:
"If others are good to me,
I am also good to them.
If others are not good to me,
I then guide them with advances and retreats, that is all."
Yán Huí said:
"If others are good to me,
I am also good to them.
If others are not good to me,
I am still good to them."
The three disciples each held different views,
and asked the Master.
The Master said:
"What Yóu holds
is the speech of barbarians.
What Cì says
is the speech of friends.
What Huí says
is the speech of kin."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"If a man is without goodness,
why should I regard him as a brother?"
9.8 Duke Jǐng of Qí indulged in drink,
got drunk, took off his clothes and cap,
and played the qín to amuse himself.
He turned to his attendants and said:
"Do virtuous men also enjoy this?"
The attendants said:
"The ears and eyes of virtuous men are like those of others;
why would they alone not enjoy this!"
Duke Jǐng said:
"Harness the carriage to welcome Yànzǐ."
Yànzǐ heard of this,
and came in full court attire.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Today, I have this pleasure;
I wish to share it with you, Minister."
Yànzǐ said:
"Your words are mistaken.
In the state of Qí, anyone over five chǐ tall
has the strength to overcome both Yīng and you,
yet they dare not cause disorder;
it is because they fear ritual.
Thus, if the Son of Heaven lacks ritual, he cannot protect the altars of soil and grain;
if the feudal lords lack ritual, they cannot protect their states.
If a superior lacks ritual, he cannot command his subordinates;
if a subordinate lacks ritual, he cannot serve his superior.
If a minister lacks ritual, he cannot govern his family;
if brothers lack ritual, they cannot live together for long.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'If a man has no ritual,
he might as well die quickly.'"
Duke Jǐng looked ashamed,
left his mat, and apologized:
"I am unvirtuous,
with unworthy attendants
who have misled me with indulgence,
leading to this.
I ask to execute my attendants to atone for my fault."
Yànzǐ said:
"Your attendants are not at fault.
If you, my lord, love ritual,
then those with ritual will come,
and those without ritual will leave.
If you, my lord, hate ritual,
then those without ritual will come,
and those with ritual will leave.
What crime have your attendants committed?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"Excellent!"
Then he changed his clothes and sat properly,
and three rounds of wine were served.
Yànzǐ took his leave and departed.
Duke Jǐng bowed and saw him off.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"If a man has no ritual,
why does he not die quickly!"
9.9 The *Tradition* says:
Táng Yī Ruò knocked on Confucius's door and said:
"Is Qiū here?
Is Qiū here?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"The noble person honors the worthy and accommodates the multitude,
praises the good and pities the incapable,
is kind to both insiders and outsiders,
and what he himself does not desire,
he does not impose on others.
Why do you speak my teacher's name?"
Táng Yī Ruò said:
"Why do you, so young, speak so sharply!"
Zǐgòng said:
"If a large carriage is not strong, it cannot bear its load;
if the qín and sè are not taut, they cannot produce their music.
Your words are sharp,
therefore I respond sharply."
Táng Yī Ruò said:
"I initially thought you had the strength of a swan,
but now I see you are just a fledgling."
Zǐgòng said:
"Without the strength of a swan,
how could it lift its wings?"
The Book of Songs says:
"Like cutting and filing,
like carving and polishing."
9.10 Duke Jǐng of Qí went hunting at Zhāohuá Pond,
when Yán Zhūojù, who was in charge of the birds, lost them.
Duke Jǐng was angry and wanted to kill him.
Yànzǐ said:
"Zhūojù has four capital offenses,
I beg to enumerate them and then execute him."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Agreed."
Yànzǐ said:
"Zhūojù!
You were in charge of our lord's birds and lost them—
this is the first offense.
You caused our lord to kill a man over birds—
this is the second offense.
You caused the feudal lords of the four states to hear of this,
making them think our lord values birds over scholars—
this is the third offense.
If the Son of Heaven hears of this,
he will surely demote our lord,
endanger his altars of grain and soil,
and cut off his ancestral temple—
this is the fourth offense.
With these four offenses,
he certainly deserves death without pardon,
I beg to carry out the execution."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Stop!
This is also my fault.
I wish you would apologize to him on my behalf."
The Book of Songs says:
"He is the upholder of the state's rectitude."
9.11 Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Xiè Hú:
"I wish to appoint a governor for Xīhé,
who would be suitable?"
Xiè Hú replied:
"Jīng Bóliǔ is a worthy man,
he would probably do."
The marquis was about to appoint Jīng Bóliǔ as governor of Xīhé.
Jīng Bóliǔ asked his attendants:
"Who recommended me to our lord?"
They all said:
"Xiè Hú."
Jīng Bóliǔ went to see Xiè Hú and thanked him, saying:
"You have magnanimously overlooked my faults,
and recommended me to the lord.
I humbly bow in gratitude."
Xiè Hú said:
"Recommending you was public duty,
bearing a grudge against you is my private feeling.
Public duty has been fulfilled,
but my grudge against you remains as before."
He drew his bow and shot at him,
the arrow traveled ten paces and disappeared—
this can be called courage.
The Book of Songs says:
"He is the upholder of the state's rectitude."
9.12 In Chǔ there was a man skilled in physiognomy,
his predictions never failed,
and he was renowned throughout the state.
King Zhuāng summoned him and asked about it.
He replied:
"I cannot read people's faces,
but I can judge them by their friends.
Observing commoners,
if their friends are all filial and fraternal,
sincere, cautious, and law-abiding,
then their households will surely prosper daily,
and their persons will surely become more secure daily—
these are what we call fortunate men.
Observing those who serve their lord,
if their friends are all honest and trustworthy,
virtuous and fond of goodness,
then their handling of affairs will improve daily,
and their official rank will advance daily—
these are what we call fortunate ministers.
Observing a ruler,
if his court ministers are mostly worthy,
his attendants mostly loyal,
and when the ruler errs,
they all remonstrate and correct him—
then the state will become more secure daily,
the ruler more respected daily,
and his fame more illustrious daily—
this is what we call a fortunate ruler.
I cannot read people's faces,
but I can judge them by their friends."
The king said:
"Excellent!"
His method of employing the worthy and using the capable to hegemonize the world
began with encountering this advice.
The Book of Songs says:
"That man,
is the ornament of the state."
9.13 Confucius was traveling in the wilderness of Shǎoyuán,
when he saw a woman weeping in the marshes,
her voice very mournful.
Confucius
sent a disciple to ask her,
saying:
"Madam, why do you weep so mournfully?"
The woman said:
"Just now, while cutting mugwort for fuel, I lost my mugwort hairpin,
that is why I grieve."
The disciple said:
"To lose a mugwort hairpin while cutting mugwort—
what is there to grieve about?"
The woman said:
"It's not the loss of the hairpin that pains me,
but that I cannot forget the old."
9.14 The Tradition says:
When a gentleman hears the Way,
he takes it in through his ears,
stores it in his heart,
examines it with benevolence,
preserves it with integrity,
practices it with righteousness,
and expresses it with humility—
therefore people cannot but listen with open minds.
When a petty man hears the Way,
he takes it in through his ears,
and speaks it out through his mouth—
merely talking about it.
It is like eating one's fill and then vomiting it out—
not only does it not benefit the skin and flesh,
but it also goes against one's will.
The Book of Songs says:
"How can it be settled?"
9.15 Confucius was wandering with Zǐgòng, Zǐlù, and Yán Yuān on Róng Mountain.
Confucius sighed deeply and said:
"Each of you speak your aspirations,
and I will observe them.
Yóu, what about you?"
He replied:
"I wish to have white plumes like the moon,
red plumes like cinnabar,
to strike bells and drums—
their sound heard above by heaven,
and shaking the earth below—
leading troops to attack,
only Yóu is capable of this."
Confucius said:
"A brave warrior!
Cì, what about you?"
He replied:
"I wish to wear plain clothes and a white cap,
to be an envoy between two states,
without carrying a weapon of any size,
or a peck or dou of grain,
and make the two states as close as brothers."
Confucius said:
"An eloquent diplomat!
Huí, what about you?"
He replied:
"Salted fish should not be stored in the same basket as orchids and angelica,
Jié and Zhòu could not govern in the same era as Yáo and Shùn.
Since the two have spoken,
what is there for Huí to say?"
Confucius said:
"Huí has a mean heart."
Yán Yuān said:
"I wish to serve as minister to an enlightened king and sage ruler,
so that city walls need no repair,
moats need no digging,
yīn and yáng are harmoniously balanced,
every household is well-provided and every person content,
and weapons from the arsenals are melted to make farm tools."
Confucius said:
"A great scholar!
Yóu, come here—
with your limited scope, what can you attack?
Cì, come here—
with your glib tongue, what can you envoy?
I wish to wear the cap of office and serve as your steward."
9.16 A worthy scholar does not eat from shame,
nor gain from disgrace.
Lǎozǐ says:
"Which is dearer, fame or life?
Which is greater, life or wealth?
Which is worse, gain or loss?
Therefore excessive love must lead to great expense,
abundant hoarding must lead to heavy loss.
Knowing contentment avoids disgrace,
knowing when to stop avoids danger—
thus one can long endure.
Great perfection seems flawed,
yet its use is unimpaired.
Great fullness seems empty,
yet its use is inexhaustible."
The straightest seems bent,
The most eloquent seems tongue-tied,
The most skillful seems clumsy,
Yet their usefulness is inexhaustible.
No crime is greater than excessive desire,
No misfortune greater than discontent,
Thus knowing contentment's satisfaction brings constant fulfillment."
9.17 Mèngzǐ's wife was alone in her room,
sitting with legs spread.
When Mèngzǐ entered and saw her,
he told his mother:
"My wife is impolite,
I request to divorce her."
His mother asked:
"Why?"
He replied:
"She sat with legs spread."
His mother said:
"How did you know?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"I saw it with my own eyes."
His mother said:
"It is you who were impolite,
not your wife.
Doesn't the Book of Rites say:
'When about to enter a gate,
ask who is inside.
When about to ascend the hall,
raise your voice.
When about to enter a room,
keep your eyes down.'
This means not to take others unprepared.
Now you went to her private quarters,
entered without making sound,
causing her to be seen sitting with legs spread -
this is your impoliteness,
not your wife's."
Thereupon Mèngzǐ blamed himself,
and dared not divorce his wife.
The Book of Songs says:
"When gathering mustard and turnips,
do not reject their roots."
9.18 Confucius exited the east gate of Wèi,
meeting Gūbù Zǐqīng,
and said:
"Disciples, steer the carriage aside.
Someone is coming
who will certainly read my fortune.
Take note."
Gūbù Zǐqīng likewise said:
"Disciples, steer the carriage aside.
A sage is coming."
Confucius descended and walked,
as Gūbù Zǐqīng approached and observed him for fifty paces,
then followed gazing for fifty more paces.
Turning to Zǐgòng, he asked:
"Who is this man?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"He is my teacher,
the so-called Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ."
Gūbù Zǐqīng said:
"Is this Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ?
I have indeed heard of him."
Zǐgòng asked:
"What is your opinion of my teacher?"
Gūbù Zǐqīng said:
"He has Yáo's forehead,
Shùn's eyes,
Yǔ's neck,
and Gāo Yáo's mouth.
Viewed from the front,
he radiates majesty like a king.
Viewed from behind,
he has high shoulders and weak spine.
These are what make him inferior to the four sages."
Zǐgòng sighed.
Gūbù Zǐqīng said:
"Why do you worry?
His soiled face is not ugly,
his rush-like mouth needs no support.
Gazing from afar,
he appears weary like a homeless dog.
Why do you worry? Why do you worry?"
Zǐgòng reported this to Confucius.
Confucius accepted all except
the "homeless dog" comment,
saying:
"How dare I claim that?"
Zǐgòng said:
"The soiled face not being ugly,
the rush-like mouth needing no support -
I understand these.
But why reject the homeless dog comparison?
Is it worth disputing?"
The Master said:
"Cì,
have you not seen homeless dogs?
After the coffin is placed in outer coffin,
ritual vessels arranged for sacrifice,
they look around finding no one,
wishing to offer their service.
Above, there are no enlightened kings,
below, no worthy officials or feudal lords.
The kingly way declines,
governance and teaching fail,
the strong bully the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the common people follow their whims,
with no one to maintain order.
This man surely thinks I wish to take this role,
how dare I claim it!"
9.19 In cultivating oneself, one cannot be careless.
Excessive desires damage conduct,
slander destroys accomplishments.
Trouble arises from anger,
misfortune begins with minor faults.
Stains are hard to wash away,
failures cannot be retrieved.
Without deep reflection and foresight,
what good is regret later?
Relying on luck
is an axe that cuts one's nature.
Indulging desires
is a horse chasing misfortune.
Deceit and exaggeration
are roads heading toward disaster.
Being slandered by others
is the house of hardship and poverty.
Therefore the gentleman doesn't rely on luck,
restrains his desires,
devotes himself to loyalty and trustworthiness,
avoids being slandered by anyone,
then his reputation will be honored,
and he will be called a gentleman.
The Book of Songs says:
"Why does he stay?
He must have companions."
9.20 The gentleman's dwelling
is secure like a warm fur coat,
peaceful like an overturned bowl.
When the world follows the Way,
feudal lords fear him.
When the world lacks the Way,
common people scorn him.
Not only today,
but since ancient times it has been so.
Long ago, Fàn Lí traveled
and lived among Qí's butchers.
Suddenly transforming like a dragon,
his benevolence and righteousness fluctuating,
his emotions surging and sighing,
he shared heaven and earth's worries.
Thus when a gentleman dwells somewhere,
how can he remain complacent?
The Book of Songs says:
"The sorrow in my heart,
who can understand it?"
9.21 When Tián Zǐfāng went to Wèi,
the crown prince met him outside the city with hundred chariots.
The prince bowed twice,
paying respects to Tián Zǐfāng,
but Tián Zǐfāng didn't descend from his carriage.
The prince was displeased,
saying:
"May I ask what qualifies one to act arrogantly toward others?"
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"I've heard of those who acted arrogantly with all under heaven and perished,
and those who acted arrogantly with a single state and perished.
From this perspective,
then poverty and low status qualify one to act arrogantly.
If one's ambitions are unfulfilled,
one can just put on sandals and go to Qín or Chǔ -
where can one go and not find poverty and low status?"
Thereupon the prince bowed twice and withdrew.
Tián Zǐfāng never descended from his carriage.
9.22 Dài Jìnshēng, wearing worn clothes and hat, went to see the King of Liáng.
The king said:
"Previously I offered you the salary of senior minister,
