but you didn't stay.
Now have you come to visit me?"
Dài Jìnshēng laughed cheerfully,
looked up and sighed deeply:
"Alas!
From this I see
you're not worth associating with.
Haven't you seen pheasants in great marshes?
They peck once every five steps,
yet become full by day's end.
Their feathers glossy and bright,
shining like sun and moon,
they flap wings and compete in singing,
their voices echoing through hills and marshes - why?
They delight in their own nature."
Placed it in the granary,
where it constantly pecked at fine grains and millet,
becoming full before the morning was over,
yet its feathers remained haggard,
its spirit sank lower,
and it hung its head without singing.
Was the food not good enough?
It was because it could not fulfill its true purpose.
Now, I have traveled a thousand miles without regard to the distance to follow you, my lord—
is it because I lack sufficient food?
Secretly, I admire your Way.
I initially thought you were a lover of scholars,
unparalleled in the world,
but now I see that you do not truly value
scholars; it is clear."
He bid farewell and left,
never to return.
9.23 King Zhuāng of Chǔ sent an envoy with a hundred catties of gold to invite Mr. Běiguō.
The gentleman said:
"I have a wife who manages the household,
I wish to go in and discuss it with her."
He then said to his wife:
"Chǔ wants to make me its chancellor.
If I become chancellor today,
I will have carriages and riders in procession,
with a feast spread out before me.
What do you think?"
The wife said:
"You make your living by weaving sandals,
eating congee and patching shoes,
yet you have no worries or fears—why is that?
It is because you do not contend with the world.
Now, if you have carriages and riders in procession,
the comfort they bring is no more than room for your knees;
with a feast spread before you,
the delicacies you enjoy are no more than one portion of meat.
To exchange the comfort of knee-room
and the taste of one portion of meat
for the burdens of Chǔ's worries—
is that acceptable?"
Thereupon, he declined the invitation,
and left with his wife.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"That virtuous and fair lady,
with whom I can converse intimately."
9.24 The *Traditions* state:
Long ago, the Róng general Yóu Yú was sent to Qín,
and Duke Mù of Qín asked him about the essentials of gain and loss.
He replied:
"Those who in ancient times possessed states never failed to be reverent and frugal,
while those who lost their states never failed to be arrogant and extravagant."
Yóu Yú then elaborated on why the Five Emperors and Three Kings declined,
and even why commoners were ruined.
Duke Mù agreed with him,
and then told his interior scribe Wáng Liào:
"A sage in a neighboring state
is a worry for a rival state.
Yóu Yú is a sage—
what should we do about him?"
Wáng Liào said:
"The king of Róng lives in a remote and backward land,
and has never seen the music and beauties of the central states
You should send him female musicians to corrupt his will,
disrupt his governance,
so that his ministers will surely become estranged.
Then, ask for an extension on Yóu Yú's behalf,
creating a rift between ruler and minister,
after which we can make our move."
Duke Mù said:
"Excellent."
He then sent Wáng Liào with two rows of female musicians to present to the Róng king,
requesting an extension for Yóu Yú.
The Róng king was greatly pleased,
and granted it.
Thereupon, he set out wine and listened to music,
ceaselessly day and night,
indulging recklessly all year,
until many of his horses died.
When Yóu Yú returned,
he repeatedly advised the king to no avail,
and left for Qín.
A Qín prince welcomed him and appointed him as a high minister.
Subsequently, Qín annexed twelve states,
expanding its territory by a thousand *lǐ*.
9.25 Zǐxià visited Zēngzǐ,
and Zēngzǐ said:
"Come in and eat."
Zǐxià said:
"Aren't you incurring expense for me?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"A gentleman has three kinds of waste,
but food and drink are not among them.
A gentleman has three joys,
but bells, chimes, lutes, and zithers are not among them."
Zǐxià said:
"May I ask about the three joys?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"To have parents to respect,
a ruler to serve,
and children to leave a legacy to—
this is the first joy.
To have parents whom one can admonish,
a ruler whom one can leave,
and children whom one can be angry with—
this is the second joy.
To have a ruler whom one can persuade,
and friends whom one can assist—
this is the third joy."
Zǐxià said:
"May I ask about the three wastes?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"To study when young,
and forget when grown—
this is the first waste.
To serve a ruler with merit,
yet lightly abandon it—
this is the second waste.
To befriend someone long and then break off in the middle—
this is the third waste."
Zǐxià said:
"Excellent!
To carefully devote oneself to a single word of advice
is better than a lifetime of recitation;
and to serve one true scholar
is greater than the achievement of governing ten thousand people.
One must not be unaware of this.
I once weeded my field poorly,
and for a whole year it yielded no harvest.
Even soil is like this—
how much more so people?
If you treat others with sincerity,
even the distant will become close.
If you treat others with emptiness,
even relatives will become distant.
Sincerity meeting sincerity
is like glue and lacquer.
Emptiness meeting emptiness
is like thin ice under the midday sun.
How can a gentleman not be mindful of this!"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The spirits hear this,
and bring ultimate harmony and peace."
9.26 When a servant of Yànzǐ's wife came out of the house wearing plain clothes of ramie,
Tián Wúyǔ mocked him, saying:
"What is someone like that doing coming out of your house?"
Yànzǐ said:
"He is a household servant."
Tián Wúyǔ said:
"Your rank is that of a mid-level minister,
with an estate of seven hundred thousand *mǔ*—
why keep such a person in your service?"
Yànzǐ said:
"To abandon the old for the young is called blindness;
to value the noble and forget the humble is called chaos;
to be pleased by appearances is called perversity.
How could I follow the way of perversity, chaos, and blindness!"
9.27 When the fenghuang first rises,
it flutters just ten paces,
and the sparrows in the hedges
chuckle at it with mocking cries.
But when it ascends to the heights,
with each dip and rise,
soaring through the clouds,
the hedgerow sparrows suddenly realize how far they fall short.
A scholar in coarse hemp garments, often threadbare,
eating coarse greens and never full,
is seen as shameful by worldly men.
But when he steps forth, he settles a hundred debates;
when employed, he prolongs the people's lives;
then worldly men suddenly realize how far they fall short.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"He is the model for the people of the state—
why should he not live ten thousand years!"
9.28 The king of Qí sent his daughter with a rich dowry,
wishing to marry her to Tú Niú Tǔ, the ox butcher.
Tú Niú Tǔ declined on grounds of illness.
His friend said:
"Will you just die in your stinky butcher shop?
Why refuse this?"
Tǔ replied:
"His daughter is ugly."
His friend said:
"How do you know that?"
Tǔ said:
"I know from my butchering."
His friend said:
"What do you mean?"
Tǔ said:
"When my meat is good,
I still have to reduce the price a bit to sell it.
When my meat is bad,
even if I add more to it,
it still won't sell."
Now, having sent you off with rich gifts,
you are ugly, and that is the reason."
His friend later saw him,
and indeed he was ugly.
The "Zhuan" says:
"Eyes like split apricots,
teeth like arranged shells."
9.29 The "Zhuan" says:
Confucius visited Kǎngzǐ,
with Zǐzhāng and Zǐxià following.
Confucius entered and sat down,
and the two disciples engaged in debate,
which remained unresolved the whole day.
Zǐxià's tone was very agitated,
and his complexion greatly altered.
Zǐzhāng said:
"Have you not heard our Master's discussions?
He speaks gently and respectfully,
his dignified demeanor is reverent;
he remains silent before speaking,
attains understanding through deference.
How lofty he is!
How broad and magnanimous!
The Way finds its home in him!
The debates of petty men,
on the other hand, are self-righteously opinionated;
they speak of others' faults,
glaring eyes and gripping wrists,
rapid speech with vehement protests,
mouths frothing and eyes reddening.
If by chance they win the argument,
they laugh shrilly in triumph.
Their dignified demeanor is crude and vulgar,
their tone and expression are base and common.
This is why the gentleman holds them in contempt."
10.1 Duke Huán of Qí was chasing a white deer
when he reached the region of Màiqiū
and met a man
who said: "Who are you?"
The man replied:
"I am a native of the Màiqiū region."
Duke Huán asked:
"Old man, how old are you?"
He replied:
"I am eighty-three years old."
Duke Huán said:
"How wonderful!"
He drank with him
and said:
"Old man, why not offer me a longevity blessing?"
The man replied:
"A rustic does not know how to offer a longevity blessing to a king."
Duke Huán said:
"Then use your own longevity to wish for mine!"
The native raised his cup and bowed twice, saying:
"May my lord have firm longevity;
may gold and jade be deemed worthless,
and the people be treasured."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent blessing!
I have heard that
supreme virtue is not solitary,
and good words must be repeated.
Old man, why not add another?"
The native raised his cup and bowed twice, saying:
"May my lord love learned scholars and not dislike being questioned.
May the worthy be at your side,
and those who remonstrate gain entry."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent blessing!
I have heard that
supreme virtue is not solitary,
and good words must come in threes.
Old man, why not add another?"
The native raised his cup and bowed twice, saying:
"May the officials and common people not incur blame from my lord,
and may my lord not incur blame from the officials and common people."
Duke Huán, displeased, said:
"This saying
does not match the previous two;
old man, you should change it."
The native shed tears,
saying: "I beg Your Majesty to ponder this deeply:
this saying
is superior to the previous two.
I have heard that if a son incurs his father's blame,
he can apologize through his aunts or sisters,
and the father will pardon him.
If a subject incurs his ruler's blame,
he can apologize through attendants,
and the ruler will pardon him.
But when Jié incurred the blame of his subjects,
to this day no one has apologized for him."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent!
Thanks to the blessings of the ancestral temple
and the power of the state altars,
I have met you here, old man."
He helped him into his carriage,
drove him back personally,
and presented him at the temple to assist in governance.
The reason Duke Huán could assemble the feudal lords nine times
and unite the world once,
without using military force,
was
not solely due to Guǎn Zhòng,
but also because he met this man here.
The "Odes" say:
"With many officials, grand and dignified,
King Wén secured his repose."
10.2 Bào Shū recommended Guǎn Zhòng, saying:
"There are five areas where I am not equal to Guǎn Yíwú.
In generosity, kindness, and gentle affection,
I am not his equal.
In winning the people's trust with loyalty and good faith,
I am not his equal.
In establishing rituals and laws across the land,
I am not his equal.
In judging cases and reaching fair decisions,
I am not his equal.
In standing with drum in hand at the army gate,
and inspiring soldiers' courage,
I am not his equal."
The "Odes" say:
"With many officials, grand and dignified,
King Wén secured his repose."
10.3 When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was exiled and passed through Cáo,
Lǐ Fúxū followed him,
but then stole Chóng'ěr's supplies and fled.
Chóng'ěr had no food,
and was too weak from hunger to travel.
Zǐtuī cut flesh from his own thigh to feed Chóng'ěr,
enabling him to continue.
When Chóng'ěr returned to his state,
many in the country did not support him.
Then Lǐ Fúxū came to see him, saying:
"I can bring stability to Jìn."
Duke Wén sent a messenger to reply:
"How dare you show your face before me, claiming you can stabilize Jìn!"
Lǐ Fúxū asked:
"Is the lord washing his hair?"
The messenger said:
"No."
Fúxū said:
"I have heard that when one washes the hair, the heart is inverted;
when the heart is inverted, the words become perverse.
Now the lord is not washing his hair,
so why are his words so perverse?"
The messenger reported this.
Duke Wén received him,
and Lǐ Fúxū looked up and said:
"Having been long away from the state,
your officials and people have many who wronged you.
Now that you have returned, they all fear for themselves.
I, Lǐ Fúxū, not only exhausted your supplies,
but hid in the deep mountains,
leaving you to starve,
so that Jièzǐtuī had to cut his thigh.
All under heaven have heard of this.
My crimes are great indeed,
worthy of punishment to the tenth degree of kinship,
which would not suffice to atone.
But if you truly pardon my crimes,
and let me ride in your carriage through the state,
when the people see it,
they will know you do not hold past wrongs against them,
and everyone will be at ease."
Thereupon Duke Wén was greatly pleased,
followed his advice,
and had him ride in the carriage through the state.
When the people saw it,
they all said:
"Even Lǐ Fúxū is not only spared but rides in the carriage,
what have we to fear!"
Thus Jìn was greatly pacified.
Therefore the "Documents" say:
"King Wén humbly labored,
attending to the work of settlement and fields."
As for Lǐ Fúxū,
he was one whose crimes deserved no pardon.
The "Odes" say:
"With many officials, grand and dignified,
King Wén secured his repose."
10.4 The "Zhuan" says:
It speaks of the difficulty of being a king.
When the great mandate arrives,
the Grand Ancestor,
Grand Historian, and Grand Invocator
don plain garments and hold tablets,
facing north to mourn the Son of Heaven, saying:
"The great mandate has come;
how long must we sorrow!"
They present the first tablet to the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"Reverently receive and offer sacrifice,
eternally uphold Heaven's mandate,
fear it without end,
and dare not rest in your person."
The second mandate was bestowed upon the Son of Heaven,
stating:
"Revere it!
Day and night remain devout,
and never slacken in your personal conduct.
All the people look up to you."
The third mandate was bestowed upon the Son of Heaven,
stating:
"The Son of Heaven faces south to receive the imperial throne,
taking governance as his concern,
never finding pleasure in the position itself."
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven's will is hard to trust,
yet none is harder to be than the king."
10.5 The nobleman cultivates gentleness and frugality to seek benevolence,
reverence and humility to seek propriety,
remaining self-possessed when attaining them,
and self-possessed when not.
Thus the nobleman's relation to the Way
is like the farmer tilling his fields:
even if the harvest fails,
he would never exchange his occupation for another.
Dàwáng Dǎnfǔ had sons named Tàibó,
Zhòngyōng, and Jìlì.
Lì had a son named Chāng.
Tàibó, knowing that Dàwáng considered Chāng worthy and wanted Jì to succeed him,
departed for Wú.
When Dàwáng was near death,
he instructed Jì:
"After I die,
go yield the throne to your two elder brothers.
If they refuse to come,
you will have acted righteously and can rule in peace."
After Dàwáng passed away,
Jì went to Wú to inform Bó and Zhòng,
who followed Jì back.
The ministers wanted Bó to establish Jì as successor,
but Jì again declined.
Bó said to Zhòng:
"Now the ministers want me to establish Jì,
yet he keeps declining.
How should we resolve this?"
Zhòng replied:
"In such matters there are principles to follow,
essential for supporting the humble.
We may establish Jì."
Thus Jì assumed the throne and nurtured King Wén,
who indeed received the Mandate and became king.
Confucius said:
"Tàibó alone perceived,
Wángjì alone understood.
Bó saw his father's aspiration,
Jì knew his father's heart.
Therefore Dàwáng,
Tàibó, and Wángjì
may be said to have seen the beginning, known the end, and been able to carry out the will."
The Book of Songs says:
"From Tàibó to Wángjì.
This Wángjì,
by nature was fraternal.
Being fraternal to his elder brother,
he greatly enhanced blessings,
bestowing radiance,
receiving honor without loss,
until he possessed all four quarters."
This refers to that.
When Tàibó returned to Wú,
the people made him their ruler,
which lasted through twenty-eight generations until Fūchāi's destruction.
10.6 King Xuān of Qí and King Huì of Wèi met for a hunt in the suburbs.
The King of Wèi asked:
"Do you also possess treasures?"
The King of Qí replied:
"I have none."
The King of Wèi said:
"Though my state is small,
I still have ten pearls measuring an inch in diameter that illuminate twelve chariots ahead and behind.
How can a state of ten thousand chariots lack treasures?"
The King of Qí responded:
"What I consider treasures differs from Your Majesty.
I have a minister named Tánzǐ
whom I sent to guard Nánchéng,
whereupon the Chǔ people dared not invade,
and twelve lords along the Sìshuǐ all came to pay homage.
I have a minister named Pànzǐ
whom I sent to guard Gāotáng,
whereupon the Zhào people dared not fish eastward in the river.
I have a minister named Qiánfū
whom I sent to guard Xúzhōu,
whereupon the Yān people sacrificed at their northern gate,
the Zhào people at their western gate,
and over seven thousand households followed him back.
I have a minister named Zhǒngshǒu
whom I tasked with preventing theft,
whereupon lost items on the road went unclaimed.
These men illuminate for me beyond a thousand miles,
how could they be compared to merely twelve chariots!"
The King of Wèi felt ashamed,
and left displeased.
The Book of Songs says:
"When speech is harmonious,
the people are settled."
10.7 In the Eastern Sea lived a warrior
named Zīqiū Xīn,
renowned throughout the land for his valor.
Encountering a divine abyss,
he said:
"Water the horse here."
His servant said:
"Any horse watered here
will surely die."
He insisted:
"Water it as I command."
The horse indeed sank.
Zīqiū Xīn removed his court robes, drew his sword, and dove in,
for three days and three nights,
emerging after slaying three jiaodragons and one dragon.
The thunder god pursued and struck him,
for ten days and ten nights,
blinding his left eye.
Yàolí heard of this,
went to see him,
asking:
"Is Xīn here?"
He was told:
"He's accompanying a funeral."
Yàolí went to see Xīn at the gravesite.
Saying:
"I heard the thunder god struck you for ten days and ten nights,
blinding your left eye.
Heaven's wrath should not last a full day,
mortal's wrath should not wait a heel's turn.
Yet you haven't taken revenge till now,
why is that?"
He scoffed and left,
stirring immense indignation at the gravesite.
Yàolí returned home,
and told his disciples:
"Zīqiū Xīn
is the world's bravest warrior.
Today I shamed him before others,
so he will certainly come to attack me.
At dusk, do not close the gate,
at night, do not bolt the doors."
Zīqiū Xīn indeed came that night,
holding his sword to Yàolí's neck,
saying:
"You have three capital crimes:
shaming me before others,
is crime one.
Leaving the gate open at dusk,
is crime two.
Leaving doors unbolted at night,
is crime three."
Yàolí replied:
"Allow me one word.
Your coming to confront me
shows lack of prowess, first.
Drawing your sword without stabbing
shows lack of prowess, second.
Blade before words
shows lack of prowess, third.
If you kill me now,
it would be like death by poison."
Zīqiū Xīn sheathed his sword and left, saying:
"Alas!
The one I cannot match
in all the world is only this man!"
The Tradition says:
Lord Mùyí preserved the state with words,
now Yàolí preserved his life with words.
Should not speech be refined,
as demonstrated here?
The Book of Songs says:
"When speech is harmonious,
the people are settled."
10.8 The Tradition says:
Qí sent an envoy to present a swan to Chǔ,
but the swan grew thirsty,
so the envoy let it drink on the way,
where it broke the cage and escaped.
The envoy proceeded to Chǔ,
saying:
"The Qí envoy was to present a swan,
but it grew thirsty,
drank on the way,
broke the cage and escaped.
I considered fleeing,
but that would sever communication between our lords.
I considered drawing my sword to die,
but people would think my lord values birds over scholars.
The broken cage is here,
I beg to soil your affairs with it."
The King of Chǔ admired his speech,
appreciated his words,
thus retained and rewarded him,
making him a permanent honored guest.
Therefore, an envoy must be skilled in rhetoric,
demonstrate sincerity and trustworthiness,
clarify his spirit and will,
untie knots and straighten out grievances,
and only then can he be sent on a mission.
The Book of Songs says:
"How pleasant are the words."
10.9 Biǎn Què passed by the Marquis of Guó,
where the crown prince had suddenly fallen ill and died.
Biǎn Què went to the palace,
saying:
"I heard that something grave has occurred in the state,
could it be an emergency?"
The reply was:
"The crown prince has suddenly fallen ill and died."
Biǎn Què said:
"Go in and say that the physician Qín Yuèrén from Zhèng can cure him."
A retainer fond of medicine came out to respond,
saying:
"I heard of an ancient physician named Dìfù.
When Dìfù practiced medicine,
he used reed mats as seats,
straw dogs as offerings,
faced north and prayed,
uttering just ten words,
and all those carried in on litters were restored to health.
Can your methods compare to this?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
The retainer continued:
"I heard of a medieval physician named Yūfū.
When Yūfū practiced medicine,
he used carved wood for brains,
fragrant grass for bodies,
blew through orifices to stabilize the brain,
and the dead came back to life.
Can your methods compare to this?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
The retainer said:
"If your methods are like this,
it is like looking at the sky through a tube,
poking the ground with an awl—
what you observe is vast,
but what you see is small;
what you aim at is huge,
but what you hit is minimal.
With your methods,
how could you possibly revive the young master?"
Biǎn Què said:
"Not so.
There are cases where a blind toss hits a mosquito's head,
or covering the eyes still distinguishes black from white.
The crown prince's illness is what is called 'corpse syncope.'
If you doubt it,
let me go in and examine him. The crown prince's inner thighs should still be warm,
and his ears may have a faint sound as if from crying.
In such cases,
he can still be revived."
The retainer then went in to examine the crown prince,
and reported the condition to the Marquis of Guó,
who, upon hearing it,
ran barefoot,
and reaching the door said:
"You have honored us from afar,
and graced this humble ruler.
If you are so kind as to cure him,
then this child of the dust
may be blessed by heaven and earth to live long as a human.
If you do not treat him,
he will sooner than dogs or horses fill the ditches."
Before he finished speaking, tears soaked his lapel.
Biǎn Què entered,
sharpened his needles and stones,
selected the three yang and five transport points,
prepared the guiding furnace,
applied the eight yang cleansings,
with Zǐtóng administering medicine,
Zǐmíng applying moxibustion to yang points,
Zǐyóu performing massage,
Zǐyí restoring the spirit,
Zǐyuè supporting the body,
whereupon the crown prince was revived.
The world heard of it,
and all said Biǎn Què could raise the dead.
Biǎn Què said:
"I cannot raise the dead;
I only make those who should live rise."
If the dead can still be medicated,
how much more the living?
Alas!
A failing ruler's governance
has no medicine to revive it.
The Book of Songs says:
"Beyond the reach of medicine."
Meaning it is doomed to perish.
10.10 Chǔqiū Xiānshēng, clad in straw raincoat and rope belt,
went to see Mèngcháng Jūn.
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"You are old, sir,
your years are advanced,
and you are often forgetful;
what could you teach Wén?"
Chǔqiū Xiānshēng said:
"What! You say I am old?
What! You say I am old?
Do you intend to have me throw stones and leap far?
Chase carriages and race horses?
Pursue deer and fight tigers?
Then I would die,
how could I be merely old?
But if you would have me plan deeply and strategize far?
Resolve doubts and decide uncertainties?
Speak upright words and face the feudal lords?
Then I am just in my prime,
what old age is there!"
Mèngcháng Jūn blushed in shame,
sweating to his heels,
and said:
"I was wrong!
I was wrong!"
The Book of Songs says:
"The old man is earnest."
10.11 Lord Jǐng of Qí was traveling on Niúshān,
and gazing north at Qí,
said:
"How beautiful is our state!
Lush and verdant Tàishān!
If in ancient times none had died,
then where would I, this humble ruler, go from here?"
He bowed his head, tears wetting his lapel.
Guózǐ and Gāozǐ said:
"Indeed!
We rely on your grace,
eating coarse food and poor meat,
riding worn-out horses and crude carts,
and still we do not wish to die,
how much more you, my lord!"
They bowed weeping.
Yànzǐ said:
"How joyful
is my outing today!
I have seen one timid ruler and two flattering ministers.
If in ancient times none had died,
then Tàigōng would still be alive today.
You, my lord, would now be wearing straw raincoat and hat standing in the fields,
worrying only about your tasks—
what leisure would you have to think of death!"
Lord Jǐng felt ashamed and raised his cup to penalize himself,
then penalized the two ministers as well.
10.12 Duke Mù of Qín was about to hunt
but lost his horse.
After searching for three days, he found it on the sunny side of Jīngshān,
where some rustics were eating it together.
Duke Mù said:
"This is the meat of a spotted horse;
those who eat it without wine will die."
Duke Mù then sought wine,
and had them all drink before leaving.
The next year, the Jìn army fought Duke Mù,
and Jìn's left and right flanks surrounded and attacked him,
with six layers of armor already pierced.
The over three hundred men who had eaten the horse
all said:
"Our lord is benevolent and loves his people;
we cannot but die for him."
They turned to attack Jìn's left and right flanks,
saving Duke Mù from death.
10.13 The Tradition says:
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was fond of courage.
While his mother was alive and well,
he fought three battles and fled three times.
His friends criticized him,
and the ruler shamed him.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ accepted the reproach,
his expression unchanged.
After his mother died and three years had passed,
Lǔ raised an army,
and Biàn Zhuāngzǐ requested to join.
When he saw the general, he said:
"Before, I was still with my mother,
so I fled three times in battle,
disgracing myself.
Now my mother is gone;
I ask to redeem my fault."
He then charged the enemy and fought,
capturing an enemy chief and presenting him, saying:
"Let this redeem one flight."
He captured another enemy chief and presented him,
saying:
"Let this redeem the second flight."
The general stopped him,
saying:
"Enough!"
He did not stop,
and again captured armored heads to present them,
saying:
"I ask to use this to redeem my three defeats."
The general stopped him,
saying:
"Enough!
Let us be brothers."
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ said:
"I endured defeat to support my mother,
now my mother has passed away,
my debt is repaid.
I have heard that
a principled scholar does not live in disgrace."
Then he charged at the enemy,
killed seventy men and died.
The gentleman heard of it and said:
"His three defeats redeemed his responsibility,
yet he extinguished his lineage and severed his ancestry;
his scholar's integrity was somewhat demonstrated,
but in filial piety he did not see it through."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Nothing is without a beginning,
but few can bring it to an end."
10.14 If the Son of Heaven has seven remonstrating ministers,
even if he is unprincipled,
he will not lose his empire.
In the past, King Zhòu of Yīn harmed the people,
defied the Way of Heaven,
even cutting off the legs of morning waders,
disemboweling pregnant women,
drying the flesh of Guǐ Hóu,
and mincing Méi Bó.
Yet the reason he did not fall was
because he had Jīzǐ and Bǐgān.
Wēizǐ left him,
Jīzǐ was imprisoned as a slave,
Bǐgān remonstrated and died,
and only then did Zhōu send troops to destroy him.
If a feudal lord has five remonstrating ministers,
even if he is unprincipled,
he will not lose his state.
King Fūchāi of Wú was unprincipled,
even driving a whole market's people to bury HéLǘ.
Yet the reason he did not fall was
because he had Wǔ Zǐxū.
After Zǐxū died,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè wanted to attack him.
Fàn Lǐ remonstrated:
"Zǐxū's strategies
are not yet forgotten in the king's heart."
Three years after Zǐxū's death,
Yuè was able to attack.
If a high official has three remonstrating ministers,
even if he is unprincipled,
he will not lose his family.
The Jì family was unprincipled,
usurping the Son of Heaven's rites,
performing the eight-row dance,
sacrificing at Tài Shān, using the "Yōng" and "Chè."
Confucius said:
"If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be tolerated!"
Yet they did not fall,
because Rǎn Yǒu and Jì Lù were their stewards.
Thus it is said:
"He who has outspoken remonstrating ministers sees his state prosper;
he who has silent flattering ministers sees his state perish."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Unenlightened is your virtue,
so none stand by your side or flank.
Your virtue unenlightened,
thus you have no aides, no ministers."
This speaks of the great king sighing,
lamenting that Yīn Shāng perished for lack of supporting, remonstrating ministers.
10.15 Duke Huán of Qí was traveling,
when he met a man in a gathered robe taking measured steps,
carrying a peach-wood staff.
Duke Huán, surprised, asked him:
"What is your name?
What classic do you follow,
what text do you dwell in?
Why have you been exiled,
why do you avoid me?"
The man said:
"My name is Èr Táo,
and táo means 'to perish.'
If one daily guards against perishing,
what troubles can one have?
Thus the fallen state's altar warns the feudal lords,
and the commoner's warning lies in the peach-wood staff."
Duke Huán was pleased with his words,
and rode with him together.
The next year in the first month, commoners all wore them.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The mirror of Yīn is not far."
10.16 Duke Huán of Qí set out wine,
commanding the feudal lords' ministers:
"Those who are late shall drink one jīngchéng."
Guǎn Zhòng was late,
and was to drink one jīngchéng.
He drank half of it,
and discarded the rest.
Duke Huán said:
"Father Zhòng should drink one jīngchéng,
why discard it?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard that
when wine enters the mouth, the tongue comes out;
when the tongue comes out, words are misspoken;
when words are misspoken, one loses one's life.
Rather than lose my life,
is it not better to discard the wine?"
Duke Huán said:
"Well said!"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Indulging excessively in wine."
10.17 Duke Jǐng of Qí sent Yànzǐ south as an envoy to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ heard of it,
and said to his attendants:
"Qí is sending Yànzǐ as envoy to my state,
he will arrive soon."
The attendants said:
"Yànzǐ
is a master debater of the world.
To discuss state affairs with him,
we are no match.
To debate ancient strategies with him,
we are no match.
Your Majesty might sit with Yànzǐ alone,
have officials bind a man to pass by the king,
the king asks about him,
and they say he is a man of Qí skilled at theft,
hence bound.
This should be able to embarrass him."
The king said:
"Good."
When Yànzǐ arrived,
he sat with him.
Planning urgent state matters,
debating the gains and losses of the era,
repeatedly the king was cornered,
and fell silent with nothing to add.
After a while,
bound prisoners were brought past.
The king said:
"What are these?"
The officials replied:
"These are men of Qí skilled at theft,
bound and brought to the officials."
The king laughed heartily and said:
"So Qí is a land of caps and sashes,
the influence of debaters,
yet they are skilled at theft?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Indeed.
They surely took it.
Has the king not seen the trees south of the river?
Called oranges,
planted north of the river,
they turn into trifoliate oranges.
Why?
The soil makes it so.
When this man was in Qí,
he stood with cap and sash,
solemn as Bó Yí in integrity;
now in Chǔ he is skilled at theft—
surely the influence of the land makes it so.
Why should the king find it strange?"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"No word goes unanswered,
no virtue unreturned."
10.18 Wú Yánlíng Jìzǐ traveled in Qí,
saw some lost gold,
and called a herder to pick it up.
The herder said:
"Why do you, sir, dwell so high,
yet see so low,
appear a gentleman,
yet speak so rudely!
I have a lord I do not serve,
friends I do not befriend,
wear furs in the heat—
do you suspect I take gold?"
Yánlíngzǐ knew he was a worthy,
and asked his name.
The herder said:
"You are a man who judges by appearance,
why bother with my name!"
Then he left.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ stood watching him,
and stopped only when he was out of sight.
Confucius said:
"Do not look at what is contrary to ritual,
do not listen to what is contrary to ritual."
10.19 Yān Yuān asked Confucius, saying:
"Yuān wishes to be as content in poverty as in wealth,
as dignified in low station as in high,
to command respect without relying on courage,
to associate with scholars,
and to remain free from troubles throughout life.
Can this be achieved?"
Confucius replied:
"Excellent, Huí!
To be as content in poverty as in wealth
shows one knows sufficiency and is without desires.
To be as dignified in low station as in high
shows one is humble and observes propriety.
To command respect without courage
shows one is reverent and never fails in dealings with others.
To remain free from troubles throughout life
shows one chooses one's words carefully before speaking.
As for Huí,
he has reached the ultimate!
Even the sage kings of highest antiquity
were merely like this."
10.20 Duke Jǐng of Qí went hunting
and did not return for seventeen days.
Yànzǐ rode out to see him.
Upon arrival,
his robe and cap were disheveled.
The Duke saw this and found it strange, saying:
"Why such haste, Master?
Is there some emergency?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Indeed,
there is an emergency.
The people all believe you detest your subjects and love game.
I have heard:
When fish and turtles tire of deep abysses and approach shallow shores,
they fall prey to hooks and nets.
When birds and beasts tire of deep mountains and descend to marshes near cities,
they are caught in hunts.
Now you have been hunting for seventeen days without returning.
Is this not excessive?"
The Duke said:
"Not so.
If it's because no one attends to guests,
then the receptionist Zǐniú is there.
If it's because the ancestral temple lacks sacrifices,
then the prayer-officer Tàizǎi is there.
If it's because judgments are unfair,
then the chief justice Zǐjī is there.
If it's because state affairs, whether surplus or deficit,
then Wū Xián is there.
I have these four men
just as one has four limbs,
and they can act on my behalf.
There is nothing to worry about!"
Yànzǐ said:
"True,
it is good that the human mind has four limbs to act for it.
But if the four limbs had no mind,
would they not perish in seventeen days?"
The Duke said:
"Well said!"
Thereupon he took Yànzǐ's hand
and returned with him in his carriage.
As for Yànzǐ,
he may be called skilled in remonstrance.
10.21 King Zhuāng of Chǔ was about to raise an army to attack Jìn.
He announced to his officers:
"Who dares remonstrate will die without pardon."
Sūnshū Áo said:
"I have heard that one who fears the sternness of the whip and dares not remonstrate with his father
is no filial son.
One who dreads execution by axe and dares not remonstrate with his ruler
is no loyal minister."
Thereupon he came forward and admonished:
"In my garden there is an elm tree,
on which a cicada resides.
The cicada, just fluttering its wings in mournful song,
about to drink the clear dew,
knows not the mantis behind it,
bending its neck,
poised to seize and devour it.
The mantis, intent on eating the cicada,
knows not the oriole behind it,
lifting its head,
ready to peck and consume it.
The oriole, focused on eating the mantis,
knows not the boy with a slingshot below,
aiming to shoot it.
The boy, about to shoot the oriole,
knows not the deep pit ahead
and the hole behind.
These all speak of pursuing immediate gain
without regard for subsequent harm.
Not only insects and common people are like this;
rulers are too.
You now covet their land
and take pleasure in your officers and troops."
Thus Chǔ was saved from peril,
and Jìn was pacified,
thanks to Sūnshū Áo's efforts.
10.22 During the time of Duke Píng of Jìn,
the treasury tower caught fire.
The officers, upon hearing,
all rushed in carriages or on horseback to fight the fire.
After three days and nights,
they finally subdued it.
Only the noble Yànzǐ came with a bundle of silk to congratulate,
saying:
"Excellent!"
Duke Píng, flushing with anger, said:
"This is where pearls and jades are stored,
the state's most valued treasures,
yet heaven set it ablaze.
All the officers rushed to extinguish it,
but you alone come with silk to congratulate.
Why?
If you have an explanation, you live;
if not, you die."
The noble Yànzǐ said:
"How dare I not have an explanation!
I have heard that
a true king stores his wealth among all under heaven,
feudal lords among their people,
farmers in their granaries,
merchants in their chests.
Now the people are destitute,
coarse clothes barely covering their bodies,
chaff and husks not filling their mouths,
yet you endlessly levy taxes on their emptiness,
collecting more than half to store in the tower.
Hence heaven set it afire.
Moreover, I have heard that
in the past, Jié brutalized the land,
taxing without limit,
causing immense suffering to the people.
Thus Tāng executed him,
making him a laughingstock of the world.
Now heaven has sent disaster upon your treasury tower,
which is your blessing,
yet you fail to realize and repent.
I fear you will be laughed at by neighboring states."
The Duke said:
"Well said!
From now on,
I shall store my wealth among the people."
The Book of Songs says:
"Farming is the true treasure,
feeding the people is what's good."
10.23 Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Lǐ Kè:
"Why did Wú perish?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Because it fought frequently and won frequently."
The Marquis said:
"Frequent victories
are a blessing to a state.
Why then did it perish?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Frequent wars exhaust the people;
frequent victories make the ruler arrogant.
Arrogance leads to recklessness;
recklessness to extremes.
When both high and low reach extremes,
Wú's demise was even belated.
This is why Fūchāi met his end at Gānsuì."
The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven sent down calamity,
destroying our established king."
10.24 In Chǔ, there was an officer named Shēn Míng,
who tended a garden to support his parents,
famed for his filial piety throughout Chǔ.
The King summoned him,
but Shēn Míng declined to go.
His father said:
"The King wishes to employ you.
Why refuse?"
Shēn Míng said:
"Should I cease being a son
to become a minister?"
His father said:
"If you receive a salary from the state
and a position at court,
you will be happy and I will have no worries.
I want you to serve."
Shēn Míng said:
"Very well."
Thereupon he went to court and received the appointment,
the King of Chǔ making him Left Marshal.
That year, the rebellion of Báigōng occurred,
killing Prime Minister Zǐxī and Marshal Zǐqī.
Shēn Míng led troops to defend.
Báigōng said to Shí Qǐ:
"Shēn Míng
is a warrior of the realm.
Now he commands troops.
What can we do?"
Shí Qǐ said:
"I have heard that Shēn Míng is a filial son,
so let us threaten his father with weapons." He sent a message to Shēn Míng saying:
"If you side with me,
I will share the state of Chǔ with you;
if you do not side with me,
I will kill your father."
Shēn Míng responded with tears streaming down his face:
"I was once a filial son to my father,
but now I am a loyal minister to my lord.
Since I can no longer be a filial son to my father,
how can I not be a loyal minister to my lord?"
He took up the drumstick and beat the drum,
then proceeded to kill Bái Gōng.
His father also died in the process.
The king returned and rewarded him,
but Shēn Míng said:
"To accept the ruler's emolument
and yet avoid the ruler's calamities
is not the way of a loyal minister.
To uphold the ruler's laws
at the cost of my father's life
is not the way of a filial son.
One cannot achieve both in action,
nor can both reputations stand together.
How tragic!
If I were to continue living like this,
what example would I set for the scholars of the world?"
Thereupon, he cut his own throat and died.
The Book of Songs says:
"Advance or retreat, both are dangerous."
10.25 In ancient times, Tài Gōng Wàng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn received their fiefs and met.
Tài Gōng asked Zhōu Gōng how he would govern Lǔ.
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Respect the respectable and be intimate with relatives."
Tài Gōng said:
"From this, Lǔ will weaken."
Zhōu Gōng asked Tài Gōng:
"How will you govern Qí?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Promote the worthy and reward achievements."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"In later generations, there will inevitably be rulers who are overthrown and killed."
Thereafter, Qí grew increasingly powerful,
achieving hegemony,
but after twenty-four generations, the Tián clan replaced it.
Lǔ gradually declined,
and was extinguished after thirty-four generations.
From this perspective,
the sages were able to foresee subtle signs.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only this sage,
can see a hundred miles ahead."
